en: Title: Rāmārcanacandrikā. Author: Ānandavana, disciple of Mukundavana.
Extent: 69 folios. Age: Saṃvat 1929. Subject: Tantra. Date:
Saṃvat 1929, Āśvina, bright fortnight, 31st day.
In the *Rāmārcanacandrikā*, page 69, verse 2300, in the manuscript of Vīrūlakhāri (fol.
1a): *Oṃ svasti śrīgaṇeśāya namaḥ | śrīgurave namaḥ | śrīrāmacandrāya namaḥ | To cross the ocean of worldly existence, that Lord whose boat is the three Vedas...* [text continues].

I bow to that supreme Śrī Rāmacandra, the stainless, innate radiance, in whom there is constant manifestation, birth, persistence, and dissolution; in whom the Vedas do not exist, nor mind, nor ego, nor even the streams of sensory perceptions. Victorious is the illustrious sage Mukuṃda, whose body pervades the universe, who is the auspicious embodied form of the Lord of the Raghus, who is a poet uniquely skilled in awakening the meaning of the scriptures, whose character is defined by peace and other virtues, who is the sole sun for dispelling the blindness of ignorance, the ever-desirable wish-fulfilling gem of higher knowledge (vijñāna), and the singular ground of eternal bliss. [The text continues with: Vedāntavā...

In which [work] the supreme goal shines forth, where there are no births that grant desires, and where the wise have always attained the state of bliss—in such a manner, I shall describe this supreme manual (*varta*) known as *Mukunda*.

Having churned the entire *Uttara-tāpanīya* and the excellent *Kalpa* of Māruti, as well as the *Kalpas* and *Saṃhitās* of Brahmā, Agasti, Vasiṣṭha, and Vāmadeva, along with the scriptures consisting of mantras and the *Sītā-kalpa*, I proclaim this *Śrī-rāmārcana-caṇḍrikā*, which destroys the impurities of the Kali age. It is composed of various passages found in those respective texts.

For the sake of ease, the sequence [of topics] is properly set forth in brief as conceived by Vātaka. First, the characteristics of the teacher and the disciple are stated: one who is peaceful, self-controlled, of noble birth, humble, and pure in appearance; who is of good conduct, well-known, pure, skillful, and highly intelligent; who belongs to an [ascetic] order, is devoted to meditation, and is expert in mantras and tantras; and who is capable of both restraint and grace—such a person is called a "teacher" (guru). This is the definition of a teacher. [The disciple should be] peaceful, humble, pure in soul, full of faith, and capable of retention. He must be competent...

One who is of noble birth, wise, of virtuous conduct, and wealthy—one endowed with such qualities as these becomes a disciple, and not otherwise. O child, the status of teacher and disciple exists only through their mutual dependence. Thus it is stated in the *Sārasaṅgraha*: "A true guru should observe a disciple for one year once he has taken him under his care. Furthermore, in that same work, the defect of a king or a person of high honor falls upon the wife, and likewise, the sins of a disciple certainly reach the guru. This is the word of Śiva in the *Devī-āgama*: "The bed, seat, vehicle, sandals, and shoes of the guru..."

"One should never step over a threshold, water for the feet, or a shadow. Likewise, in that same [text]: "One should abandon arrogance; one should avoid performing separate worship, initiation (*dīkṣā*), exposition, or exercising authority in the presence of the Guru. Such are the characteristics of a disciple. Since instruction without initiation is defective, initiation must come first; for it effects the destruction of sins and brings about the divine state for the practitioner (*sādhaka*).

Even therein, one should purify the mantra according to the distinctions of *siddha*, *sādhya*, and so forth, by means of [the numbers] two, three, eleven, nine, two, four, ten, six, eight, and sixteen.

The wise person, having observed the letters starting from the birth-star (janmarkṣa) in the ten, fourteen, and eighteen elemental squares—namely the fifteen squares of Pātāla, Fire, and Moon—should write the letters of the mantra in sequence. Among these four groups of four squares, one square is designated as the first; then, within the individual squares, moving clockwise from the letter of the birth-star, the wise should recognize the *siddha*, *sādhya*, *susiddha*, and *ari* [categories] according to their order. That which is *siddha* will be accomplished in time.

The *sādhya* [friend] is accomplished through recitation (*japa*) and fire-oblations (*homa*); the *susiddha* [friend], merely by being grasped, uproots and destroys the enemy. The *siddha* [friends] are said to be kinsmen, while the *sādhya* [friends] are remembered as servants. The *susiddha* [friends] are to be known as nourishers, and enemies are remembered as destroyers.
Through recitation, the *siddha* becomes a kinsman; through superior service, the servant [becomes so]; the nourisher fulfills one's desires, while the destroyer causes ruin.

A *Siddha* mantra is certainly accomplished according to what has been stated; a *Siddha-sādhya* is accomplished through double that amount; a *Siddha-susiddha* is accomplished by reciting half [of that]; and a *Siddha-ari* destroys one's kinsmen. A *Sādhya-siddha* is accomplished with double [the effort], while a *Sādhya-sādhya* is useless; a *Sādhya-susiddha* accomplishes it through triple [effort], and a *Sādhya-ari* destroys those born of one's own lineage. A *Susiddha-siddha* is accomplished through mere recitation, a *Susiddha-sādhya* through double that amount, a *Susiddha-susiddha* through the seizing [of the mantra], and a *Susiddha-ari* destroys one's own family. (3)

An *arisiddha* (enemy-successful) mantra kills one's sons; an *arisādhya* (enemy-to-be-accomplished) kills one's daughters; an *arisusiddha* (enemy-very-successful) kills one's wife; and an *ariari* (enemy-enemy) kills the practitioner himself. One should separate the names given by the mother and father, as well as those derived from one's lineage (*abhijana*), by means of their various vowels and consonants. Likewise, one should separate the seed-syllables (*bīja*) of the mantra; thereafter, one should begin the purification. The anusvāra (*viṃdu*), the two dots (*dvividu*), the upadhmānīya, and those produced by the tongue and the feet—these are obtained through combined pronunciation. Furthermore, there are redundant syllables (*adhikākṣara*), missing syllables (*ayabhraṃśākṣara*), and the four parts of the *lakṣa* (the phonetic markers). [The vowels are: *ṛ*, *ḷ*, *ḹ*.

One should purify each of these syllables of the name together with the syllables of the mantra: consonants with consonants, and likewise vowels with vowels. The first [syllable] of the month should be purified by the first [syllable] of the mantra, and the second by the second. When the syllables in the mantra or the name are unequal, then one should begin from the mantra and apply them until they become equal.

O fair-faced one, that mantra in which the first and last syllables are *siddha* (accomplished) will, in a very short time, bestow all accomplishments (*siddhis*). That which is joined with the beginning of the *sādhya* (to be accomplished) is... [excellent].

In the beginning it is accomplished with difficulty, but at the end it is easily accomplished and bestows the power of all desires. One for whom there is an enemy both in the beginning and at the end should be abandoned along with his mantra; a mantra that has enemies in the three positions (beginning, middle, and end) is considered equal to death. When there is an enemy at the beginning and it is accomplished in the middle, it is "attainable" (sādhya) at the end; the accomplishment of its purpose comes with great hardship, and its fruit will be very small. If there is an enemy at the end, while the first and middle parts are "attainable," the work will be delayed, and in the end, everything will perish.

Whether [the mantra] is *siddha* or *susiddha*, a wise man should avoid with effort a mantra that is excessively heated by the examination of its separation from the waters. One should not examine the *siddha* and other states of mantras consisting of syllables joined with *piṇḍas* belonging to Nṛsiṃha, Arka, Varāha, and the Praṇava. In the case of a three-syllabled *mālā-mantra* obtained in a dream, or in all Vedic mantras, one should never examine their *siddha* status and so forth. Thus ends the purification regarding *siddha*, *sādhya*, and the rest. Now I shall explain the distinction between one's own *kula* and another *kula* for practitioners; [these are] *u*, *ū*, *ga*, *ja*, *ḍa*, *da*, *va*, *ḷ*, *ṣma*.

The letters *ṛ, ṝ, ḷ, ḹ* belong to the Earth; *ṇ, ñ, ṅ, na, ma* belong to Water; *ṭha, ṭha, dha, bha, va, śa, ṣa, ha* belong to Fire; *i, ī, e, ai, kha, ḍha, ṭha, tha, pha, ra, kṣa* belong to Fire; *ā, e, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, ya, svā, mā, ru, tā* belong to Wind; and *ḷ, ḹ, ṅ, ñ, ṇ, na, ma, sa, ha* belong to Ether. The first letter of the practitioner and the first letter of the mantra—if they share the same element and deity—are beneficial as they belong to one's own family. Water is the friend of Earth, and Wind is the friend of Fire. Wind is the enemy of Earth and Water, while Fire is the enemy of Wind. Ether is the friend of all. If [the letters] are of different families, it is harmful. If they are of the same family, it is beneficial. If they are of different elements, it is neutral. If they are of the same element, it is excellent. If they are of different deities, it is harmful. If they are of the same deity, it is beneficial. If they are of the same class (varga), it is excellent. If they are of different classes, it is harmful. If they are of the same class and same element, it is most excellent. If they are of different classes and different elements, it is most harmful. If they are of the same class but different elements, it is neutral.
