One should not mix what is obstructed (*ruddha*) in this manner; thus ends the wheel of one’s own *kula* and *akula*. Now, another classification of mantras beginning with "infant" (*bāla*) and so forth is described: starting from a single-syllable mantra up to sixteen syllables is "infant" (*bāla*); from there up to twenty syllables is "grown" (*prauḍha*); those beyond that are considered "old" (*sthavira*). Those ending in *svāhā* are feminine in nature; those ending in *namaḥ* are neuter; and those mantras ending in *huṃ phaṭ* are proclaimed to be masculine. These three types of mantras are recommended for subjugation (*vaśya*), pacification (*śānti*), and malevolent rites (*abhicāra*). Thus ends the classification of infants and others. [Now follows] the conjunction of zodiac signs (*rāśimelana*).

From this, one should also determine the position of the zodiac signs (*rāśi*) corresponding to the letters of the name: *ai ī* is Aries; *u ū ṛ* is Taurus; *ḷ ḹ* is Gemini; *e ai* is Cancer; *o au* is Leo; *aṃ aḥ śa ṣa sa ha la kṣa* is Virgo; the *ka*-group is Libra; the *ca*-group is Scorpio; the *ṭa*-group is Sagittarius; the *ta*-group is Capricorn; the *pa*-group is Aquarius; and the letters beginning with *ya* are Pisces. One should count from the letter of the practitioner's name up to the letter of the sign of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Friends are said to be those at the first, fifth, and ninth positions; those at the second, sixth, and tenth are servants; and those at the third, seventh, and eleventh are enemies. Those at the fourth, eighth, and twelfth are neutral. [Note: The final line appears to be a fragmentary mnemonic verse regarding the number of syllables in the names of the deities.]

Six, twelve, six, four, and eight are the slayers [of the planets]. Thus is the conjunction of the zodiacal signs (*rāśi*). *Āśvinī* belongs to the divine class (*devagaṇa*); *Bharaṇī* belongs to the human class (*manuṣyagaṇa*);

*Kṛttikā* belongs to the demonic class (*rākṣasagaṇa*). *Ṛ, Ḷ, Ḹ, Ro, Hiṇī* belong to the human class; *E, Mṛgaśīrṣa* belong to the divine class; *Ai, Ārdrā* belong to the human class; *O, Au, Punarvasu* belong to the divine class; *Ka, Puṣya* belongs to the divine class;

*Kha, Ga, Śleṣā* belongs to the demonic class; *Gha, Ṅa, Maghā* belongs to the demonic class; *Ca, Pūrvaphalgunī* belongs to the human class; *Cha, Ja, Uttaraphalgunī* belongs to the human class; *Jha, Ña, Hasta* belongs to the divine class; *Ṭa, Ṭha, Citrā* belongs to the demonic class... [and so on].

The letter *kṣa* belongs to the Rākṣasa [class] for Aśvinī; *ḍha* for Bharaṇī; *ṇa* for Kṛttikā; *vi* for Rohiṇī; *śā* for Mṛgaśirā; *khā* for Ārdrā; *rā* for Punarvasu; *kṣa* for Puṣyā; *ta* for Āśleṣā; *thā* for Maghā; *da* for Pūrva-phalgunī; *anu* for Uttara-phalgunī; *rā* for Hasta; *dhā* for Citrā; *de* for Svāti; *va* for Viśākhā; *rā* for Anurādhā; *kṣa* for Jyeṣṇā; *ta* for Mūla; *thā* for Pūrva-āṣāḍhā; *da* for Uttara-āṣāḍhā; *nu* for Śravaṇā; *rā* for Dhaniṣṭhā; *kṣa* for Śatabhiṣaj; *sa* for Pūrva-bhādrapadā; *ma* for Uttara-bhādrapadā; *nu* for Revatī; *ṣya* for Aśvinī; *bha* for Bharaṇī; *ma* for Kṛttikā; *śra* for Rohiṇī; *va* for Mṛgaśirā; *ṇo* for Ārdrā; *de* for Punarvasu; *va* for Puṣyā; *ya* for Āśleṣā; *ra* for Maghā; *dha* for Pūrva-phalgunī; *ni* for Uttara-phalgunī; *ṣṭā* for Hastā; *rā* for Citrā; *kṣa* for Svāti; *sa* for Viśākhā; *la* for Anurādhā; *śa* for Jyeṣṭhā; *ba* for Mūla; *pū* for Pūrva-āṣāḍhā; *rva* for Uttara-āṣāḍhā; *ā* for Śravaṇā; *ṣā* for Dhaniṣṭhā; *ḍhā* for Śatabhiṣaj; *ma* for Pūrva-bhādrapadā; *nu* for Uttara-bhādrapadā; *ṣya* for Revatī. The wise practitioner should count these letters in a clockwise direction starting from the syllable of his own name:
*janma* (birth), *sampat* (prosperity), *vipat* (misfortune), *kṣema* (well-being), and *pratyari* (enemy). The practitioner [should determine his status] according to this sequence.

Dhaḥ is the supreme friendliness; those who cause birth and other such states again and again, and who bring about calamities, should be avoided day after day by the wise. Thus ends the section on the types of constellations (*nakṣatra*). The time for awakening from sleep is said to be that of the mantras. Mantras consisting of the nature of Agni and Soma are to be understood for the performance of fierce and gentle rites respectively. It is taught that those mantras which abound in the letters *gha*, *mṛ*, and *ta* are fiery (*āgneya*), while those ending in the vocative case (*saṃbuddhi*) are lunar (*saumya*). When the vital breath (*prāṇa*) moves in the right [nostril], the fiery mantras awaken; when the breath is situated in the left, the lunar mantras awaken.

When the vital breath (*prāṇa*) has entered both channels (*nāḍī*), all [the letters] attain awakening; once awakened, they always bestow their fruit upon the practitioners (*mantrins*). Alternatively, the time of awakening is to be known as the union of the Śiva and Śakti through the conjunction of the vital breath and the mind; after that follows the time of sleep. This is the time of perfect awakening. Having encapsulated [the mantra] with the *saṃpuṭa* [method], one should take the letters from the peaceful *ā* up to the excellent *bindu* (*m*). Then, those same letters with the *visarga* (*ḥ*) fall [in sequence] until the solitary letter *kṣa*. If, having reached this state, the desired [mantra] is awakened, it quickly grants success. Now, regarding the wealth of syllables...

Now, the purification that bestows success is being described. The letters of the name of the person to be overcome (*sādhya*) are multiplied by the numbers one, two, twelve, fifteen, six, four, three, five, eight, nine; likewise, the letters of the practitioner’s name (*sādhaka*) are multiplied by the numbers ten, one, seven, four, eight, seven, seven, four, six, and three. Having determined the remainder of both after division by forty-five, the debt (*ṛṇa*) should be added to the credit (*dhi*). The meaning of this is as follows: the letters of the *sādhya*’s name—both vowels and consonants—are separated and multiplied by the aforementioned numbers (one, etc.). Likewise, the letters of the practitioner’s name...

One should multiply by the numerical values [of the letters] such as *rāṇya*, *ṣida*, and *gādi*. From the collection of vowels and consonants beginning with the name and ending with *pha*, there are four groups divided according to the four classes starting with *ka* and *ṭha*:

the *a*-group consisting of *a* through *aḥ*; the *ka*-group from *ka* to *ṭa*; and the *va*-group from *va* to *ha*. These four groups each consist of eleven syllables. When these are divided by eight—starting from *ka*, *ṭha*, and *va*—the remainder of both the group to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and the group of the practitioner (*sādhaka*) [is determined].

The remainder is the debt to be given by one who possesses a superior form; having understood the wealth, one should bestow the mantra. If the mantra becomes a debtor, then that mantra is a giver of auspiciousness. If the mantra is the creditor and its numerical value is greater, the wise man should recite that mantra. One should also recite the mantra when it is equal, but not when the wealth is excessive. One should know that zero (śūnya) signifies death; therefore, one should avoid zero. The purity of the zodiac signs (rāśis) should be known [by calculating] the enemy, the killer, and the expenditure. The wise should count from the sign of one's own birth (sva-rāśi) up to the sign of the mantra. [The houses are: the ascendant (lagna), wealth (dhana), friends...

The third, sixth, eighth, and twelfth houses represent enemies, wife, death, and the destruction of virtue, desire, and wealth respectively; these are the twelve signs (*rāśis*). Thus ends the purification of the signs (*rāśiśuddhi*). Thus concludes the method for calculating debt and wealth (14, 27, 2, 12, 15, 6, 4, 3, 8, 8, 9). Other defects of mantras should also be understood by the wise from other texts. Herein are written the consecrations (*saṃskāras*) of mantras:
*oṃ*, *ā*, *u*, *ṛ*, *ḷ*, *e*, *ai*, *o*, *au*, *aṃ*, *aḥ*. From the *Dātilaka*: "Birth, then life, thereafter striking, and likewise awakening; then the consecration (*abhiṣeka*). [End of fragment].

Ka, kha, ga, gha, ṅa; ca, cha, ja, jha, ña; ṭa, ṭha, ḍa, ḍha, ṇa; ta, tha, da, dha, na; pa, pha, ba, bha, ma; ya, ra, la, va; śa, ṣa, sa, ha. The purification of mantras consists of these ten rites: *līkaraṇa*, *āpyāyana*, *tarpaṇa*, *dīpana*, and *gupti*. *Janana* (birth) is known as the extraction of the mantra-syllables from the midst of the consonants [from *ka* to *ha*]. A wise person should recite the syllables of the mantra with the *praṇava* (Om) interspersed between them.
[The remaining sequence is: *eta*, *va*, *bha*, *ma*, *ya*, *ra*, *la*, *va*, *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, *ha*.

Those expert in *mantra* and *tantra* declare that [this] is the "reviving" (*jīvana*). Having written out the letters of the *mantra*, one should strike it with sandalwood water; each such striking, consecrated by the wind-mantra (*vāyu*), is declared to be "reviving. (3) Having written the *mantra*, the practitioner should perform "awakening" (*bodhana*) with *karavīra* flowers, numbering as many as the syllables of that *mantra*, ending with the *dravya* mantra. (4) According to the procedure prescribed in his own *tantra*, he should sprinkle the *mantra* with *aśvattha* leaves, numbering as many as the syllables of the *mantra*, for the sake of purification. (5) Having contemplated the *mantra* mentally, he should burn it away with the *jyotis-mantra*. (The *jyotis-mantra* consists of: *sāraṃ vyomāgnimanuyuk daṇḍī jyotiḥ manu*.)

Sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) with water from *kuśa* grass over which the mantra has been recited syllable by syllable is considered by the wise to be the purification of the three impurities (*mala-traya*) of the mantra-practitioner. The mantra consisting of *Tāra* (Om), *Vyoma* (H), *Agni* (Ra), *Manu* (Ya), *Yuda* (Kṣa), *Daṇḍī* (Pha), and *Jyotis* (Sa)—that is, *Oṃ Hrakṣaphaṭ Saḥ*—is used for sprinkling the mantra with water from *kuśa* grass over which it has been recited syllable by syllable. By means of that same mantra, performed according to the rules, this is known as *āpyāyana* (nourishing). Sprinkling the mantra with water using that very mantra is known as *tarpaṇa* (satisfying). The conjunction of *Tāra* (Om), *Māyā* (Hrīṃ), and *Ramā* (Śrīṃ) is called the *dīpana* (igniting) of the mantra. Concealment (*gopana*) is the non-disclosure of the mantra while it is being recited. Thus ends the section on the mantra.

Now we shall describe the extraction of the mantra of Rāghava. This king of mantras, which is like a celestial tree, was proclaimed by Brahmā in the Kalpas and other scriptures as the bestower of perfect success upon practitioners. It consists of a single syllable, is situated in fire (Ra), contains the bed of Viṣṇu (A), and is adorned with a half-moon (Ū). Brahmā is the sage, Gāyatrī is the meter, and Rāma is the deity. One should perform the placement of the limbs using the long vowels joined with the half-moon. On the bank of the Sarayū, on a seat of lotuses at the altar of the Madāra tree, one should meditate on the dark-complexioned Lord seated in the Vīrāsana posture, beautiful with the Jñānamudrā, his left thigh [resting upon...].

Having placed those [syllables] upon the *brahmarandhra*, served by Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, and beholding himself within the Self as one whose splendor is immeasurable, he should meditate on the Supreme Self and recite the mantra with the sun as its target.

Whether it be the fire, Nārāyaṇa, the channels, the digestive fire, or even the absolute alone—this two-syllabled king of mantras bestows the fruits of both enjoyment and liberation. If it consists of a single syllable, it is said to have six limbs through the first [syllable]; it is sixfold by means of the *tāra* (om), *māyā* (hrīṃ), *ramā* (śrīṃ), *naṃ* (nam), *jña* (jña), and the seed-syllable of speech (*aiṃ*). This single-syllabled king of mantras grants all desired fruits. And the two-syllabled [mantra] is *candrabhadra*.

(p. 4b) That [mantra] is of two kinds and consists of four syllables; the seer (ṛṣi) and other details for these should be known by the wise as before. With the *pratiṣṭhā* [vīja], *ra*, *ma*, and *va*, the wind (*ya*), this five-syllabled mantra is remembered. Viśvāmitra is declared the sage, *paṅkti* the metre, and Rāmabhadra the deity. The seed (*vīja*) is the first syllable, and the power (*śakti*) is the next in sequence. One should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the mantra upon the earth-center, the heart, the navel, the two arms, and the two feet. The six-limbed [protection] is as before; alternatively, one may perform the weapon-ritual (*astraka*) with the five-syllabled mantra. In the middle of the forest, at the foot of a wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpataru*), upon a seat of flowers and creepers, [he is seated] with Lakṣmaṇa holding a bow and arrows.

One should meditate upon the Lord, the slayer of the ten-faced Rāvaṇa, who is being watched by Jānakī with a fan in her hand; he has a head shining with a mass of matted locks, is dark-complexioned, surrounded by hosts of sages, and has a parasol held over him by Lakṣmaṇa.
Furthermore, [one should visualize] Sugrīva and Vibhīṣaṇa as before, atop the Puṣpaka chariot. One seeking victory should specifically recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.

The six-syllabled mantra—consisting of the five syllables beginning with *sva-kāma-śakti-vāk-lakṣmī-tārā*—is of six types and bestows the fruits of the four aims of human life (*caturvarga*). [It consists of] the fifty letters of the Mātṛkā mantra...

Preceded by *tye*, it may consist of one syllable, or it may be manifold, such as *lakṣmī*, *vāṅmanmatha*, *tārā*, and so forth. A mantra beginning and ending with a single seed-syllable—such as *śrīṃ*, *māyā* (*hrīṃ*), or *manmatha* (*klīṃ*)—should have four syllables or six syllables; it bestows all desires. This mantra may end in *svāhā*, *huṃ phaṭ*, or it may not end at all. Brahmā, Sammohana, Śakti, Dakṣiṇāmūrti, Agastya, Śrīśiva—these are declared to be the sages (ṛṣis) in their respective order. The metre is Gāyatrī, and the deity is Śrī Rāma; or else, O Goddess, [the sage] is Viśvāmitra from the Kāma-bīja.

One should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the six syllables as before—of the sage (muni), the metre (chanda), the goddess (devī), and so forth, with Rāmabhadra as the deity, and the seed-syllable (bīja) and power (śakti)—in the cranial aperture (brahmarandhra), between the eyebrows, at the heart, the navel, the throat, and the feet. Alternatively, one should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) using the six long-voweled seed-mantras or the individual letters of the mantra. Then, one should meditate upon the Lord at the root of the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpataru) within a golden pavilion, inside the celestial chariot named Puṣpaka, seated upon a throne surrounded by its furnishings. Upon a four-petalled lotus, the God shines with the luster of sapphire (indranīlamaṇi), seated in the hero’s posture (vīrāsana), adorned with the gesture of exposition (vyākhyāmudrā). Or [one may meditate on him] thus.

On page 5a): One should recite the mantra while meditating on Him who is seated upon Mṛṇāla, served by Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, endowed with all ornaments, and possessing the beauty of a youth in his prime. Alternatively, one may remember Hari through the recitation of the mantras beginning with Smara. The mantra "Rāma" ending with "Candrabhadra," preceded by the *oṃ* syllable and followed by "namaḥ," is known as the eight-syllabled (*aṣṭākṣara*) mantra when joined with the *tāra* (oṃ). When preceded and followed by the *tāra*, that same mantra becomes nine-syllabled (*navārṇa*), though it may be of various forms. The mantra "Tāra-Rāma" (oṃ rāmāya), ending in the dative case, followed by "Krodhāstra" and "Vahnitalpagā" (svāhā), is another eight-syllabled mantra. Its seer (*ṛṣi*) and other attributes are like those of the six-syllabled mantra. One should utter the seed-syllable of the qualities (*guṇabīja*) and the *māyā* (hrīṃ), followed by "Rudrā... [Note: The text appears to be truncated here].
Furthermore, this mantra of Śivomā consists of eight syllables and bestows wealth. Sadāśiva is declared to be the Ṛṣi, and Gāyatrī is said to be the metre.

Śivomā-Rāmā-Candra is proclaimed as the presiding deity. The limbs [of the mantra] are formed by the long *māyā* (the seed-syllable *hrīṃ*) joined with the syllables of the *tāra* (*oṃ*). We worship Rāma, the three-eyed one, who bears the crescent moon, the supreme wielder of the trident, whose entire body is smeared with ashes, and who wears matted hair. We worship her who is delightful to Rāma, the limit of beauty, the one who adorns the boundary, holding the noose, the goad, the bow, and the arrow.

One should meditate on the three-eyed Lord who holds the earth, Sītā, and the bow, and thus mutter the mantra one hundred thousand times. One should offer oblations with bilva leaves, fruits, flowers, sesame seeds, or lotuses, soaked in the three sweets (honey, ghee, and sugar). Then the treasures desired by the gods will come of their own accord. This mantra, ending with "O Beloved of Jānakī," consists of eighteen syllables. Vasiṣṭha is the seer (ṛṣi), the Svarāt is the meter (chandas), and Rāma, who took the hand of Sītā, is the deity (devatā). The first syllable is the seed (bīja), the syllable "Ṭhiṭha" is the power (śakti), and it is considered that the limbs (aṅgas) are formed with the Kāma-bīja. [The head (śiras) is assigned to the heart.]

One should place the ten syllables of the mantra upon the forehead, between the eyebrows, the palate, the throat, the heart, the navel, the two shanks, the knees, and the feet. [One should meditate on] Rāghava, seated upon a lion-throne atop a heap of flowers, in the city of Ayodhyā, within a golden pavilion variegated with jewels and adorned with canopies of Mandāra flowers and festoons of arches;
being praised by demons, monkeys, and auspicious gods who have partaken of divine drinks, and attended by bowing sages; his left side adorned by Sītā and graced by Lakṣmaṇa; he is dark-complexioned.

One should meditate upon him with a serene face, adorned with all ornaments, and the wise practitioner should thus recite the mantra for one hundred thousand syllables. Rāmaṅ etaṃ dhanuṣpāṇi yeṅ etaṃ syād vahnisundarī—this is the ten-syllable mantra. Brahmā is remembered as the sage (ṛṣi), Virāṭ is the meter (chandas), and the deity is declared to be Rāma, the destroyer of the Rākṣasas. The first syllable is the seed (bīja), and the second is the power (śakti); by means of these, the limbs (aṅgas) are assigned as before. One should perform the assignment of the syllables (varṇanyāsa), the meditation (dhyāna), and the rules for the preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa) as stated for the ten-syllable mantra; one should remember [the deity] holding the bow and arrows. *Oṃ hṛdbhaga*.

The *vīja* is "Rāma" and the *śakti* is "Caṅe," joined with the *tāra* (Om). Its seer (*ṛṣi*) and meditation (*dhyāna*), etc., are as before; it consists of twelve syllables, with the word "Śrī" at the beginning and "Jaya" in the middle.

That [mantra] of thirteen syllables, with its seer and other details as before, grants all desires. With the three parts repeated twice, the limbs (*aṅga*) are formed, and the meditation is like that of the ten-syllable mantra. With the *tāra*, the heart (*hṛt*), "Bhagavate Rāmaṃ," then "Ṅe," and thereafter the word "Puruṣāya," ending with the heart—this is the eighteen-syllable mantra. Viśvāmitra is the seer, the Gāyatrī is the meter, and the deity of this mantra is Rāmabhadra, the crusher of the pride of the Ten-faced one (Rāvaṇa).

Then one should fashion the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*): *Ṛtaḥ*, *Tāram*, *Vījanatiḥ*, *Śaktiḥ*, *Ṣaḍaṅgam*, and thereafter *Kauśaleṃdra-savyasaṃdhamanantaram*. Then, for the sake of the welfare of all the worlds, one should utter "Rāvaṇāntaka-vāmānam" followed by "Svādu-prasannavadanaḥ" in the dative case (*caturthī*). In the grove of Nandigrāma, which was adorned with clusters of trees and fragrant flowers, and where there was dancing on all sides accompanied by the sounds of drums, kettledrums, conchs, and trumpets, and the chanting of auspicious hymns of victory—there, [he saw] sandalwood and saffron...

In a place perfumed with the scent of sandalwood, camphor, and agallochum, filled with breezes carrying the fragrance of various flowers, and adorned by the songs of celestial nymphs and Gandharva women, one should meditate in the heart upon Rāmabhadra—who is seated upon the Puṣpaka chariot in the form of a lion-throne, accompanied by Sītā and the son of Sumitrā, graced by his crown of victory, bearing a bow and arrows, dark-complexioned, and attended by Sugrīva and Vibhīṣaṇa; who, having slain Rāvaṇa, protected the three worlds from the distress caused by his magic—and thus the sage should recite the mantra ten hundred thousand times. "I am first Rāmabhadra, together with Agni"—thus [he should contemplate] thereafter.

Then, trembling with fear, he [Rāvaṇa] granted the supreme hero, the best of men, the destroyer of the ten-faced one (Rāvaṇa), the state of sovereignty over the body of the Rakshasas. Next, I shall cause him to give the mantra of thirty-two syllables. Viśvāmitra is the sage (*ṛṣi*) of this mantra; the *anuṣṭubh* is the meter (*chandas*); and Lord Rāmabhadra is proclaimed as the deity (*devatā*). The arrangement of the limbs (*aṅga-kalpanā*) consists of four parts for the hands, four for the feet, and four for the secret organ. One should place the letters of the mantra on the head, the forehead, the two eyes, the two ears, the two cheeks, the bridge of the nose, the mouth, the two arms, the two breasts, the navel, the heart, the two sides, the two shoulders, the two thighs, the private parts, the anus, and the joints of the feet. The meditation (*dhyāna*) and the mantra are also as previously described.

One should recite three hundred thousand times while focusing on Rāma as yellow in color; one afflicted by poverty should recite this mantra with the *tāra* (Oṃ) prefixed. The mantra is: *oṃ namo bhagavate raghunandanāya rakṣoghna-viśada-madhura-prasanna-vadanāyāmita-tejase balāya rāmāya viṣṇave namaḥ*. This garland-mantra (*mālā-mantra*) consists of forty-seven syllables. The sage (*ṛṣi*) is Pitāmaha (Brahmā), the meter (*chandas*) is Anuṣṭubh, and the deity (*devatā*) is Rāma, consecrated for kingship. The seed-syllable (*bīja*) and power (*śakti*) are according to the [prescribed] sequence.

One should place the syllables in the following locations: the tongue, the face, the forehead, the space between the eyebrows, the two eyes, the two ears, the two nostrils, the two cheeks, the two lips, the teeth, the region of the mouth, the middle of the arms, the tips of the fingers, the throat, the heart, the navel, the private parts, the sides, the back, the belly, and the seat of the navel. The meditation for the ten-syllable mantra is said to consist of seven, six, seventeen, eleven, six, eight, and six [units]. One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times with bilva fruits, flowers, and leaves combined with the three sweets (honey, ghee, and sugar), or with the three types of honey.

Or else, one should perform the *homa* with lotuses ten times the [required] portion, and likewise perform the *tarpaṇa* (libation) in all cases. Among all the *Rāma-mantras*, the six-syllabled king of mantras is established in many ways:
once, twice, thrice, fourfold, fivefold, as well as sixfold, sevenfold, eightfold, and so on. Śiva alone knows the true nature of the divisions of the *Rāma-mantra*.

This six-syllabled mantra ends in "Sītā," ends in the dative case, and concludes with "Svāhā"; it is declared to be both independent and subordinate to its limbs (*aṅga*). Janaka is its *ṛṣi*, and the meter is *gāyatrī*.

On page 6b): The goddess Sītā is declared to be the deity of this mantra; *śrīṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and *svāhā* is the power (*śakti*). One should fashion the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) by joining these with the long vowels in their respective positions. One should worship her upon a Vaiṣṇava pedestal and meditate on her as united with Rāghava—of the same complexion as him, with lotuses in her hands, and intent on gazing at Rāma. One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times (*lakṣa*) and thereafter accomplish one's desired goal. Now, the king of mantras spoken by Agastya for Lakṣmaṇa is set forth: having extracted the letter preceded by *ra* (i.e., *la*) together with the moon (*indu*, i.e., the nasal bindu), joined with *lakṣmaṇa*, followed by *ṅe* (the dative case ending), and endowed with *namaḥ*—this is the mantra of Lakṣmaṇa. Agastya is its seer (*ṛṣi*). Its meter is... [The text breaks off].

In this context, the *yantra* is described: Lakṣmaṇa is declared to be the deity; *Laṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and indeed *Śakti* is its power. In the application (*viniyoga*) for the four aims of human life (*puruṣārtha*), one should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) using one's own seed-syllable conjoined with the long vowels. One should worship Rāma—who has two arms, a body radiant as gold, eyes fixed upon a lotus, holding a bow and arrow in his hands, and whose mind is intent on service to [Rāma]—upon a Vaiṣṇava pedestal provided with the limbs (*aṅgas*) but devoid of the supreme [central] form. Having performed the preliminary rite (*puraścaryā*) of seven hundred thousand recitations, once perfected, the practitioner should achieve success. This same procedure applies to Bharata and likewise to Śatrughna. Thus it is said.

These [deities] are also considered primary; whether at the beginning or at the end of the worship of Rāghava, their worship must also be performed by those desiring the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation. Lakṣmaṇa, however, is always to be worshipped primarily and eternally on the pedestal of Rāma; his worship must be eternal just as that of Rāma. If one who is firm in his vows desires the fruit of the worship of Rāma, he should with effort perform the worship of Lakṣmaṇa in detail. There are many varieties of the Śrī Rāma mantras.

O Sage, that peace must certainly be accomplished by practitioners for the sake of Saumitri as well. With a concentrated mind, seekers of liberation (mumukṣus) should tirelessly recite the mantra of Lakṣmaṇa one hundred and eight times, or ten thousand times, or even a hundred times. Those who recite the mantra of Rāma without first reciting the mantra of Lakṣmaṇa do not attain the fruit of victory, nor indeed does the discernment between enemy and friend arise for them in this world. He who, established in solitude, recites the mantra of Lakṣmaṇa daily, is liberated from all sins and obtains all his desires.

(p. 7a) Indeed, this mantra was taught by Śārṅgin (Viṣṇu) for the sake of ritual application; in former times, by means of this very [mantra], Arjuna completely conquered all directions and established Dharmarāja (Yudhiṣṭhira) in his ancestral, supreme kingdom. This mantra, centered on recitation (*japa*), is the sole means for attaining a kingdom. If one, being self-controlled and concentrated, should recite this mantra one hundred thousand times (*lakṣa*), he will undoubtedly regain his lost kingdom before long. Then, having consecrated himself, one should meditate upon Rāsa with intense devotion; having recited this [mantra] fifty thousand times, he shall attain it.

Standing in solitude and meditating on [Hanumān] as liberated from the serpent-noose, one shall obtain sovereignty; by reciting ten thousand (*ayuta*) times, one shall indeed be released at that very moment from shackles and other bonds. Meditating on Añjaneya, who has brought great medicinal herbs that remove all pain, a person shall escape untimely death by reciting ten million (*nayuta*) times. Meditating thus upon the destroyer of Indrajit’s life-force while taking refuge [in him], one should recite with great speed and perseverance against a host of enemies. Meditating on the one whose mind was intent on cutting off the tip of Śūrpaṇakhā’s nose, Indra and the other gods were [subdued] by a thousand recitations.

One should know that for the sake of serving the lotus feet of Rāma, having prepared the gateway and reciting [the mantra] ten thousand times in solitude, one destroys many great diseases such as epilepsy and leprosy at that very moment. Restraining the senses, with a restricted diet, performing seven thousand recitations day after day, and worshipping according to the rules with one hundred and eight flowers and white lotuses, the sage should offer milk-rice mixed with sugar as an oblation according to the ritual. Having anointed [the image] with sandalwood paste mixed with camphor, he should [offer it] dedicated to the God.

O best of the twice-born, by worshipping [the deity] constantly, one shall be liberated from leprosy (kuṣṭha), which is difficult to treat and manifold, including various skin diseases such as circular patches (maṇḍala) and others distinguished by their types; all these, even if difficult to cure, shall perish in an instant. Restricting one's diet exclusively and having conquered the senses for six months, one who recites [the mantra] according to this rule is liberated from consumption (kṣaya).

With a concentrated mind, reciting the mantra while offering oblations of black gram cakes (māṣāpūpa) and food, one is liberated from wind-related diseases (vātaroga), even those that are many, in an instant. Having consecrated water with the mantra three times daily with a concentrated mind, [one should drink it].

Having drunk [the water] with pure devotion during the twilight (saṃdhyā), one is liberated from all diseases. Having destroyed poverty, the one of noble vows (subrata) attains prosperity. There shall never be contact with poison or other ailments. By washing his body and face every day with devotion and a concentrated mind, he shall conquer even the most terrible diseases arising in the mouth, eyes, and so forth. By drinking consecrated water, he shall conquer many diseases of the stomach. By making a gift of an image of the Lord according to the rules and with devotion, one is liberated from all diseases; of this there is no doubt. And for one desiring a daughter, [there is success] in marriage.
O ascetic, by meditating on Śaktimān, reciting the mantra one hundred thousand times, and offering oblations of parched grain (lāja) ten times that number, one shall quickly obtain a desired maiden.

One who is initiated, constantly restrained and observant regarding the mantras of the weapons, and who for three months daily remembers [the deity] according to rule with undistracted mind, preceded by worship—reciting seven thousand [times] while having conquered the senses—he certainly becomes a knower of the essence of all sciences. Having performed a sacrifice of wonderful prowess like Viśvāmitra, one who meditates [on the deity] with ten thousand recitations is liberated from fears after a long time. At the junction of day and night (saṃdhyā)...

The knower of mantras, having performed the ritual rinsing of the mouth according to rule with the root mantra, being self-restrained at the three junctions of the day and having personally completed his daily rites, and having received initiation according to the prescribed method preceded by the permission of the Guru, is liberated from all sins and goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu. Furthermore, one who is free from desire and worships the All-pervading Lord, having obtained initiation according to the rules from a Guru who is stainless, devoted to his own conduct, self-controlled, a householder, and one who has conquered the senses— following that Guru’s instruction and performing the *puraścaryā* rite according to the injunctions— is freed from the entire multitude of merits and demerits.

One whose mind is pure and who utters this sound shall attain the eternal state that is free from rebirth. Whether one has desires or not, having obtained what is wished for and being liberated from captivating enjoyments, and having become a rememberer of past births for a long time, he attains the supreme abode of Viṣṇu. Just as the practitioner of the Śrī Rāma mantras transcends the origin of sin, so too those who utter the mantra of Lakṣmaṇa attain the highest goal. Some mantras may exist merely for the sake of specific speech, while others are means for the removal of sins; yet this one alone is known to yield the fruit of both enjoyment and liberation. I shall now declare the mantra of Añjaneya, the sole means for both enjoyment and liberation.

This wealth has been revealed by Śaṅkara, desiring the welfare of the worlds. Upon seeing one intent on the practice of this mantra, bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, ḍākinīs, and brahmarākṣasas flee in all directions.

This unsurpassed king of mantras is both the primary essence and its constituent limb. Having first uttered the word *namaḥ*, then the word *bhagavate*, then the word *aṃjaneya*, then the word *ṅe* (Oṃ), and likewise the word *mahābala*, followed by the wife of Vahni (Svāhā)—this is the supreme mantra of Hanumān. This eighteen-syllable mantra is declared to grant success from the very outset; it is known as the Mālā-mantra, the supreme mantra of Māruti that grants all accomplishments.

Having first uttered the syllable *praṇava* (Oṃ), one should recite the words *namo hanumate*, followed by the word *prakaṭa* (manifest), and likewise the word *parākrama* (valour). Then, joined with the word *ākrānta* (having traversed), one should utter the phrase "the circle of the directions.

Then, saying "he who has whitened the three worlds with his canopy," and having said "vajradeha" (diamond-bodied), one should likewise utter the word "avatāra" (incarnation) of Rudra. One should then utter the vocative case ending, followed by the words "the burner of the city of Laṅkā," "the leaping across the ocean," "the slayer of the ten-necked Rāvaṇa," the word "consolation for Sītā," "born from the womb of Añjanā," and "O you who bring joy to Śrī Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, O monkey-sage!"

One should utter the word "Mountain-lifter," which is common to both the Unmanifest Illuminator (Nyaprakāśaka) and Sugrīva; likewise the word "O one who has observed celibacy since childhood" (Vālabrahmacārin); likewise the word with a deep sound; likewise "Destroyer of all caves" and "Cutter of all fevers. Then one should recite the syllable *Tāra* (*Om*). Having uttered the three *Māyā-hā*s (*Hrīm Hā Hrīm*), then the words "Come, O Slayer" (*Hatyāvehi*); then "Take away all poison" (*Sarvaṃ viṣaṃ hara*) and "Agitate the supreme power" (*Paraṃ balaṃ kṣobhaya*). One should repeat twice "Accomplish all tasks" (*Sarvākāryāṇi sādhaya*). *Huṃ Phaṭ Svāhā*—this is the mantra known as the "Garland" (*Mālā*), which grants all desires. The Seer (*Ṛṣi*) is Īśvara.

The meter is said to be Anuṣṭubh, Hanumān is declared to be the deity, "Haṃ" is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and the two final letters (*ja* and *au*) are the power (*śakti*). The three syllables [of the name] are declared to be the peg (*kīlaka*), and again, the piercing is performed with the root [syllable]. The fruit is proclaimed to be the propitiation of Hanumān in the month of Māgha. One should place [the mantra] on the two thumbs with "Obeisance to the Blessed One, the Son of Añjanā" (*namo bhagavate cāñjaneyāya*). Immediately after, one should place it on the two index fingers with "To the Form of Rudra" (*rudramūrtaye*). Likewise, clearly on the two middle fingers, one should place it with "To the Son of Vāyu" (*vāyusutāya*). Similarly, one should place it on the two ring fingers with "To Him whose Womb is Fire" (*agnigarbhāya*). And the wise practitioner should place it on the two little fingers with "To the Messenger of Rāma" (*rāmadūtāya*). [The remainder is] the Brahmāstra.

The weapon-mantra (astra-mantra) has been proclaimed for the purpose of warding off [obstacles]. Having thus performed the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) as prescribed by the Sage, one should meditate with undistracted mind upon [the deity] who is the color of crystal, possessing the luster of gold, two-armed, with palms joined in reverence (*añjali*), and whose lotus-face is beautified by a pair of earrings. One should perform the preliminary rite (*puraścaryā*) ten thousand times before a *liṅga* of Śiva or on a Vaiṣṇava or Śaiva pedestal, offering worship daily without the surrounding circuits (*āvṛtis*), eating only at night, and having conquered the senses. O Sage, for the cessation of minor diseases, by reciting [the mantra] one hundred and eight times for three days in solitude, one shall be liberated from them instantly.

Furthermore, by reciting [the mantra] one hundred and eight times for three days for the sake of pacifying minor spirits (*bhūta*), one is liberated from the fear of spirits. By reciting it exactly one hundred and eight times for the pacification of *bhūtas*, *pretas*, *piśācas*, and so forth, one will certainly be freed from that fear; of this there is no doubt. For the sake of pacifying major diseases and the like, one who is restricted in diet should recite it one thousand and eight times, and thereby one will surely be liberated. For kings desiring victory, there is nothing other than this: one who is restricted in diet should meditate upon the Slayer of Rākṣasas and recite [the mantra] ten thousand times while remaining self-controlled.

One shall conquer even the formidable enemy; by remembering Sugrīva, the peacemaker, one attains peace with even a powerful foe without a doubt. By chanting the mantra ten thousand times while offering oblations of *kaṃdhya* (a specific plant) into the fire, O sinless one, one may burn down the enemy kingdom, and even the Ocean of Milk itself. For one seeking victory over hosts of foes, there is no other means superior to this.

He who worships Hanumān, the soul of all the gods, within his home, shall be saluted by others; through that mantra, his prosperity shall be unshakable. He shall obtain long life, O God, and become victorious over all.

By merely uttering the name of Hanumān, who causes the agitation of the elements such as Māyā, enemies are always born as friends. Indeed, for the devotees of Śiva and Viṣṇu, only the six rites have been shown;
there is no other means than this mantra of Hanumān. For those terrified by thieves, tigers, and the like, he alone is the supreme refuge.

For those whose kingdoms have been seized, those who have been insulted by others, those separated from their beloveds, and those obstructed in battle by enemy troops—let them set out from their own homes at the time of departure, placing Hanumān before them.

One should go with urgency to see the object of sight, constantly remembering it even during sleep, as if one were pursued by thieves, spirits, or others. Then, the state of Hanuman, beginning with Vāsudeva and the rest, bears fruit; one should go to that place where the fruit has ripened. "Āyuḥ, āḥ, rudrāya"—this mantra produces immediate conviction. This twenty-four-syllable mantra removes the disease of the spleen (*plīharoga*).

The auspicious cloth, folded eight times over the leaf of the *vāgalli* plant, should be placed entirely upon the abdomen, made of bamboo. One should heat a stone taken from the forest over a fire until it is red-hot, and then apply it [to the abdomen]. The mantra...

Having consecrated it seven times with this mantra, one should then likewise consecrate the *vicaru* (the medicinal powder) seven times. From the bursting stream [of the powder], one will undoubtedly become the Goddess Lakṣmī herself. One should draw the form of Hanumān on a cloth in the shape of a tail using *kokilākṣa* as a pen and the eight fragrant substances beginning with camphor. Having extracted the eighteen-syllable mantra and placed the name in its midst, if one binds it upon the head, one certainly conquers the three worlds. Alternatively, one may conquer an army; one should draw the shadow [of the deity] while reciting the *Mātṛkā* during a lunar or solar eclipse.

One should perform oblations until liberation is attained, using sesame, mustard seeds, and other materials, each in a tenth part of the quantity. During the time of battle, by displaying a banner mounted upon an elephant or a horse, the defeat of the enemy army becomes certain. He who recites the *mālā-mantra* of Hanumān becomes free from debt; in battle, his body becomes as hard as a thunderbolt and his prowess equal to that of Hanumān. Now I shall describe a protective rite (*rakṣā*) that bestows all accomplishments, which paralyzes all armies and brings all beings under one's control. [One should write the mantra] with *rocanā* and saffron on a beautiful birch-bark leaf. Su...

One should draw an eight-petaled lotus diagram using a pen made of colored powder. In its center, one should write the name of the person for whom the rite is intended; on the eight petals, the root mantra; and outside of that, the garland mantra. This should be encircled three times by the syllable *Hrīṃ*. Having thus prepared the diagram, one should wear it—encased in the three metals—on the waist, the arm, or the head. For one who maintains this protection, no obstacle shall arise. In battle, in the royal court, in gambling, or in legal disputes, he shall suffer no defeat. His body becomes like adamant and possesses great strength; weapons do not strike him. He is free from the afflictions of calamities and the like, as well as from poison, both stationary (*sthāvara*) and mobile (*jaṅgama*). No fear exists for him, nor even among women.

(p. 9b) Even those who are intensely dear to him do not cause him suffering, nor do houses or domestic attachments; there is no fear of water or fire, nor of tigers, thieves, or wild beasts. All fevers, including the powerful *tryāhika* (tertian) types and others, as well as great diseases such as consumption (*yakṣman*), are destroyed by the power of the King of Yantras. The root mantra is declared to consist of eight syllables: the *Tāra* (Om), followed by *Hakāra* (Ha), *Agni* (Ra), *Śaṅkha* (Sa), endowed with the six long vowels and the *Bindu*, and ending with the *Praṇava* (Om).

One should extract [the mantra] beginning with *Tāra* and *Vajrakāya*, and then *Tuṭṭe*. He is described as having tawny-brown hair, possessing great strength, with upward-pointing hair, a red face, and a tongue like lightning.

Then [one should utter] *hāraudrapadam*, then *daṃṣṭotkaṃṭakahakahakarālin*, then *mahādṛḍhaprahāriṃścalam* for the sake of slaying the Lord of Laṅkā, then the word *mahāsetuvadha*, then *mahāśailapravāhavan* for the sky-walker, then *ehi bhagavan śrama*, then the word *mahāpadam*, then the word *balaparākrama*, then *bhairavājñāpaya iti ehi ehi*, then *mahāraudradīrghapucchena veṣṭaya vairiṇam bhañjaya*, [this] word repeated twice, then *huṃ phaṭ*. This mantra of one hundred syllables, consisting of twenty-five more [than seventy-five], is proclaimed as the "Mālā" (Garland) mantra for diseases such as fever and the like.

"Maṃtakaḥ smṛtaḥ"—thus is the extraction of the Śrī Rāma mantra. It is understood that the four [deities] beginning with Gaṇeśa are limbs (*aṅga*) of Rāma, based on the general scriptural injunction: "All the gods praise [him]. All mantras that have come down from the King of Mantras are to be known as enjoined by the Vedas, even if not explicitly stated, because his form is the Supreme Brahman itself. One should worship Gaṇeśa in the southeast, Sūrya in the southwest corner, Umā in the northwest, and Īśa (Śiva) in the northeast, in due order. *Śa-śi-vi-sū-ga-vi-śa-śi-ga-śa-śi-vi-ga-vi-sū-ga-śā* (This is the seed-mantra).

The sequence [of mantras] has been stated in brief for the five [deities] starting from Fire; however, when deprived of their own proper places, these deities bestow suffering, grief, and disease. Having offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) to the Principal Deity, the worship of Gaṇeśa and the others should follow. If Gaṇeśa is the principal deity there, it should proceed according to the sequence of the Sun. As for their many mantras, they should be learned by the wise from other texts; here, out of fear of making the book too voluminous, they are told in brief. One should utter the seed-syllables of Tāra (Om), Śrī (Śrīṃ), Śakti (Hrīṃ), Smara (Klīṃ), and Bhū (Lūṃ), followed by "Gaṇapatim," then "ṅentaṃ varānte varadaṃ sarvayuktaṃ janaṃ ca me," and afterwards one should say "vasaṃ ca. Then... [the rest of the sentence follows].

(p. 10a) This mantra of Mahāgaṇapati consists of twenty-eight syllables and has fire as its beloved [seed]. Gaṇaka is its seer (ṛṣi), and the Gāyatrī meter is endowed with the Trivṛt [stoma]. Mahāgaṇapati is declared to be the deity, saluted by the world. The sixth [syllable] is the seed (*bīja*), the end and the beginning are the power (*śakti*), and Śrī is the face; the heart is Smara [Kāma]. For the attainment of all desired fruits, this application (*viniyoga*) is proclaimed. With the seed-syllable at the beginning of the *Tārā* [mantra], one should conceive of the long portions. [He holds] a citron fruit, a mace, a sugarcane bow, a lotus, a discus, a lotus, a noose, a blue lotus, the tip of a grain of rice, his own tusk, and a jewel.

I worship the moon-crested Lord whose face is like a lordly elephant, who possesses a ruddy luster, and who is joyfully embraced by his beloved Pārvatī, who rests upon his own body like a beautiful lotus.

In front of him is a bilva tree, and on both sides are the two supreme lords (Śiva and Viṣṇu) seated upon a vaṭa tree; behind them are the two gods of excessive floral arrows (Kāmadeva and Cupid) seated upon a pippala tree.
To the left are Priyaṅgu and Mahīvarāha. On his right and left sides, one should meditate upon the two treasures, Śaṅkhanidhi and Padmanidhi, shining like pearls and rubies, raining down jewels.

"Always bestow wealth by means of a rain of jewels, pearls, and corals contained within the jar held in your own lotus hand; scatter an unceasing stream of gems for the sake of the complete prosperity of the practitioner. One should extract [the mantra] as "Tāram ghṛṇiḥ sūryapam ādityam. This is declared to be the eight-syllable mantra of the Sun. Bhārgava is its seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is its meter (chandas), and the Sun is the deity (devatā) of this mantra.
It has been proclaimed by the sages as bestowing both seen and unseen fruits. The limb-mantras are now shown: "Satyāya" is the heart, and again, "Brahmaṇe" is the head.

The *Śikhā* mantra is declared for Viṣṇu, the *Varman* is assigned to Rudra, and the *Netra* mantra belongs to Agni. The *Astra* mantra, beginning with "Oṃ ghṛṇi sūrya āditya," should be known as being for all [deities]. Thus is the arrangement of the limbs (*aṅgakalpanā*). I worship the Lord of Day (the Sun), who possesses the luster of a bandhūka flower, who has three shining eyes, wears a crown of rubies, and whose hands hold a pair of red lotuses and grant protection, adorned with armlets, bracelets, and earrings. The mantra known as *Prāsāda*, consisting of the letter 'sa' (sāṃ) joined with grace (*anugraha*) and adorned with a bindu at its head, is proclaimed for the devotees of the gods.

The Ṛṣi is Vāmadeva; the metre is said to be Paṅkti; Sadāśiva is the deity; *Vam* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and *Auḥ* is remembered as the power (*śakti*). The six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) are formed by joining the root seed-syllable with the long vowels. One should meditate upon the Lord, who is adorned with five faces having the colors of pearl, yellow, a water-cloud, a pearl-oyster, and the *japā* flower; who is worshipped by the five-faced [deities]; who wears the crescent moon on his head and possesses the luster of ten million full moons; who holds a trident, a skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*), a sword, a thunderbolt, fire, a lordly serpent, a jar, a goad, a noose, and displays the gestures of granting boons (*abhaya*) and fearlessness (*vara*); and who shines with dark ornaments and blazing [flames]. The Fire-god (*Lakuśīśa*) mounted upon the Wind-god (*Agni*) is known as Bhuvaneśī, who rides upon the left eye and the half-moon.

The sage of this [mantra] is Ṛṣiṃśakti, the metre is Gāyatrī, and the deity is Śaṃdogāyatrī. Its seed-syllable (*bīja*) is *haṃ*, and its power (*śakti*) is Īśa; one should employ it for one's desired purpose. One should fashion the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) by joining the seed-syllable with the six long vowels. I worship the Mother of the Universe (*Jagadambikā*), who resembles the rising sun, who has three eyes and a smiling face, and who holds a noose, a goad, and the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons.

Like a king, she is the source of auspiciousness for the Siddhas and others. The method of worship should be understood primarily from the extensive text. Thus ends the extraction of the mantras of the limb-deities. And now the greatness as spoken by Agastya...

I shall now declare the great reason for its preeminence regarding the illustrious King of Mantras; having heard it, one attains the supreme goal. Among all the best of mantras, the Vaiṣṇava is said to be the most excellent; among those of Gaṇeśa, Śiva, Śakti, and Sūrya, it is the bestower of desired fruits. Even among all the Vaiṣṇava mantras, the Rāma-mantras yield superior results. Compared to the mantras of Gaṇeśa and others, they are millions upon millions of times more efficacious. O best of Brahmins, even without initiation, without the performance of *puraścaryā*, and indeed without the ritual of *nyāsa*, these mantras grant success through mere recitation (*japa*). Among them, this six-syllabled mantra is the one that grants fruit without effort. This six-syllabled [mantra]...

This mantra, which wards off all calamities, is proclaimed as the king of mantras, the most excellent of all. It burns away daily misfortunes, those arising from fortnights, months, and seasons, entirely and without remainder, like fire consumes wool. Thousands of killings of Brahmins committed knowingly or unknowingly, tens of thousands of thefts of gold, drinking of liquor, and violations of the Guru’s bed, as well as thousands of crores of minor sins—all these perish through the recitation of the Rāma-mantra. Thus it is said; and likewise the Śruti [declares] the Tāraka Brahma-mantra.

He who constantly recites this [mantra] transcends the study of the Vedas; he transcends the killing of a learned Brahmin (pāṣaṇḍa); he transcends the killing of an embryo; he transcends the killing of all beings; he transcends saṃsāra. Having become liberated in soul, he attains the state of being truly born (the immortal state). There is no mantra equal to this even in the entire universe. When Rāma is propitiated by means of this, He becomes pleased very quickly. While the procedure for the practice of all mantras in general belongs to Rāghava, the specific details should be understood from their respective sources. Thus ends the majesty of Rāma’s mantra, the meaning of the king of Śrī Rāma mantras.

The *Saṃhitopaniṣad* is established here as the root, bestowing the accomplishment of all goals. The letter *ra* signifies fire and culminates in light; it is said that the Supreme Self consists of Being, Consciousness, and Bliss (*saccidānanda*).

The consonant is the partless Brahman, while the vowel is *prāṇa* and *māyā*. The union of the consonant with the vowel is known as the "joining of the breath" (*prāṇayojana*). Because the letter *ra* is composed of light, the addition of the letter *ā* is performed. The letter *ma* is proclaimed as "I" (*mām*) because its purpose is upward ascent. Having cast off this very *ātman*, there remains the single-syllabled mantra *Aum*. This is it.

The seed-syllable (bīja) is the equilibrium of *samāyā*, which is called Brahman; it possesses the nasal drop (*bindu*) and is also the Puruṣa, possessing the forms of Śiva, the Sun, and the Moon. Its flame-like form is Light (*jyotis*), and its *nāda* is considered Nature (*prakṛti*). Both Nature and Puruṣa are the equilibrium of Brahman itself. The seed-syllable consists of the *bindu* and *nāda*; Fire is considered the digit of the Moon. The entire universe, consisting of Fire and Moon, is established within the seed-syllable of Rāma. Just as a great tree exists potentially within a small seed, even so this entire world of moving and non-moving beings exists within the seed-syllable of Rāma—thus says the Śruti.

Thus is the meaning of the seed-syllable (*bīja*). Now, as the literal meaning of this mantra is being clarified, the dual nature of the seed-syllable is seen within the name "Rāma. When the seed-syllable is free from *māyā*, it is celebrated as the Supreme Brahman, which grants liberation to practitioners; therefore, the single letter *m* is considered the giver of liberation. Because he possesses the form of *mā*, Rāma bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*). The first syllable, *vā* (the *v* sound), represents the meaning of the term *tat* ("That"), while the *makāra* represents the meaning of the term *tvam* ("Thou"). Those who know the reality of the Self understand that the union of these two is expressed by the word *namaḥ*. While the statement "That art Thou" (*tat tvam asi*) and others grant only liberation, [this mantra] grants both.

Since this bestows both liberation (*mukti*) and worldly enjoyment (*bhukti*), it excels even that; for yogis always delight in that which sustains their own selves. It is celebrated as both *nirguṇa* (devoid of qualities), being consciousness-bliss (*cidānanda*), and *saguṇa* (possessing qualities). It is sung as the name signifying the individual soul (*jīva*), and likewise as "Ātmārāma" (one who delights in the Self). Furthermore, it is called the "fourth" (*turyā*) because of its identity with that. This mantra is the designator (*vācaka*) and Rāma is the designated (*vācya*); when these two are united in yoga, it yields fruit for all practitioners, of this there is no doubt. Just as one becomes present through the name that designates it, so too—

The mantra consisting of the individual soul (jīvātman) becomes manifest before the practitioner; likewise, the mantra consisting of the individual soul is composed of consciousness. For the sake of the purpose of those who worship the second [Brahman], which is partless and bodiless, there is the conceptualization of forms for Brahman. There is the conceptualization of male, female, limbs, weapons, and so forth for the deities residing in those forms. Because it protects through contemplation (*manana*), it is called a *mantra*; it is produced from the root-source of all mantras arising from the *mūlādhāra*. Because it is the root-nature and the very foundation of all mantras, it is remembered as the *mūlamantra*. The seventy million great mantras and the secondary mantras (*upamantras*) are its branches.

All such vowels, which are the mothers of the phonemes, have arisen from the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*). Whatever has been studied by him, all that is accomplished; the wise man who knows the root-mantra as revealed by the Guru becomes liberated while living merely by knowing the root. The power of atomicity (*aṇimā*) and other sovereign powers arise before long. Such is the meaning of the King of Mantras. All human beings, embodied souls, have the right to this—those seeking liberation, the dispassionate, and likewise those belonging to the various stages of life (*āśrama*). Rāma is to be meditated upon like the *praṇava* (Om), especially by ascetics (*yatis*), because it is so stated in the Śruti.

The nature of this King of Mantras is clearly as follows: *Oṃ*, the half-mora (*ardhamātrā*), the bindu, and the nāda; these are the syllables in sequence. Because it causes one to cross over [saṃsāra], it is called "Tāraka"; let this be understood from what is declared in the Śruti. Then Bharadvāja asked Yājñavalkya: "What is the Tāraka? What does it transcend? Yājñavalkya replied: "The Tāraka is *Dīrghānala* preceded by the bindu. Again, *Dīrghānala* is followed by *Ṇāya namaḥ*, *Candrāya namaḥ*, and *Bhadrāya namaḥ*. This *Oṃ* is of the nature of Brahman, designated as Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*); thus it should be meditated upon. The letter *A* is the first syllable, and the letter *U* is the second."

The letter *ma* becomes the third syllable; the half-mora (*ardhamātrā*) becomes the fourth syllable; the *bindu* becomes the fifth syllable; the *nāda* becomes the sixth syllable; and that which is the *tāraka* (the savior) becomes the bearer of the burden (*bhāraka*). "Know that very *tāraka* to be Brahman"—so says the Śruti. "Rāma" is the supreme mantra to be recited (*japya*), designated as Brahman; likewise, "Rāma-Rāma" is called the *tāraka*. There are thousands of such Śrutis and Smṛtis. Śrī Rudra himself declares this very thing at Avimukta to one who is about to die at Maṇikarṇikā: *(Page 12a)*... [the letter] *ma* becomes the third syllable, the half-mora becomes the fourth syllable, the *bindu* becomes the fifth syllable, the *nāda* becomes the sixth syllable, and that which is the *tāraka* becomes the bearer of the burden. "Know that very *tāraka* to be Brahman"—such is the Vedic revelation. "Rāma" is the supreme mantra to be recited, known as Brahman; likewise, "Rāma-Rāma"—this is called the *tāraka*. There are thousands of such scriptural and traditional texts. Śrī Rudra himself proclaims this very truth at Avimukta to the dying man at Maṇikarṇikā.

"Even from the Śruti, which states, 'Rudra, dwelling on Mount Mardhoda, expounds the Brahma-tāraka,' it should be understood that this [knowledge] is superior to all others by those who know the excellence of the place. In the Agastisaṃhitā, however, this very point is established:

'Those of purest vows, Śūdras, the righteous, servants of the twice-born, women devoted to their husbands, and others—whether born in the inverse or natural order—all people down to the Cāṇḍālas are eligible here. The Śruti speaks of the six castes (ṣaḍ-varṇa), while the Smṛti consists of two castes; when there is a conflict between these two, it is resolved by such a systematic arrangement. Thus says the Śruti."

On account of the contradiction with Smṛti, Śruti alone is more authoritative; relying on the absence of a fixed rule, this statement is the regulator: the six-syllable mantra for Brāhmaṇas and others, while for the three [lower castes] it is two-syllabled. For others, the supreme Tāraka must be taught by the Lord of the Region (Deśikendra), but without the Praṇava, mantras, and the Gāyatrī, because of the prohibition in Śruti. If one should know the Sāvitrī, Lakṣmī, the Yajus, or the Praṇava for a woman or a Śūdra, he falls into a terrible sin. Therefore, if he teaches anything at all, he becomes an Ācārya and dies by that very act—so says the Tāpanīya Śruti. And thus said Agastya:

This mantra should be taught by a Brahmin as being appropriate [for his disciples]. It should not be less than two syllables, nor more than six syllables, because it would be deficient in its essential requirements. The Śruti also declares: "The yogis always delight in the Name, which is Truth and Bliss. It is sung of as *Ātmārāma* (one who delights in the Self). Furthermore, that which is identical with it is called the Fourth (*Turyā*). This mantra is to be expressed as *Cakorāma*; there is no doubt that it bestows the fruit of yoga upon all practitioners. Just as one becomes intent upon the goal through the Name that expresses it...

(p. 12b) For the sake of those who worship [Him], Brahmā—who is composed of consciousness (*cinmaya*), non-dual, partless, and bodiless—assumes the conception of form. There is the conception of deities residing in forms, and the conception of male, female, limbs, weapons, and so forth. Because it protects through contemplation (*manana*), the mantra is a wish-fulfilling tree for the practitioner (*mantrin*). Because it is the root of all mantras, arising from the *mūlādhāra*, and because its own nature is the root, it is remembered as the "Root Mantra" (*mūlamantra*). The seventy million great mantras and similar secondary mantras (*upamantra*) are all merely phonemes, vowels, and consonants; they are the root...

All that arises from the root-mantra has been studied and heard by him; all that has been performed by him. The wise one who understands the root-mantra as revealed by the Guru becomes liberated while living (jīvanmukta) merely through the knowledge of the root. The power of sovereignty over the atoms and directions arises even for those born of low lineage. Such is the meaning of the King of Mantras. All men have the right to this, whether they are seekers of liberation, the detached, or householders; however, it should always be meditated upon like the *praṇava* (Oṃ), especially by ascetics (*yatis*). Because it is declared in the Śruti, the King of Mantras possesses the quality of being a "savior" (*tāraka*).

It is clearly [composed of] Om, the half-measure (ardhamātrā), the bindu, and the nāda; these syllables are the Tāraka because they deliver one across [saṃsāra], as declared in the Śruti; let this be understood. Then Bhāradvāja asked Yājñavalkya: "What is the Tāraka? What is the Tarati? Yājñavalkya replied: "The Tāraka is Dīrghānala preceded by the bindu; Dīrghānala again is 'namaḥ māyāya', 'namaḥ candrāya', and 'namaḥ bhadraya'. Thus, 'Om'—which is of the nature of Brahman, known as Being-Consciousness-Bliss—is to be meditated upon. The letter 'A' becomes the first syllable within the Self."

"By the word 'Rāma,' the Supreme Brahman is designated"—this is the method regarding the qualification [for initiation]. Now I shall describe the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), the unsurpassed ritual of initiation (*dīkṣā-vidhi*) by which [success] is not attained even through a hundredfold practice. In the month of Madhu (Caitra) there will be suffering; in Mādhava (Vaiśākha), a collection of jewels; in Jyeṣṭha, death occurs; in Āṣāḍha, the destruction of kinsmen. In Śrāvaṇa, prosperity certainly comes; in Bhādrapada, loss [of wealth]; in the month of Āśvina, there is indeed auspiciousness in every respect for all people; in Kārttika, knowledge arises; and in Mārgaśīrṣa, happiness also occurs. In Pauṣa...

(p. 13a) In Māgha there shall be the destruction of ignorance; in Phālguna there shall be an increase in intelligence and prosperity; one should avoid the intercalary month (*malamāsa*). Thus is the purification of the month (*māsaśuddhi*). It should be performed on Sundays, Thursdays, Saturdays, Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays. Thus is the purification of the day (*vāraśuddhi*). One should perform the consecration with mantras (*mantrābhiṣecana*) under the asterisms of Aśvinī, Rohiṇī, Svātī, Viśākhā, Hastā, Jyeṣṭhā, and the three *uttarā*s. In the Nārada-tantra it is said: "Rohiṇī, Śravaṇa, Ārdrā, Dhaniṣṭhā, the three *uttarā*s, Puṣya, and Śatabhiṣaj are declared to be the asterisms for initiation (*dīkṣā*). Thus is the purification of the asterism (*nakṣatraśuddhi*). [On] the full moon...

The fifth, second, seventh, thirteenth, and tenth lunar days are praised as granting all desires; according to the *Mantrasārasaṃgraha*: "The second, fifth, and especially the sixth, as well as the twelfth or even the thirteenth, should be observed. This concludes the purity of the lunar day (*tithi-śuddhi*). Regarding the purity of time (*kāla-śuddhi*): on a day when the five limbs [of the sun] are pure, during the rising of the moon and its asterism, at the rising of Jupiter and Venus, in a pure ascendant calculated by the twelve [houses], and when the moon and stars are favorable, it is recommended for all rites. Thus ends the [section on] Sūtra.

At the time of a solar eclipse, nothing else need be sought; there is no other time equal to the moment of a solar eclipse. Whatever is performed there yields its fruit in full. On the occasion of a solar eclipse, there is no need for consideration of the lunar day, the weekday, or the direction; it grants the desired result. Whatever is received from a preceptor at that time results in the swift accomplishment of the mantra without effort. Therefore, those desiring the perfection of their mantra should, with every effort, perform the ritual bathing at a sacred ford (tīrtha) with the mantra during a solar or lunar eclipse while staying with the preceptor.

Regarding the *tantu* and *dāmana* festivals, one performing the initiation (*maṃtradīkṣā*) should purify the month, the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), and so forth; this is the time for exceptions. However, the seeker (*upāsaka*), being pure in soul, should strive to satisfy the Guru with various wonderful offerings, endowed with devotion and faith, so that the Guru, being satisfied and gracious, may himself grant the mantra as a boon. Such is the sequence of duties. The Guru, having already been purified, should perform the auspicious sowing of sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*) on the seventh day after the day of purification, following a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) and fasting. He should not... [text ends]

On the previous day, one should perform the *svastivācana* (rite for auspiciousness) for the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha* according to the procedure prescribed in one's own *gṛhya-sūtra*. Then, having properly drawn the *sarvatobhadra* diagram using four colors—blue, yellow, white, and black—one should place two handfuls of grain upon it. Therein, one should set down a water-pot (*kalaśa*) filled with water from sacred sites (*tīrtha*), wrapped in a pair of cloths, endowed with five gems, enriched with blossoms of mango and *aśvattha* trees, adorned with branches, provided with a coconut and its husk, and made radiant on all sides by auspicious items; having thus prepared it, one should include all festive elements.

There, one should worship Hari with the hymns (*sūktas*) of the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāma* Vedas, as well as with the mantras of the *Smṛtis*, the *Purāṇas*, the *Āgamas*, and the Vaiṣṇava scriptures. One should honor the Brāhmaṇas with garments, earrings, and finger-rings, and have them recite the hymns along with the prescribed mantras during that auspicious festival. The Guru, according to the ritual procedure for that [rite], should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and so forth;

having duly performed the array of ritual placements (*nyāsa*), he should worship Him according to the Tantra. One should worship Puruṣottama with the previously mentioned articles of worship, and celebrate the festival with the aforementioned dances, songs, and other festivities.

One should cause [the temple] to be decorated and give to the meritorious and illustrious householders a very extensive offering of perfumes, flowers, water, betel-leaf, fine garments, ornaments, and so forth, as well as food along with various kinds of drinks; it is likewise given to others. Having thus performed the festival there, one should perform the night vigil (*jāgaraṇa*). Thus, one should worship the Lord three times a day, both by day and by night. One should mutter [the mantra] six thousand times.

After the worship, the Guru should perform the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) according to the rules at night and on the following day, as well as in the morning, performing everything as before. Having worshipped according to the injunctions, one should then perform the fire-ritual. (From the *Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā*)

The characteristics of that sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) have been described. A wise man should cause a pavilion (maṇḍapa) to be constructed in the northeast portion of the house, measuring six, twelve, eight, or sixteen cubits on all sides, provided with four doors and adorned with arches (toraṇas) and other ornaments. In the middle of that [pavilion], he should cause a square pit to be made, dug two spans (vitasti) deep and four finger-breadths (caturaṅgula) wide. For Brahmins, it should be joined with three finger-breadths; for Kṣatriyas, with two finger-breadths more; for Vaiśyas, with one finger-breadth more; and for Śūdras, it should be only one cubit in measure. Therein, the first girdle (mekhalā) should be twelve finger-breadths in width.

It [the first rampart] is four finger-breadths high on all sides. Above that, one should construct a second rampart, four finger-breadths high and properly extended by eight finger-breadths on all sides. Furthermore, above that, a third rampart should be made; it too is four finger-breadths wide and likewise high. On the western side, the *yoni* (vulva-shaped opening) is situated in the middle, facing east.
It is six finger-breadths wide and twelve finger-breadths long. Its back is raised like an elephant’s trunk, with a hollow in the middle and a slightly elevated neck.

In a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) measuring one cubit (*hasta*), the neck should be made with effort by those desiring the fruits of enjoyment and liberation; it should be the size of a *ṣṭayava*. Alternatively, the pit may have a navel (*nābhi*) or consist of a single girdle (*mekhalā*). A pit endowed with such characteristics bestows the fulfillment of desired goals. If a pit contains defects—whether being deficient or excessive—it yields many faults; therefore, one who desires auspicious results should examine it thoroughly before constructing it. Or, for a concise fire-ritual (*homakarman*), a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) the size of an arrow (*iṣu*) may be used. Thus ends the description of the sacrificial pit. One should prepare the altar for worship in the northwest or the northeast, measuring one cubit...

One should draw the yantra, which is extensive according to the tantra, square on all sides, using rice-powder of blue, yellow, white, black, red, crimson, smoky, and pale colors. When the initiation for a king is performed elsewhere, one should first draw ten lines in the four directions, forming seven squares. Therein, the wise one should fashion an eight-petaled lotus surrounded by three circles, as well as the orbs of the Moon, Sun, and Fire. Outside of that, there should be a square; within the pericarp, there should be a hexagon. The eastern [section] should be yellow and the western white.

Likewise, one should place the red [deity] in the east, the black in the south, the pale-red (pāṭala) situated in the southeast, the blue-colored in the southwest, the smoke-colored (dhūmra) in the northwest, and the white (gaura) is prescribed in the northeast;
this is the sequence for the eight petals. Having properly drawn the conch, discus, mace, lotus, bow, and arrows within the maṇḍala using pigments, one should worship Rāma there.

One should perform offerings, fire-sacrifices (homa), worship, and so forth with means acquired through righteous means; otherwise, even if performing it with devotion among the twice-born, one goes downward. [One should also draw] sixteen squares.

(p. 14b) One should wipe clean the area for the purpose of the yantra. Then, having wiped two rows [of squares] starting from the cardinal directions and the corners, one should establish the house of Earth (the central square). Having drawn equal lines in the intermediate directions, there are the twelve zodiac signs (*rāśis*) therein. Then, for the sake of the enclosure, one should wipe away two outer [rows]. In the remaining two rows, with six squares on all sides, there are the gates; the primary and secondary ornaments (*śobhā-upaśobhā*) are formed by many [squares], and the half-moons are formed by groups of three. This is the general procedure for the initiation into the five *āyatanas*. O Sage, in this very manner, having worshipped within the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), one should offer oblations. Thus ends the description of the altar (*vedikā*). The *śruva* ladle is the measure of a forearm.

One should first construct a square for the purpose of the fire-pit (*agni-kuṇḍa*), measuring seven or five finger-breadths (*aṅgulas*) in sequence. The neck (*garbha*) should be one-third of that; it should be adorned with a door at its end. Having dug a pit equal in width and height, one should clear the area outside below it. From the remainder of the five-finger measurement, one should fashion four beautiful girdles (*mekhalā*) using half of that remaining portion. One should make the opening three parts wide and as long as a thumb, or perhaps one and a half thumbs; at its front, there should be a mouth, four finger-breadths wide.

The handle should be five finger-breadths, or even three or two; its middle and end should be very beautiful, well-hollowed, and placed in a pleasant spot for as long as the little finger [can reach]. The remaining staff should be made according to one's taste, variegated, four-cornered, and exactly one cubit in length. One should fashion the *śruva* ladle with four beautiful, rounded corners, measuring two finger-breadths [in width]; it should be made so that, when placed on a small base, it appears as lovely as a cow’s hoof-print. O Sage, one should fashion the *sruk* and *śruva* ladles from a beautiful, unblemished leaf of the *pālāśa* tree, or else from the *aśvattha*.

When the fire-offering (homa) has been briefly concluded, one should then properly smear the area around the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with cow dung. First, while seated upon a comfortable seat (viṣṭara), one should perform the fire-sacrifice (agnikārya), reciting the mantra with the mind focused on the vital breaths (prāṇas) and with undistracted intellect, until the wind circulates through all the limbs—this is the firm rule.

Having established the fire within the sacrificial pit according to one's resolve, one should draw a six-pointed star, a hexagon, or a triangle in the center of the lines; then, having sprinkled [the site] and moved [the fire], one should respectfully offer the seat (viṣṭara).

On folio 15a): One should contemplate the fire produced there by the Lord Nārāyaṇa through his union with Lakṣmī during her fertile period according to the *grāmyadharma* rite. Alternatively, having churned the fire according to the prescribed rule and brought it even from the house of one who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), one should establish it here after carefully kindling it with *kuśa* grass. Having sprinkled it with water consecrated by the *yajñika* mantras, one should kindle it again with sacrificial wood. Then, having performed *prāṇāyāma*, and having strewn *kuśa* sprouts around [the fire] according to the procedure taught in one's own *gṛhya-sūtra*, O Sage, the knower of mantras should place the vessels for Vāsudeva and the other deities according to the rules, and having inspected them, he should prepare the fuel.

Having placed the strainers upon them and sprinkled them again, one should bring the vessel back, fill it completely with auspicious water, offer *akṣata* grains and a strainer, and having purified it there, place that vessel in the northern direction; this is called the *praṇītā* by the wise. There, one should worship the Lord Viṣṇu along with Brahmā and the Brahmins. Having consecrated the clarified butter (*ājya*) according to the rules, while reciting "Sruksravāvomi," one should perform for the fire the rites beginning with conception (*garbhādhāna*) and ending with marriage. One should offer oblations eight times for each individual rite while the deity is being worshipped.

Having completed [the rite] ending with *hnau vauṣaṭ*, one should begin another ritual and complete that in the same manner. One should again offer oblations for the *agnimukha* (commencement of the fire-rite), beginning with the placing of fuel (*idhmādhāna*) up to the *ājyabhāga* portions. Thus, when the fire-rite is well-performed, one should cook the *caru* for Viṣṇu. One should worship the Leader of the Raghus along with His limbs (*sāṅga*) and attendants (*āvāhana-mantra*) in the fire. One should offer sixteen oblations each of *samidh* wood, clarified butter (*ājya*), and ghee; and with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*), one should offer to the retinue as well. O Sage, one should offer three oblations to all the attendants beginning with Vaināyaka, and to the door-guardians, the limbs, and the retinue.

One should offer oblations again to the deities of the altar; having offered those, one should then give oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) for their attainment. One should offer with the respective materials, all of them being pleasing and made of cooked rice (*caru*). Having first offered to the deities of the gateway and the pedestal, one should then offer three oblations separately to each deity from the beginning up to the Vaiṣṇava deities. Then, having offered the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation with clarified butter, O best of sages, and having properly sprinkled water all around according to the rite, one should perform the purification of the *praṇītā* vessel, offer the oblation, and present the sacrificial fee (*brahma-dakṣiṇā*) according to the extent of one's own means, without greed.

Free from delusion, he should then dismiss the Brahmin and feed other Brahmins. He should then re-unite the deity residing in the midst of the fire with his own self. Having contemplated them as thus become one, while reciting the *Svastivācana* and being honored by the learned with words of benediction (*āsīrvāda*), he shall become happy. Then, having consumed the remainder of the oblation—measured like a *kuṇḍayaṇḍa* and consecrated with the *Gāyatrī* mantra—he should offer a *bali* to that very [deity]. Whether it be a regular (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), or optional (*kāmya*) rite, this "mouth of the fire" (*agnimukha*) is prescribed for all [offerings], both internal and external, with food. Everywhere—

One should perform the *abhyudaya-śrāddha* and the sowing of sprouts (*aṅkurāropaṇa*) at the very beginning for the sake of the success of the rite; such is the rule for the fire-oblation (*homa*). Then, one should again offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) to Rāma, who resides within the water-pot (*kalaśa*). Next, having brought forward the disciple—who is free from sin and bowed with devotion—and having performed breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) and the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) according to the rules, one should, together with many Brahmins, consecrate him upon his head with the waters of that pot while reciting the mantra "surāstvām abhiṣiñcantu" and other mantras: "May Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara consecrate you! May Vāsudeva, the Lord of the World, as well as the all-pervading Āsaṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha, grant you victory. May Ākhaṇḍala (Indra), the divine Agni, Yama, Nairṛti, Varuṇa, Pavana, the Lord of Wealth (Kubera), and Śiva, together with Brahmā and Śeṣa—the guardians of the quarters—protect you always.
Kīrti, Lakṣmī, Dhṛti, Medhā, Puṣṭi, Śraddhā, Kriyā, Mati, Buddhi, Lajjā, Vapu, Śānti, Māyā, Nidrā, and Bhāvanā—may these consecrate you.
May the planets—Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn, as well as the Sun and the Moon—being honored, consecrate you with tranquility, nourishment, splendor, and forgiveness.
May the gods, Dānavas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Pannagas; the sages, Manus, cows, and divine mothers; the wives of the gods, trees, Nāgas, Daityas, and hosts of Apsarases;
