weapons, missiles, kings, and vehicles; medicinal herbs, jewels, and the various limbs of Time; and the rivers and oceans [consecrate you].

"May the mountains, the sacred fords (tīrthas), the clouds, and the rivers consecrate you for the attainment of all desires and goals. Thus are the consecration mantras (abhiṣeka-mantra) in the *Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā*. Having repeatedly recollected: "Nārāyaṇa himself, as Rāma, may he abide within his disciple; he who is omnipresent exists everywhere; may that ocean of mercy be gracious," one should consecrate him with those waters. Then, having clothed him in fine garments, applied sandalwood paste and other unguents, and caused him to wear earrings and a ring, one should thereafter deposit the Vaiṣṇava Mātṛkā and the deposition of the principles (tattva-nyāsa).

Confidently, he should perform the *nyāsa* of the cage of that deity's form (*mūrti-pañjara-nyāsa*) as well as the *nyāsa* of the seers (*ṛṣi*) and so forth, according to the rules as before, upon the body of the disciple.

Then, placing his own hand upon the disciple’s head, he should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times. Thereafter, he should impart the mantras preceded by the offering of water, saying: "May you become one who yields equal fruit for both of us. Thus the eminent sage, the preceptor, being pleased and granting boons to that disciple, should meditate on the self-luminous knowledge (*vidyā*) departing from himself; the blessed disciple should meditate on it as having arrived.

With a special smile, the disciple, having accomplished his purpose, should with devotion report everything to that preceptor—whatever it may be and however much—as he has been pleased in mind. He should offer cows, land, gold, forests, houses, fields, and so forth, in great quantity, or at least half of that, or even a tenth part; or, without hardship, he should give food, clothing, and other items according to his means. In the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam it is said: "O friend, this is what must be done by disciples as a repayment to the preceptor: namely, the offering of all things and one's very self to the preceptor with a pure disposition. No other method is sufficient.

One should diligently please the preceptor with agallochum (vyāghru), and please the preceptor’s son, wife, and others with gold and other gifts, as well as with various honors, clothing, and ornaments, out of devotion. Having given the Vedic sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the preceptor in the manner described, and considering oneself to have accomplished one's purpose, one should feed the Brahmins. After giving them their sacrificial fees as well, one should complete everything.

Strengthened by the benedictions of the Brahmins and the blessings of the preceptor, the knower of mantras should dismiss the preceptor and the others, and then eat. Thus is the *laghumaṇu* [the abbreviated rite].

"O Brahmin, for one who has accomplished his purpose, there is no doubt regarding food"—thus ends the method of initiation (*dīkṣā*). Now I shall describe initiation in brief, along with the conduct required for the preceptor (*ācārya*) and the restraint thereof. One should remember the reality (*tattva*): at that time, initiation depends solely on the vision of the Divine and according to the command of the Guru. There is no need for [waiting for] a lunar day, nor worship, nor fire-oblation (*homa*), nor bathing, nor the performance of recitation (*japa*); rather, the cause of initiation is the attainment of the vision of one's own true Guru. That alone is the auspicious moment, that alone is the good day; that alone is the strength of the stars, the strength of the moon, the strength of the Vidyā, and the strength of destiny. O Lord of Lakṣmī, I meditate upon Your pair of feet.

This is the general time for initiation (*dīkṣā*). Having placed a new water-pot (*kumbha*) upon the *sarvatobhadra* diagram during a *muhūrta*, and having worshipped it with scents and flowers, covered it with cloth, and filled it with all medicinal herbs (*sarvauṣadhi*), five gems (*pañcaratna*), and five sprouts (*pañcapallava*); then, having performed the worship of the deity, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations (*homa*). One should cause the well-adorned disciple to sit upon the altar near the fire. Then, one should consecrate him with water from the sprinkling-vessel (*prokṣiṇī*) and with water from the peace-pot (*śāntikumbha*), both empowered by the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) recited one hundred and eight times. Thereafter, one should accomplish the mantra...

One should place the *traṃhasta* upon the head; saying "May you be equal [to me]," one should offer unbroken rice grains (*akṣatān*) and then the disciple should honor the Guru. Thus ends the abbreviated initiation (*saṃkṣepadīkṣā*). If someone here is unable [to perform this], then having sprinkled unbroken rice grains placed in the center of a lotus with water eight times while reciting the root mantra (*mūla*), and having placed them on the head, one should whisper [the mantra] into the ear. This is the procedure for the oral instruction (*upadeśa*).

The oral instruction is said to be merely the proclamation of the mantra at a holy ford (*tīrtha*), a site of accomplishment (*siddhakṣetra*), or a temple of Śiva. The oral instruction shall be of two kinds: the brief and...

The internal [practice] is said to be for renunciants (*nyāsins*), while for others both are prescribed. The power (*śakti*) consisting of five colors is declared to be known as *vidyā*; the sixth is the essence of sound (*nāda*).

Contemplating the Self through withdrawal (*saṃhṛti*) is the contemplation of the reality (*tattva*) of the Self; it is also the contemplation of the Self within the Self. The contemplation of the unity of both, however, is that which brings an end to worldly existence; this is the internal [practice].
External worship consists of the propitiation of substances and so forth, and that belongs to the householder. This was stated by Śambhu to Śāmbhavī in the *Saṃhitā*: "Not the house..."

O lady with a moon-like face, one attains auspiciousness both in this world and the next through knowledge alone, even without giving gifts, performing fire-sacrifices (*homa*), and so forth. If a householder does not give gifts, nor offer oblations, nor perform worship according to the rules, he fails to do what ought to be done; yet, O beautiful woman, there is no authority for a celibate student (*brahmacārī*) to give such things. Who would disregard all the preceptors and their sons? Furthermore, in this degenerate age (*kaliyuga*), forest-dwellers lack the capacity [for ritual acts]; thus, for a wandering mendicant (*parivrāj*), there is liberation through knowledge alone, without the need for giving, fire-sacrifices, and the like.

One becomes liberated from all the demons of suffering; it cannot be otherwise. O lotus-faced one, both the wandering mendicant who is detached and the householder who is likewise detached sink into the Kumbhīpāka hell. Householders who possess merit and seek auspiciousness through auspicious means should perform worship with the necessary materials, give gifts of food, and offer honor. Even forest-dwellers and ascetics, if they were to do this daily, would not be able to turn back from saṃsāra due to the fault of violating the prescribed order; indeed, they would become fallen from their exalted state and partakers of misery.

Non-violence is the supreme dharma, and this is their path. Indeed, those various [merits] cannot be obtained except through non-violence; they are attained solely through the means of worship fashioned by meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*). For those engaged in yoga, external [rituals] are not praised; rather, they dwell having envisioned Rāma as the Self who is worthy of praise. Among them, there is no evil-doer, nor is anyone else such. "I am the one to be worshipped by Rāma with substances cultivated by his attendants, and therefore I am the servant of householders" — thus it is said.

Thus ends the first chapter of the *Śrīrāmārcanacandrikā*, composed by Ānandavana, disciple of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrīmān Mukundavana. The knowers of reality declare that reality to be non-dual knowledge, which is designated as Brahman, the Supreme Self (*Paramātman*), and the Blessed Lord (*Bhagavān*). Sages who do not conceal [this truth], being endowed with knowledge and dispassion, perceive the Self within themselves through devotion acquired from sacred scripture. Therefore, for men...

(p. 17b) "The perfection of that Dharma which consists of contentment with one's own caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*), according to the divisions [of scripture], is the pleasing of Hari. Therefore, with a single-minded focus, the Blessed Lord, the Master of the Sātvatas, should always be heard, glorified, meditated upon, and worshipped. Without the unmanifest Brahman as his witness, one shall not proceed to the Supreme Brahman without obstacle. For the group of six enemies is difficult to conquer; therefore, one should worship the Embodied Brahman (*mūrtabrahman*). Thus, without firmness in devotion, whatever practice of one’s own duty—such as the propitiation of other deities and so forth—may be performed, it would perish instantly; for that reason, from that very moment..."

Like one who possesses his own celestial mansion, being established in his own dharma, he should rise during the *brāhma-muhūrta* and meditate upon the Joy of the Raghus. The wise man should contemplate Him who is called the Savior (*tāraka*), the supreme auspiciousness, preceded by "Śrī," with "Jaya" in the middle, and ending twice with "Jaya. He should remember at dawn Rāma—the ornament of the Solar dynasty, known through the Vedāntas, the fearless one who assumed the guise of a king, accompanied by Vaidehī and Lakṣmaṇa, the delight of His own people, and Rāma for the pacification of the poison of the serpent of worldly existence. At dawn, I shall chant His deeds to destroy [all evil]. Rā... [The text ends here].

2. To that destroyer of Death (Kṛtānta), who was made the subduer of the ocean, who destroyed the bondage of worldly existence through the story of the binding of the ocean, and who thereafter delighted in the kingdom of Vibhīṣaṇa—[to him I bow]. 3. May that [Lord] grant me supreme devotion, whose action destroys the impurity of the Kali age and bestows protection; he who, while residing within as the Supreme Consciousness-Self of exquisite beauty, is directed by Rāma, who possesses an external body as a guru. 4. He who, with his mental faculties offered to Śrī Rāmacandra, recites these three verses at dawn, shall obtain longevity, prosperity, fame, and infinite happiness.

The King of Kośala—who, for the sake of his elder brother’s purpose, renounced his kingdom and wandered through the forest; who, by means of the two lotuses that were his beloved’s hands, straightened the path for the two heroic brothers, Hanumān and Lakṣmaṇa; who, terrified by the expansion of the earth brought about by the wrath of Śūrpaṇakhā over her disfigurement and separation from her lover, built a bridge across the ocean;

and who extinguished the forest fire of the demons—may he protect us! Thus, one should perform the recollection (smaraṇa) during the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā): facing north during the day, and facing south at night; wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (nivītī) while voiding urine.

(p. 18a) Regarding purification after voiding urine: outside, one should perform cleansing with water using one application of earth on the penis, five on the anus, ten on the left hand, and seven on both hands; for householders, this sequence is doubled and so forth, while for forest-dwellers and renunciants, it is half of that. This is the rule for voiding urine. Having performed the cleansing of the feet, one should then drink pure water three times, wipe the mouth twice, and touch the two nostrils with the thumb and forefinger; the pair of eyes with the thumb and ring finger; and the pair of ears with the little finger and thumb.

The procedure for sipping water (ācamana) is as follows: [one touches] the navel region with two fingers, the heart with the palm, and the head with all the fingers. Regarding the brushing of teeth: from the mantra beginning with "daṃtollekho vitastā bhavati parimitā āyuḥ," one should brush with a twig of the *kṣīri* (milk-exuding) trees or others in the morning—such as the *vaṭa*, *khadira*, *paśu*, *tāmra*, *arka*, or *bilva*. After eating, one should perform six mouth-rinses (*gaṇḍūṣa*) twice; however, on the *naṃdā* days, the *bhūta* days, the eighth lunar day (*aṣṭamī*), the full moon (*parvan*), and during the *jaya*, *arkapāta*, and *annādyāya vyūhadhvam somāṃ rā* [occasions], one should not use twigs, but rather use the ring finger (*doḥśinī*) and the other fingers [for rinsing].

"Born from the mouth of Brahmā, you destroy disease along with infamy and misfortune. This is the mantra for cleaning the teeth. Having thoroughly purified all [the cavities] and become pure, one should enter the seat;
on a seat such as the *svastika*, one should meditate upon Rāghava in his own form: "I am Rāma and none other; I am Brahman alone, not subject to sorrow;

I am of the nature of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*); I possess the nature of eternal liberation. With this contemplation, by the very command of the primordial God Śrīnātha Viṣṇu, who consists of the consciousness of the three worlds, [one should proceed].

"Having arisen from that state, I shall continue the journey through saṃsāra for the sake of what is dear to me. I know dharma, yet I have no inclination toward it; I know adharma, yet I have no aversion to it. Whatever I do, I do so as directed by the Lord who dwells within my heart. This is the procedure for the prayer. Having performed the rite according to the rules in a clean place, one should wear the auspicious sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) with the mantra "That which is the Brahmasūtra. Facing south, one should arrange the hair upwards; then, remembering the *Oṃkāra* and the *Gāyatrī*, one should tie it.

(p. 18b) Having taken washed garments, *darbha* grass, and likewise clay and sesame seeds, one should go to the water of a river or similar source and bathe according to one's own prescribed rules. If one performs daily (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites with unwashed clothing, one does not obtain that fruit; it becomes fruitless. With hands and feet washed and having sipped water (*ācamana*), one should, with a composed mind, make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "By his command, I shall perform this bath as an ancillary part of the worship of Rāma. The bath may be performed by immersion in a lake, pond, ocean, or river, or by applying ashes, cow-dung, or the dust of a bull. If there is misfortune, [it is performed] with [the aforementioned materials].

One should remember the Lord, whose form is the Mantra, the lotus-eyed one situated in the sky, who is the embodiment of the mantra; who resembles the rising sun, is four-armed Vāsudeva, bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, adorned with a crown and a forest garland; whose limbs are smeared with divine sandalwood paste, who has a beautiful smile and auspicious eyes; who is served by Nārada and others, and possesses shining, massive bracelets and tinkling bells. By means of the pure *bāpima* mantras alone, there shall be the attainment of the five [goals]. Having extracted the *piṇḍas*, one should avoid those born in rivers ending in *pura* and *payas*. Those located east of Siṃha and above Karkaṭa that have reached the ocean are undesirable on the shore. One should meditate on the Lord who resides in the sky, whose form is the mantra. [He is] Vāsudeva, resembling the rising sun, four-armed, bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, wearing a crown and a forest garland; his limbs are anointed with divine sandalwood paste, he has a beautiful smile and auspicious eyes; he is served by Nārada and others, and possesses shining, massive bracelets and tinkling bells.

One should contemplate his lotus-feet, which bear necklaces, armlets, and earrings, and jeweled anklets, marked with banners, umbrellas, and goads; one should receive the stream of water falling from those feet upon one’s own head, and as it enters through the *brahmarandhra*, one should wash one’s own body with it, thereby cleansing all impurity within the body. At that very moment, one becomes free from passion (*viraja*), like a crystal.

This is known as the excellent mantra-bath, performed more than a thousand times. Having performed this, one should then perform the Vedic bath and thereafter the hymn-bath, placing the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) upon the body and performing *prāṇāyāma*.

Having drawn forth the holy water from the orb of the sun with the *aṅkuśa-mudrā* while reciting the syllable *vaṃ*, one should bathe it with the *kavaca-mantra* and veil it. Having protected it, one should consecrate it with the root mantra eleven times (*rudra-saṃkhyayā*). Then, one should perform the casting of water with the *astra-mantra* twelve times (*arka-saṃkhyayā*). Submerging oneself therein, one should meditate upon Śrī Rāma while reciting the mantra according to one's capacity.
Emerging and forming the *kuṃbha-mudrā*, one should take the water from the Śālagrāma stone mixed with the fragrance of *tulasī*, whirl it three times in the conch, and cast it into oneself.

(Leaf 19a) He who, without drinking the water from a *śāligrāma* stone, should pour it upon his head, is declared a slayer of a Brahmin. Whatever holy places (*tīrtha*) exist on earth, they all reside in the ocean; and all those holy places along with the oceans reside at the right foot of a Brahmin. Then, in brief, he should offer libations (*tarpaṇa*) to the gods, humans, and ancestors. Having washed away the filth by carefully scrubbing the two thighs, he should diligently rinse his mouth (*ācamana*) and put on two clean garments, an undergarment and an upper robe, which are uncut, with their fringes intact, and white. Seated upon a seat, he should perform the ritual rinsing of the mouth according to the tradition of the Bahvṛcas.

One should have a seat made for the three [twice-born] that is smooth and shaped according to the requirements of the ritual; however, for others, one should have it made four-legged and square. The wise should avoid a seat made of clay from a cow-pen, or one that is broken, or one made of *pālāśa* or *pippala* wood, or one bound with iron, or one that is hollowed out like a bird's nest. One should not sit with the feet extended while performing giving (*dāna*), sipping water (*ācamana*), fire-offerings (*homa*), eating, worship of the deities, Vedic study (*svādhyāya*), or libations (*tarpaṇa*). One who sits with a foot placed upon the seat, or upon the knees or the shanks, or who wears a cloth wrapped around the legs, is said to be "sitting with extended feet" (*prauḍhapāda*). Thus ends the rule for bathing.

Having drunk [water] with the first three [names beginning with] Keśava, one should wash both hands with two [names]; likewise, one should wipe the lips with two [names] and perform the wiping upward (unmārjana) with two [names]. Having washed one hand with one [name], and likewise the feet with one, one should sprinkle the head with one [name]. Then, with the [names] beginning with Śaṅkarṣaṇa, one should touch the mouth, nose, eyes, ears, navel, chest, and arms. Having performed the sipping of water (ācamana) in this manner, one becomes Nārāyaṇa himself. [The names are: Keśava, Nārāyaṇa, Mādhava, Govinda, Viṣṇu, Madhusūdana, Trivikrama, Vāmana...

With these names—Śrīdhara, Hṛṣīkeśa, Padmanābha, Dāmodara, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Vāsudeva, Pradyumna, Aniruddha, Puruṣottama, Adhokṣaja, Nṛsiṃha, Acyuta, Janārdana, Upendra, Hari, Kṛṣṇa, Caturthī, and Namaḥ—one should perform the Vaiṣṇava recitation. One should meditate on Keśava at the forehead, Nārāyaṇa on the belly, and Mādhava on the heart. One should meditate on Govinda at the base of the throat; one should contemplate Viṣṇu pervading the right side of the belly; and one should contemplate Madhusūdana at the armpit on that same side.

On his shoulder is Trivikrama, and on the left side Vāmana; Śrīdhara is on the left arm, and Hṛṣīkeśa on the neck. On the other [shoulder] should be Padmanābha, and one should remember Hāṭakodara on the hump. With the water used for washing those [images], one should place [the name] "Vāsudeva" upon the head. On the right hand, the Brahmin should hold the Sudarśana discus; on the others, the lotus, the fish, the conch, the tortoise, and likewise the mace. One should bear the mace on the forehead, the bow and arrows on the head, Nandaka sword on the heart, and the conch and discus on the two arms. A Brahmin marked with the conch and discus who dies in a cremation ground [attains liberation].

"Nārada has declared that this [method] is the arrival at Prayāga; thus, having wrung out the cloth, one should thereafter commence the *saṃdhyā* rites. He who performs his bath otherwise shall find it fruitless. That fool who wrings out the triple-folded cloth—his bath becomes useless, as he wrings out the water [that represents the deity]. Having bowed to the Guru, whose nature is Rāma, one should then perform the Rāma-saṃdhyā. Having meditated upon Rāma and the mantra during the evening, morning, and midday *saṃdhyās*, [one should proceed]."

The knower of mantras should recite [the mantra] over the water, purifying it with the Astra-mantra and sprinkling it with the Kavaca-mantra. Having properly formed the water into a circle with the root of a *darbha* blade, he should invoke the holy ford (*tīrtha*) with the mudrās of invocation and so forth, and worship it. "O Sun, by the truth that the holy fords within the belly of the cosmic egg have been touched by your rays, grant me this divine ford. O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, Sarasvatī, Sindhu, and Kāverī—be present in these waters! Having thus invoked and worshipped according to the rules, he should [use] that [water].

Taking the water in his joined palms, he should recite the *mālā-mantra* properly; he should pour the water held in his right hand onto his left hand. Remembering the *mālā-mantra*, he should sprinkle the water flowing from that [left hand] upon his head. Having consecrated the remainder of that water with the ten-syllable mantra, he should drink it. Again, taking water in his joined palms, he should toss it upwards three times, saying: "Salutation to Rāma residing in the *maṇḍala*; I offer this [water]. Then, being self-restrained, he should recite the Gāyatrī, thinking: "I am Rāma," starting from his birth.

Whatever sin has been accumulated through ten [repetitions], one may purify it by a hundred, a thousand, or even more recitations. One should utter the words "Tad dhiyaḥ śarāthāya," followed by the word "vidmahe," then extract the word "sītā," and thereafter say "vallabhāya. Then one should say "dhīmahīti" and "notha rāmaśca pracodayāt. This is the Rāma-Gāyatrī, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon devotees. Its preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) consists of a recitation of four hundred thousand times; all other rites such as worship and so forth should be performed as previously described. Om, etc., the Gāyatrī of the Lineage bestows liberation itself.

O Sage, even through her, one attains mastery over illusion and the like, as well as fortune such as that of Lakṣmī; and when united with Madana, she deludes the entire earth. When Rāma is propitiated by her, he bestows all desired objects and grants satisfaction. Therefore, preceded by the recitation of the root mantra, one should satisfy Rāma with "Rāmaṃ tarpayāmi namaḥ. First, having satisfied the deities of the pedestal and so forth, one should then satisfy Sītā and the others in groups of four, followed by the [deities] beginning with Hṛdaya (the Heart). In the center of each, one should satisfy the descendant of Raghu (Rāma) with his name-mantras; thus there are two hundred and forty [offerings].

O Lord of Sages, he who praises and bows down to Rāma according to his capacity, performing this correctly every day at the three junctions of the day (sandhyā) according to the rules, that practitioner of mantra shall have accomplished his purpose; this is the truth, the absolute truth, and not otherwise. Having first uttered "Oṃ Haṃsaḥ," one should recite the Ajapā [Gāyatrī]: "So'ham. The Seer (ṛṣi) is Haṃsa, the metre (chanda) is the Imperishable (avyaya), and the Deity here is the Supreme Self (Paramātman). To the Sun-Self, the heart; to the Moon-Self, the head; to the Stainless One (Nirañjana), the tuft (śikhā); to the Effulgenceless One (Nirābhāsa), the armor (kavaca); and for the weapon (astra): "May the Subtle One without body impel me. The wise say that Heaven is His head.

They say that the sky is his head, the sun and moon are his eyes, the quarters are his ears, and the earth is his feet; he who is the inner self of all beings is to be meditated upon. With twenty-one thousand six hundred breaths, one should perform the recitation (*japa*), and at the end, one should dismiss [the deity] with the thought: "May Śrī Rāma be pleased. This is the Rāma-sandhyā. Having bowed to Rāma and to the elder gurus, holding kuśa grass, water, and flowers, and likewise having avoided heretics, one should enter the home while remembering tranquility (*śama*). The fire-oblation (*homa*) for the Sun should be performed before sunrise, and for Agni, it should be during the day or night.

(p. 20b) Then, with substances such as rice and so forth, which are not forbidden, one should perform the worship of the deity with the name-mantras, offering oblations once for each. One should give gifts according to one's ability to worthy recipients and others. Thus ends the rule for the duties of the first portion of the day. In the second part of the day, the twice-born should engage in the study of the Vedas, as well as Mīmāṃsā, Logic (Tarka), the treatises on Dharma, Artha, and so forth.
A wise man should look upon the eight auspicious objects: a cow, land, a Brāhmaṇa, water, gold, the sun, oil, and a king. Thus ends the rule for the duties of the second part of the day.

On the third day of the fortnight, having fasted and nourished his family, he should acquire wealth through work that is not contrary to place or scripture. He should live by *ṛta*, *amṛta*, *mṛta*, or *pramṛta*; never by *satyānṛta* or by his own improper livelihood (*asvavṛtti*). *Ṛta* is said to be what is gleaned (*uñcha*); *amṛta* is what is obtained unasked; *mṛta* is constant begging; and *pramṛta* is agriculture. *Satyānṛta* is trade, while service to others is called one's own lowly livelihood (*asvavṛtti*). Those who have declared service to be a livelihood have not spoken correctly. One should act according to one's own will.

Those lowest of the twice-born who, having sold their own conduct and not being true servants, live by staking their very lives for hire—having eaten the food of those evil-minded ones, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. Without regard for others, standing in two parts [of the day] while reciting mantras, one should act according to the command of the Lord; for He is the giver of all and the Sovereign of All. Thus ends the rule for the duties of the third part of the day. When the day is divided into eight parts, in the fourth part, the twice-born should perform the midday bath, as well as recitation and the worship of the deities, using clay and cow-dung... [and so forth].

Having gone to the water's edge with silken garments, kuśa grass seats, finger-rings, flowers, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), sesame seeds, forehead marks (*tilaka*), sacred circles (*maṇḍala*), sandalwood paste, and so forth, and having remembered the *aleha* and *samārṣika* [mantras], one should worship Him whose fame as the purifier of all holy places (*tīrtha*) is complete, using the excellent mantras prescribed in one’s own *gṛhya-sūtra*. Having bathed and performed the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyā*), one should offer libations (*tarpaṇa*) to the gods and others with white, variegated, and black sesame seeds.

Likewise, the practitioner (*mantrī*) should first perform the bath, twilight devotions, and libations for the Lord of the World (*Bhuvaneśa*). Then, having bowed to Rāma, he should dismiss Him. After that, having gone to the temple and performed the ritual placements (*nyāsa*), [he should proceed].

One should worship Hari and enter one's own beautiful Mandara mountain with a light heart; this is the duty for the fourth part of the day. Having returned home on the fifth day, at the fifth division of the day, one should wash one's feet, perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and offer the arghya water to the Sun outside.

Then, regarding the one who worships the deity and the materials for worship, [one should offer] that fruit; [reciting] "Obeisance to Rāma, the Self, who is everything including the vital breath and the intellect"—having bowed with this mantra, one should worship the deities of the doorway. That worship which is prescribed in the Agastya-saṃhitā is now extracted and set forth in its proper sequence so that it may be performed accordingly.

It is written as follows: *Oṃ namo rāmabhadrāya*, *gaṃ gaṇeśāya tasmai namaḥ*, *saṃ savitre*, *hauṃ śivāya*, *reṃ hnīṃ śrīparaśaktaye*, *dīṃ dīpanāthāya namaḥ*, *daṃ kṣetrapālāya namaḥ*. Having worshipped [these] with flowers, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), and other offerings, the wise man should first worship the six deities of the door of Śrī Rāma situated there in front. He should worship "Salutation to the Glory of the Door" (*dvāraśrī*) above, and then "to the Threshold" (*dehalī*) below that. Then, on the right and left branches of the beautiful door, he should worship Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, Gaṅgā, and Yamunā.

Preceded by *oṃ*, [one should worship]: *oṃ bhadrāya subhadrāya godāṃ kṛṣṇāṃ ca dakṣiṇe* (Oṃ, to Bhadra and Subhadra, to Godā and Kṛṣṇā, in the south); *oṃ candrāya pracaṇḍāya revāṃ tāpīṃ ca paścime* (Oṃ, to Candra and Pracaṇḍa, to Revā and Tāpī, in the west); *śaṅkhāya padmanidhaye vāṇīṃ vainyāṃ tathottare* (To Śaṅkha and Padmanidhi, and likewise to Vāṇī and Vainyā in the north). Having well worshipped these at the four gates, one should thereafter worship above the house with: "Salutation to the Lord of the House, to the House, and to the Family Deity. Then: "Salutation to the one with the arrow, the bow, and the *phaṭ*; salutation to Vināyaka, *phaṭ*. With these two [mantras], the flower placed within the bow and arrow should be removed; then, having invoked the removal of obstacles, one should strike with the heel.

One should practice [the preliminary rites] while touching the threshold; having entered first with the right foot, one should worship the remaining [deities], the Seat of Knowledge (Vidyāpīṭha), and offer salutations to Vāstu-puruṣa. This is the procedure for the worship of the door.

A wise person should avoid a seat made of stone, wood, earth, grass, or leaves, as it bestows miseries such as poverty and the like. One should prepare a seat made of a black antelope skin (kṛṣṇājina), a tiger skin, silk (kauśeya), hemp (venna), cloth, or a woolen blanket (kaṃbala). Having settled comfortably upon that soft seat, one should first begin the arrangement of the vessels (pātrāsādana). Having prepared [them]...

One should fill the flower-mat (*puṣpa-ḍālikā*) with various flowers, such as *tulasī*, lotus, and *jāti*, as well as many kinds of garlands. One should place a water-pot (*kalaśa*), filled with pure water from a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) and consecrated by oneself and others, to one's own left side in front [of the deity]. Other articles of worship should be set down right in front. This is the preparation (*āsādana*). Then, having placed around one's neck a rosary (*mālā*) fashioned from *tulasī* wood, or made of *rudrākṣa* beads, or carved into the forms of the conch, discus, mace, lotus, or sandals, one should begin the worship.

Having properly placed upon his head a garland of *bheṭ* flowers, a garland of *āmalaka*, a garland of *puṣkara*, and a *nirmālya* garland of *tulasī*, that best of the twice-born should mark his body with the *nirmālya* sandalwood paste using the deity’s names. Or, he may place the deity’s weapons upon his two arms using those very same names. Whether he be most sinful or sinless, or even all-knowing or unborn, he undoubtedly becomes qualified for this act of worship. Thus is the wearing of the garland; one should perform the purification of living beings by means of flowers, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and other substances.

One should perform the purification of the image by washing it, applying ointments, and so forth; then, with an undistracted mind, one should perform the purification of oneself and subsequently the purification of the ground. Having properly smeared the altar, one should cause a maṇḍala to be drawn there using powders of rice and blue, yellow, white, and black [pigments]. One should draw an eight-petaled lotus, surrounded by a square, with a six-cornered [figure] in the pericarp, and in the middle of the corners, enclosed by circles. Thus, the object of accomplishment (sādhya) is adorned with beautiful lines. Having worshipped this maṇḍala, one should place the seat of the Tārās...

And it was adorned on all sides with moonlight-colored banners and archways; here and there, on the walls, pillars, and platforms, even one who should make a mandala the size of an atom before the foremost descendant of Raghu, using clay, cow-dung, or minerals, enjoys infinite fruit. Thus ends the fourfold purification. [One should perform] two hand-gestures (*mudrās*) in the form of a lotus, a svastika, or the *bhadra* and so forth. For the mantra "pṛthivī tvayi," Merupṛṣṭha is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Sūktala is the meter (*chandas*), Kūrma is the deity (*devatā*), and its application (*viniyoga*) is in the installation of the seat (*āsana*).

O Earth, you are supported by Viṣṇu; O Goddess, you are supported by Viṣṇu. Therefore, support me, O auspicious one, and make this seat pure. *Bhur bhuvaḥ svaḥ kūrma-āya namaḥ* (Salutation to the Tortoise of the three worlds).

*Ādhāra-śaktaye namaḥ* (Salutation to the Support-Power). One should worship with: *Duṣṭa-vidrāvaṇāya nṛsiṃhāya* (To Nṛsiṃha, the dispeller of the wicked). "May all beings and Piśācas depart in every direction. Without the opposition of anyone, I shall commence the Brahma-karma.
Having struck the ground three times with his heel while reciting this mantra, the wise knower of mantras, having driven away the hosts of spirits, should sit upon the seat. *Oṃ rastrāya phaṭ*.

Having performed the four types of hand-clapping and other gestures as prescribed, and having offered a continuous stream of water to the Guru, the wise practitioner should worship Vināyaka on the seat, Sarasvatī on the left side, and Durgā along with the Guru on the right side. Then, beginning from the beginning of the alphabet (A), he should bow to the lineage of Gurus:

"Salutations to Ananta; salutations to Brahmā; salutations to Vasiṣṭha; salutations to Śakti; salutations to Parāśara; then salutations to the eternal one; salutations thereafter to the son of Satyavatī (Vyāsa); and [salutations] to the feet of the Lord of Yogīs."

I bow to the venerable Govinda-pāda, whose nature is consciousness and who has Garuḍa as his feet; to the illustrious Śrī Śaṅkarācārya, the universal form (Viśvarūpa), the Lord of the Gods (Sureśvara); to Mādhava, known as Vāsudeva, the performer of all sacrifices; likewise to Gaṅgādhara, Nāgadeva, and the scholar Śrī Bhaṭṭācārya;
to those called Paramānanda-rāja and those named Dogalīśa; to Nimbāditya, the great Siddha, the lord who perceives other paths; and to the illustrious...

I bow to the kings Viṣṇusvāmin and others who propagated devotion to Viṣṇu, and to the lords and kings who were the disciples of Viṣṇusvāmin. Homage to the gurus and to the sandals of the gurus; homage to the Supreme and to the sandals of the Supreme; homage to the sandals of Ācārya Siddheśvara; homage to the sandals of the Lord of Sītā. Thus is the salutation to the gurus. Then, having paid obeisance to the Deity, one should again perform the three *tālas* (claps). Reciting "Oṃ rastraḥ phaṭ," one should brandish the right hand while remembering Kāla, thinking: "I shall perform [this rite] for the pleasure of Śrī Rāma."

(p. 22b) Having thus performed the visualization (*saṃkalpa*) for worship, one should then withdraw Māyā from the locations of the nyāsa in reverse order. One should dissolve *lakāra* into *aukāra*, *hakāra* into *sakāra*, and *malaya* into *sakāra*. Having thus diligently produced the dissolution of *aparyya-laṃ*, one should join [the breath] with the syllable *oṃ* at the thousand-petaled lotus in the *brahmarandhra*. This is the withdrawal of the Mātṛkā. Then, one should contemplate that very state within the three locations: consisting of light, unstruck (*anāhata*), and having the nature of truth, knowledge, and bliss; surrounded by the fire of the Self.

Having performed the protection (*kāraṃtrāṇa*) against *bhūtas*, *pretas*, and *piśācas*, immediately thereafter, the practitioner of mantra (*mantrī*), for the sake of removing fear and obstacles, should scatter water, flowers, and unbroken rice grains consecrated with the fire-seed syllable (*vahni-bīja*) and the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*). The wise should contemplate the individual soul (*jīva*), which is the size of the tip of a needle, as residing in the heart-lotus—the lotus born from the bulb of Brahman (*brahmakaṇḍa*), having knowledge as its stalk, the eight petals of sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) as its leaves, and detachment (*vairāgya*) as its pericarp. By means of that [soul], one should join the Supreme Self situated at the end of the twelve [finger-breadths] using the *haṃsa* mantra; then, according to the prescribed rule, one should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*).

One should perform the installation of the *jīva* (life-principle) as follows: from the feet upward to the lotus of the navel, one should contemplate the yellow-colored Brahmā, whose form is square and possesses five qualities; [reciting] *glauṃ hrāṃ hraḥ phaṭ*, [one installs] the Earth element (*bhū*) in the water [element], which is white, possesses the head-moon, belongs to Viṣṇu, and consists of taste, form, touch, and sound; [reciting] *hrīṃ hraḥ phaṭ*, [one installs] the Water element (*jala*) from the navel to the heart, which belongs to Pradyumna, is triangular, svastika-shaped, and reddish-brown, consisting of fire-form, touch, and sound; [reciting] *raṃ hnaṃ hnaḥ phaṭ*, [one installs] the Air element (*samīraṇa*) from the heart to the eyebrows, which belongs to Vāyu, is circular, white, and consists of wind-touch and sound. *Note: The term "rasa" (taste) here refers to the Earth element, while "vṛtta" (circular) and "śāṅkha" (conch-like/white) refer to the Air element.*

Having uttered "ṇaṃ dhūmraṃ yaṃ hre hvaḥ phaṭ," one should withdraw Vāsudeva, who is sound (*śabda*) and space (*kha*), from the center of the brows up to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*). Then, with "haṃ hnauṃ hnaḥ phaṭ," one should dissolve that Great Principle (*mahattattva*) into the Unmanifest Nature (*prakṛti*), and that [Nature] into the Supreme Brahman known as Rāmacandra. This is the withdrawal of the elements (*bhūtasaṃhāra*). The purification of the elements which constitute the form of the body, through contact with the Unmanifest Brahman, is considered to be this "Purification of the Elements" (*bhūtaśuddhi*). Then, having restrained the Prāṇa and Apāna breaths, [one should meditate on] that root ignorance, as well as the sin and the suffering of birth and so forth, which bestow misery.

One should contemplate his form as having the five limbs of great sins (*mahāpātaka*), being the refuge of [ordinary] sins, with the minor sins (*upapātaka*) as its body-hair, black, cruel, and extremely terrifying. At the navel, in a circle that is six-cornered, black, and joined with a drop (*bindu*), filled with the wind [seed-syllable] *ya* and ending with *oṃ yama oṃ*, one should dry [the body]. In the heart, within a red radiance shaped like a Svastika emerging from a triangle, [one should place] the seed-syllable *ra*—filled with fire—in the wind [element], [reciting] *oṃ ramoṃ*. Then, [reciting] *oṃ baṃ moṃ*, which is white and situated on the lotus of the head, shining like a thousand moons, one should dissolve that seed-syllable and cause it to be flooded with well-refined nectar; thus one should illuminate it. Thus [ends the section].

Then, having performed the dissolution of the forest-like seed-syllables and the immersion [of the universe] into the center, one should meditate upon the four thousand-petaled lotus with the mantra "Oṃ Rāma Hūṃ. Then, for the sake of attaining worship, one should again contemplate one's own body with devotion as pure, bestowing auspiciousness, and unified with the self-mantra while meditating. Through the subtle light arising from the *mūlādhāra* by way of the *suṣumṇā* path, one should place the breath under restraint at the crown of the head with the mantra "Oṃ Hūṃ Phaṭ. Thus, from the undivided Brahman comes Rāma, then the Impeller (*Puruṣa*), then Nature (*Prakṛti*), then Great Nature (*Mahāprakṛti*), and then I, who am composed of the three qualities (*Triguṇā*).

From this very Self, space was produced; from space, air; from air, fire; from fire, water; from water, earth; from earth, plants; from plants, food; from food, semen; from semen, the person (*puruṣa*). This very person consists of the essence of food (*annarasamaya*). One should bring that essence under control by means of the seed-syllable *glauṃ*. By means of the seed-syllables *oṃ*, *haṃ*, and *om*, the formation of its limbs occurs. Having meditated upon that very same [essence] as the perfected speech at the end of the mantra *so'haṃ* through the aperture of Brahma (*brahmarandhra*), [one should place] the life-force (*jīva*) there.

One should place the bark-garment upon the heart, having brought the hands into proximity. With the *Tāra* (Oṃ) and the *Prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra: "For the *Prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are the seers (*ṛṣayaḥ*);

the *Ṛg*, *Yajus*, and *Sāman* are the meters (*chandāṃsi*); or rather, the *Atichandas* is the meter; the deity is the one named Prāṇa, whose body consists of action (*kriyāmayavapuḥ*); the application (*viniyoga*) is for the purpose of the installation of the vital breaths. Oṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ aṃ—salutation to the heart (*hṛdayāya namaḥ*), which is the self of earth, water, fire, air, and ether. Oṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ īṃ—*svāhā* to the head (*śirase svāhā*), which is the self of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell.

(Leaf 23b) Oṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ ūṃ! To the self of the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose: Ūṃ! To the crest-lock (śikhā), vaṣaṭ! Oṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ eṃ! To the self of speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals: Aiṃ! To the armor (kavaca), vaṣaṭ! Oṃ paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ maṃ oṃ! To the self of speaking, grasping, moving, excreting, and experiencing bliss: Auṃ! To the three eyes (netratraya), vauṣaṭ! Oṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ laṃ kṣaṃ aṃ! To the self of mind, intellect, ego, and consciousness: Aṃḥ! To the weapon (astra), phaṭ! Oṃ Āṃ! From the navel downwards. Oṃ Hno! From the heart up to the navel. Oṃ Kroṃ! From the head down to the heart. Then: [The following mantras].

Oṃ yaṃ, obeisance to the self of the skin, at the heart; Oṃ raṃ, obeisance to the self of the blood, at the base of the arms; Oṃ laṃ, obeisance to the self of the flesh, at the crown of the head; Oṃ vaṃ, obeisance to the self of the marrow, at the two armpits; Oṃ śaṃ, obeisance to the self of the bones, from the heart to the pair of shanks; Oṃ ṣaṃ, obeisance to the self of the marrow, at the pair of feet; Oṃ saṃ, obeisance to the self of the semen, at the abdomen;

Oṃ prāṃ, obeisance to the self of the vital breath, at the mouth; Oṃ kṣaṃ, obeisance to the self of the individual soul—having performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) in this manner, one should meditate upon the deity as red.

May the Supreme Vital Power (Prāṇaśakti), who is the color of the rising sun, bestow happiness; she who is mounted upon a lotus in a lake of radiant oceans arising from the Bodhisattva, who holds in her lotus-hands the noose, the bow, the trident, the goad, and the five arrows, whose cheeks are adorned with earrings, who possesses three eyes, and whose yellow garments shine brilliantly. This is the visualization (*dhyāna*). *Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ haṃsaḥ samastaprāṇā iha prāṇā iha prāṇāḥ. Again, [I] bring that very same one back as the life-force (*jīva*).*

Having uttered "mamajīva" (my life-force) as before, and likewise having uttered "mamasarvendriyāṇi" (my all the senses), and again having uttered "mama vāṅ-manas-tvak-cakṣu-jihvā-śrotra-ghrāṇyaḥ sarve prāṇā iha yāntu svastaye suciraṃ sukhena tiṣṭhantu svāhā" (may my speech, mind, skin, eyes, tongue, ears, and nose, and all my vital breaths come here for my well-being; may they remain for a very long time in happiness, svāhā)—this is the mantra. Then, for the sake of accomplishing the sixteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) beginning with birth, one should perform sixteen repetitions of the *praṇava* (OM) and meditate upon the Supreme Power (*Śakti*). This is the re-generation of the body. "Speech is measured in four steps... [and so forth].
"Those wise ones who know do not utter that which is hidden in the cave; they speak only the fourth part of speech, which is human. Thus ends the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*).

Without the purification of the elements, all rites such as recitation (*japa*), fire-offerings (*homa*), and worship, even if performed in every way, become fruitless. Since the letters of the alphabet (*mātṛkā*) have arisen from the Self, which is one's own nature, and because they are non-different from it, the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of them for the sake of one’s own purpose is proclaimed. They say that without *nyāsa*, there is no victory [in spiritual practice].

The fruit is silent and demoniac; indeed, through the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), one becomes Rāma himself. Having become Rāma, one should mutter "Raghūṃ. The creation (*utpatti*) [of the hands] occurs from the left thumb to the right hand;

the withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) is the reverse of that. The bestowal of stability (*sthiti*) begins from the little finger. In the body as well, the one called creation extends from the head to the feet; the withdrawal is the other way around.

For one residing in a house, the placement of stability goes from the head to the feet; for a forest-dweller, it is the withdrawal; for a celibate student (*brahmacārin*), it is creation; and for a woman or a *śūdra*, it is likewise.

Thus ends the determination of the placement (*nyāsa*). One should fill [the breath] through the *iḍā* [left nostril] by means of the consonants and vowels; one should retain it with the *ka* and other [consonant] letters, and then exhale again through the *piṅgalā* [right nostril].

In the same manner, there should be filling, retention, and exhalation of the air through the *iḍā*, and then again through both [nostrils] for the triad of filling and so forth. Having thus performed the three *prāṇāyāmas*, one should begin the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*). With the letters beginning with *a* and ending with *kṣa*, [one should perform the placement] from the soles of the feet to the top of the head. Thus ends the *prāṇāyāma*. For this venerable *Mātṛkā-mantra*, Brahmā is the seer (*ṛṣi*), and the Goddess is the deity...

The Ṛṣi is R̥ṣideva Gāyatrī, the metre is Gāyatrī, the deity is Śrīmātṛkā-Sarasvatī, the seed-syllables (bījas) are the consonants, the power (śakti) is the collection of vowels, and the application ( viniyoga) is for the purpose of the limbs of the Śrī Rāma mantra being practiced. Having thus recited the Ṛṣi, metre, deity, seed-syllable, and power, one should perform the placement (nyāsa) on the head, face, heart, private parts, and feet in that order. This is the Mātṛkā-Ṛṣyādi-nyāsa. One should place each vowel individually upon the lines of the fingers and hands, and one should also place the Praṇava (Oṃ) on the palms and the backs of the hands.

*Pṛ0 24ba)* Oṃ aṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ āṃ aṃ *namaḥ* to both thumbs; Oṃ iṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ ī *namaḥ* to both index fingers; Oṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ ūṃ *namaḥ* to both middle fingers; Oṃ eṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ aiṃ *namaḥ* to both ring fingers; Oṃ paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ maṃ auṃ *namaḥ* to both little fingers; Oṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ l̥ kṣaṃ aḥ *namaḥ* to both palms and backs of the hands.

These very [syllables] are to be applied to the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*): *namaḥ* to the heart and so forth, *svāhā* to the head, *vaṣaṭ* to the crest-lock (*śikhā*), *huṃ* to the armor (*kavaca*). *Ne*... [text truncated].

With the mantra sequence *Tattvāya Vaṣaṭ* and *Astrāya Phaṭ*, one should meditate upon her whose face, arms, feet, flanks, and chest are adorned with the fifty letters of the pure Mātṛkā; who possesses a radiant matted lock and a digit of the moon; who is as white as the moon’s orb; whose hands hold a rosary, a water-pot, a lotus, and display the gesture of granting boons; who is ruddy-hued, seated upon a lotus, and whose beautiful form is graced by breasts that are neither too fleshy nor too coarse, yet heavy and marked by the lines of age; to her I bow. This is the meditation on the pure Mātṛkā. Now follows the internal placement (*antarmātṛkā-nyāsa*) of the throat, heart, and navel...

In the secret places—the two feet, the space between the eyebrows, and the lotuses of sixteen, twelve, ten, six, four, and two petals—the arrangement of the fifty letters occurs according to the sequence of the number of petals.

One should place each single letter at the end of each petal, joined with the vowel *i*. This is the internal placement of the Mātṛkā. Having thus placed [the letters] internally, one should then place them externally with the mind: on the head, the face, the circle of the forehead, the two eyes, the pair of ears, then the nose, the two cheeks, as well as the upper and lower lips, and the upper and lower rows of teeth.

One should place the sixteen vowels on the face and the crown of the head; the two *ka*-groups on the two arms; and the five *sandhis* (semivowels) on the joints of the limbs. Likewise, one should place the two *ṭa*-groups and the two *ta*-groups on the joints and tips of the feet. One should place the *pa*-group on the pair of sides, and *laṃ* on the back, the navel, and the belly. One should apply the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*) over the heart, the roots of the arms, the hips, the armpits, and the pair of heart-regions starting from the beginning of the letter *ka*. Furthermore, one should apply it to the abdomen and the bowing of the body. The placement of the fifty letters is thus prescribed in sequence, either with *oṃ* at the beginning and end, or with *namaḥ* at the end, or with the *bindu*, or even devoid of the *bindu*. This is the *Kevalamātṛkā* (the solitary alphabet).

(p. 25a) Next is the *nyāsa* with the *bindu*. As before, the *ṛṣi* and the *chandas* are the same. The limbs of the goddess Saṃhāra-Śāradā are [assigned] with the vowels joined by the *bindu*. One should bow to Varṇeśvarī, who holds in her hands a rosary of crystal, a deer, a lofty trident, and the *vidyā*; who has three eyes; whose head is adorned with the crescent moon; who is reddish in hue; who rests upon a lotus; and who is bent by the weight of her breasts. This is the meditation (*dhyāna*) on the *Mātṛkā* with the *bindu*. One should perform the *nyāsa* of the *Mātṛkā* joined with the *bindu* in forward order (*anuloma*). This is the *nyāsa* of the *Mātṛkā* with the *bindu*. Then, one should again assign the *kalās* of the *Mātṛkā* to these aforementioned locations.

One should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the syllables of the Kalās. Prajāpati is the seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is the meter (chandaḥ), and Kalāsarasvatī is the deity (devatā). The application (viniyoga) is for the attainment of desired goals. Oṃ Āṃ, salutation to the heart; Iṃ, svāhā to the head; Uṃ Ūṃ, vaṣaṭ to the tuft of hair (śikhā); Eṃ Aiṃ, huṃ to the armor (kavaca); Oṃ Auṃ, vauṣaṭ to the three eyes; Aṃ Aḥ, phaṭ to the weapon (astra). This is the six-limbed ritual of the Kalās. [She holds] in her hands a lotus, a discus, a bowstring, a deer, a book, a rosary of letters, a chisel, a trident, a skull-cup, a conch, and a shining golden pitcher.

I bow to that Bhāratī, who carries five colors—resembling pearls, lightning, clouds, crystal, and fresh *japā* flowers—through her three eyes; she is bent by her breasts and resembles the moon atop a water-jar.

Thus is the meditation (*dhyāna*) on Kulādevī. Oṃ Aṃ, salutation to Nivṛtti. Oṃ Āṃ, salutation to Pratiṣṭhā. Oṃ Ī, salutation to Vidyā. Iṃ, salutation to Īśānā. Oṃ Īṃ, salutation to Dīpikā. Ūṃ, salutation to Dīpikā. Ṛṃ, salutation to Recakā. Ṝṃ, salutation to Sūcikā. Ḷṃ, salutation to Parā. Ḹṃ, salutation to Atisūkṣmā. Eṃ, salutation to Mṛḍā. Aiṃ, salutation to Jñānā. Auṃ... [and so forth].

To Mṛtāyai: Oṃ Āpyānyai, Aṃ Vyāpinyai, Aḥ Vyomarūpāyai. Kaṃ Sṛṣṭyai, Khaṃ Ṛddhyai, Gaṃ Smṛtyai, Ghaṃ Medhāyai, Ṅaṃ Kāntyai, Caṃ Lakṣmyai, Chaṃ Iṣṭyai, Jaṃ Sthirāyai, Jhaṃ Kṣityai, Ñaṃ Siddhyai, Ṭaṃ Jarāyai, Ṭhaṃ Pālivyai, Ḍaṃ Śāntyai, Ḍhaṃ Aiśvaryāyai, Ṇaṃ Kṛtyai, Taṃ Kāmikāyai, Thaṃ Varadāyai, Daṃ Hlādinyai, Dhaṃ Prītyai, Naṃ Dīrghāyai, Paṃ Tīkṣṇāyai, Phaṃ Raudrāyai, Vaṃ Bhayāyai, Bhaṃ Nidrāyai, Maṃ Tandrāyai, Yaṃ Kṣāyai, Raṃ Krodhyai.
*Pṛ0 25ba)* The placement of the fifty *kalās* (phonemes): *nyaṃ* to Ulkā, *kriṃ* to Mṛtyu, *yaṃ* to Pītā, *vaṃ* to Śvetā, *eṃ* to Aruṇā, *laṃ* to Asitā, *kṣaṃ* to Anantā.

Then, in the place of the vowels (*svara-sthāna*), [the following are placed]: *oṃ* to Amṛtā, *āṃ* to Ānandā, *iṃ* to Pūṣā, *īṃ* to Tuṣṭi, *uṃ* to Puṣṭi, *ūṃ* to Rati, *ṛṃ* to Dhṛti, *ṝṃ* to Śaśinī, *ḷṃ* to Candrikā, *ḹṃ* to Kānti, *eṃ* to Jyotsnā, *aiṃ* to Śrī, *oṃ* to Prīti, *auṃ* to Aṅgadā, *aṃ* to Pūrṇā, and *aḥ* to Pūrṇāmṛtā. Thus ends [the sequence].

These [syllables] are to be placed: *ṣṭvaṃ* to Tāpinī; *kaṃ vaṃ* to Tāpinī; *gaṃ phaṃ* to Dhūmrā; *ghaṃ paṃ* to Marīci; *ṅaṃ naṃ* to Tālinī; *caṃ bhaṃ* to Ruci; *chaṃ daṃ* to Suṣumṇā; *jaṃ thaṃ* to Bhogadā; *jhaṃ taṃ* to Viśvā; *ñaṃ ṇaṃ* to Bodhinī; *ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ* to Dhāriṇī; *ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ* to Kṣamā; *maṃ yaṃ* to Dhūmrārcis; *raṃ ūṃ* to Ūṣmā; *laṃ jvaṃ* to Jvālinī;
*vaṃ jvāṃ* to Jvālāmālinī; *śaṃ viṃ* to Visphuliṅginī; *ṣaṃ suṃ* to Suśrī; *saṃ rūṃ* to Rūpā; *haṃ kaṃ* to Kapilā. These [are to be placed] at the joints of the pair of hands and feet.

One should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the thirty-eight *kalās*: "Oṃ *chaṃ* obeisance to Havyavāha" on the head; "Oṃ *kṣaṃ* obeisance to Kavyavāha" as the pervasive (*vyāpaka*). This is the placement of the thirty-eight *kalās*.

Then, one should diligently perform the placement of the deities Keśava and the others, along with their powers (*śakti*), by encasing the letters [of the alphabet] beginning with Māyā, following the sequence starting from the head. To illustrate: for the Keśavādi-Mātṛkā-nyāsa, Nārāyaṇa is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Gāyatrī is the meter (*chandaḥ*), Lakṛṣmī-Nārāyaṇa is the deity (*devatā*), the consonants (*hal*) are the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and the collection of vowels (*svara*) is the power (*śakti*).

The application for the desired purpose: *Oṃ śrīṃ oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya haṃsaḥ so'ham aṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ āṃ oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ so'ham oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya kruddholkāya svāhā āṃ devyai*—this is for the heart (*hṛdayam*). *Oṃ śrīṃ oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya haṃsaḥ so'ham iṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ īṃ oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ so'ham oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya maholkāya svāhā śrīṃ padminyai namaḥ*—this is for the head (*śiras*). *Oṃ śrīṃ oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya haṃsaḥ...* [continues].

(Leaf 26a) So'ham-uṃ-ṭaṃ-ṭhaṃ-ḍaṃ-ḍhaṃ-ṇaṃ-ūṃ-oṃ-hnīṃ-haṃsaḥ-so'ham-oṃ-namo nārāyaṇāya vīrolkāya svāhā | Aṃ viṣṇupatnyai namaḥ | This is the *śikhā* (topknot). Oṃ śrīṃ oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya haṃsaḥ so'ham-eṃ-taṃ-thaṃ-daṃ-dhaṃ-naṃ-seṃ-oṃ-hnīṃ-haṃsaḥ-mohaṃ-oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya dyūlkāya svāhā | Śraiṃ varadāyai | This is the *kavaca* (armor). Oṃ śrīṃ oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya haṃsaḥ so'ham-oṃ-paṃ-phaṃ-baṃ-bhaṃ-maṃ-auṃ-oṃ-hnīṃ-haṃsaḥ-so'ham-oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya...

*Sahasrolkāya svāhā*. *Śrauṃ* to her whose form is the lotus—this is the *netra* (eye-mantra). *Oṃ śrīṃ oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya haṃsaḥ so'haṃ aṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ laṃ kṣaṃ aḥ oṃ hnīṃ haṃsaḥ so'haṃ oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya anaṃtolkāya svāhā śraḥ śūlinyai namaḥ*—this is the *astra* (weapon-mantra). Thus are the *Keśavādi-mātṛkā-ṣaḍaṅga* (the six-limbed ritual application of the alphabet beginning with Keśava). [She is] Lakṣmī, who shines with the splendor of a lightning-flash and a mirror, her hands adorned with a lotus, a mirror, a jar of nectar, a lotus, a *kaumodakī* mace, a sword, and the *sudarśana* discus.
The meditation on the Mātṛkā-mantras beginning with Keśava, whose nature is Nārāyaṇa, who is indivisible and the primordial form: Oṃ hnīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ aṃ klīṃ śrīṃ hnīṃ, obeisance to Keśava and Kīrti.

This is the *saṃpuṭa* (enclosure) for all [mantras]: Āṃ to Nārāyaṇa, for Kānti; Īṃ to Sādhu, for Tuṣṭi; Īṃ to Govinda, for Puṣṭi; Uṃ to Viṣṇu, for Dhṛti; Ūṃ to Madhusūdana, for Kṣānti; Ṛṃ to Trivikrama, for Kriyā; Ṝṃ to Vāmana, for Dayā; Ḷṃ to Śrīdhara, for Medhā; Ḹṃ to Hṛṣīkeśa, for Harṣā; Eṃ to Padmanābha, for Śraddhā; Aiṃ to Dāmodara, for Lajjā; Oṃ to Vāsudeva, for Lakṣmī; Auṃ to Saṃkarṣaṇa, for Sarasvatī; Aṃ to Pradyumna, for Prīti; Aḥ to Aniruddha...

*Tyai* to Kañcukin (the one with the armor), *Jayāyai*; *Kham* to Khaḍgin (the sword-bearer), *Durgāyai*; *Gam* to Śāṅgin (the bow-bearer), *Prabhāyai*; *Gham* to Khaḍgine (the sword-bearer), *Satyāyai*; *Ṅam* to Śaṅkhine (the conch-bearer), *Caṇḍāyai*; *Cam* to Haline (the plough-bearer), *Vāṇyai*; *Cham* to Muśaline (the mace-bearer), *Vilāsinyai*; *Jam* to Śūline (the trident-bearer), *Vijayāyai*; *Jham* to Pāśine (the noose-bearer), *Virajāyai*; *Ñam* to Aṅkuśine (the goad-bearer), *Viśvāyai*; *Ṭam* to Mukundāya, *Vimadāyai*; *Ṭham* to Nandajāya, *Sunandāyai*; *Ṅam* to Nandine, *Smṛtyai*; *Ḍham* to Narāya, *Ṛddhyai*; *Ṇam* to Narakaghne, *Samṛddhyai*; *Tam* to Haraye, *Śuddhyai*; *Tham* to Kṛṣṇāya, *Buddhyai*; *Dam* to Satyāya.

Bhuktyai (for enjoyment) to Aṃśumat (the Sun), Tāyai (to her); Atyai (for the immortal) to Naṃśūri (the Moon), Kṣamāyai (for patience); Paṃ (to the Earth) to Surāya (the Lord of the Gods), Ramāyai (to Lakṣmī); Phaṃ (to Janārdana) to Umāyai (Umā); Vaṃ (to Bhūdharāya, the Mountain-Bearer) to Kledinyai (the Moistening One); Bhaṃ (to Viśvamūrtaye, the Universal Form) to Kinnāyai (Kinnā); Maṃ (to Vaikuṇṭhāya) to Vasudāyai (Vasudā); Yaṃ (to Puruṣottama, the Supreme Person) as the self of the skin, to Vasudhāyai (Earth); Raṃ (to Valine, Bali) as the self of the blood, to Parāyai (Parā); Laṃ (to Balānujāya, Kṛṣṇa) as the self of the flesh, to Parāyaṇāyai (the Ultimate Refuge); Vaṃ (to Valāya, Indra) as the self of the fat, to Sūkṣmāyai (Sūkṣmā); Śaṃ (to Vṛṣaghnāya, Indra) as the self of the bone, to Saṃdhyāyai (Saṃdhyā); Ṣaṃ (to Vṛṣāya, Indra) as the self of the marrow, to Prajñāyai (Wisdom); Saṃ (to Śukrātmane, the Self of Semen).

To Haṃsāya-prabhā, to Haṃ-ānātman-varāha, to Niśā; to Kṣaṃ-kriyāśaktyātman-vimalā-moghā. Oṃ hnīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ kṣaṃ klīṃ śrīṃ hnīṃ, salutation to Paramātman-nṛsiṃha and Vidyutā. Merely by this Nyāsa of Keśava and the others, it bestows the state of Acyuta upon embodied beings; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt. Thus ends the Keśavādi-Mātṛkā-Nyāsa. One should place the syllables of the Mātṛkā beginning with Vāk, Māyā, and so on, along with the Ṛśaktis and the Śrīkaṇṭhas and Ādityas, in the locations of the body.

Regarding the *Śrīkaṇṭhādi-nyāsa*: Ambarīṣa is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (*chandas*), Ardhanārīśvara is the deity (*devatā*), the consonants are the seeds (*bījas*), and the vowels are the powers (*śaktis*). Its application (*viniyoga*) is for the sake of knowledge and wisdom. *Aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ aṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ āṃ*—salutation to the two thumbs (*aṅguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ*). *Aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ iṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ īṃ*—salutation to the two index fingers (*tarjanībhyāṃ namaḥ*). *Aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ uṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ ūṃ*—salutation to the two middle fingers (*madhyamābhyāṃ namaḥ*). *Aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ eṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ aiṃ*—salutation to the two ring fingers (*anāmikābhyāṃ namaḥ*). *Aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ oṃ paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ maṃ auṃ*—[salutation to the two little fingers]... *kani...* [The text ends here].

*Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ aṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ laṃ kaṃ aḥ namaḥ* to the palms and backs of both hands. With these very [syllables], perform the *nyāsa* on the heart and other limbs. Having meditated upon the Lord (*Īśa*), who is like vermilion and gold in His two halves, the Ardhanārīśvara, adorned with the daughter of the mountain (Pārvatī) and the daughter of Hari (Lakṣmī), bearing the ornaments and marks of Hari, and holding in His eight hands the noose, the gesture of fearlessness, the rosary, and the discus—one should perform the *nyāsa* for the attainment of all desired objects of the self. *Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ aṃ śrīṃ namaḥ* to Śrīkaṇṭheśa and Pūrṇodarī; thus [one places them] on the head. 3. *Oṃ āṃ namaḥ* to Ananteśa and Virajā; [thus one places them] on the face.

One should assign [the mantras] to the locations beginning with Vṛtti: "Iṃ, obeisance to Sūkṣma and Śaśālmalī"—thus everywhere. "Īṃ, obeisance to Trimūrti and Lolākṣī. "Uṃ, obeisance to Amareśvara and Vartulākṣī. "Ūṃ, obeisance to Arghīśa and Dīrghaghoṇā. "Ṛṃ, obeisance to Bhārabhūtīśa and Dīrghamukhī. "Ṝṃ, obeisance to Atithīśa and Gomukhī. "Ḷṃ, obeisance to Sthāṇvīśa and Dīrghajihvā. "Ḹṃ, obeisance to Hareśa and Kuṇḍodarī. "Eṃ, obeisance to Jhaṭīśa and Urdhvakeśī."
Aiṃ, salutation to Aiṃbhautikeśa and Vikṛtamukhī. 3. Oṃ, salutation to Sadyojāteśa and Jvālāmukhī. 3. Auṃ, salutation to Anugraheśa and Ulkāmukhī.

Aṃ, salutation to Akrūreśa and Śrīmukhī. 3. Aḥ, salutation to Mahāśeneśa and Vidyāmukhī. 3. Kaṃ, salutation to Krodhīśa and Mahākālī. Khaṃ, salutation to Caṇḍeśa and Sarasvatī. 3. Gaṃ, salutation to Pañcāntakeśa and Gaurī. 3. Ghaṃ, salutation to Śivottameśa and Trailokyavidyā. Ṅaṃ, salutation to Ekarudreśa and Maṃtraśakti.

*ktibhyāṃ namaḥ* 3. *caṃ kūrmeśātmaśaktibhyāṃ namaḥ*. *chaṃ ekanetreśamātṛkābhyāṃ namaḥ*. *jaṃ caturānaneśalaṃbodarībhyāṃ namaḥ* 3. *jhaṃ ajeśadrāviṇībhyāṃ namaḥ*. *ñaṃ sarveśanāgarībhyāṃ namaḥ* 3. *ṭaṃ someśvareśakhecarībhyāṃ namaḥ* 3. *ṭhaṃ lāṅgalīśamañjīrībhyāṃ namaḥ* 3. *ḍaṃ dāhakeśarūpiṇībhyāṃ namaḥ* 3. *ḍhaṃ arddhanārīśvareśavairiṇībhyāṃ namaḥ* 3. *ṇaṃ umākānteśavṛkodarī*.

Bhyāṃ namaḥ 3. To the couple Āṣāḍhīśa and Pūtanī, obeisance. Thaṃ namaḥ 3. To the couple Daṇḍīśa and Bhadrakālī, obeisance. Daṃ namaḥ 3. To the couple Atrīśa and Yoginī, obeisance. Dhaṃ namaḥ 3. To the couple Mīneśa and Śaṅkhinī, obeisance. Naṃ namaḥ 3. To the couple Meṣeśa and Garjinī, obeisance. Paṃ namaḥ 3. To the couple Lohiteśa and Kālarātri, obeisance. Phaṃ namaḥ 3. To the couple Śikhīśa and Kuṇḍanī, obeisance. Baṃ namaḥ 3. To the couple Galagaṇḍeśa and Kapardinī, obeisance. Bhaṃ namaḥ 3. To the couple Dviraṇḍeśa and Vijayā, obeisance. Maṃ namaḥ 3. To the couple Mahākāla and Jayā, obeisance.

Salutation to Yaṃbālīśa and Sumukheśvarī. 3. Salutation to Raṃbhujaṅgeśa and Revatī. 3. Salutation to Laṃpinākīśa and Mādhavī. 3. Salutation to Vaṃkhaḍgīśa and Vāruṇī. 3. Salutation to Śaṃvakeśa and Vāyavī. 3. Salutation to Ṣaṃśveteśa and Rakṣopadhāriṇī. 3. Salutation to Saṃbhṛgvīśa and Sahasā. 3. Salutation to Haṃlakulīśa and Lakṣmī. 3. Salutation to Laṃśiviśa and Vyāpinī. 3. Salutation to Kṣaṃsaṃvartakeśa and Mahāmāyā. 3.

Thus [ends] the pervasive [assignment]. This is the Śrīkaṇṭhādi-nyāsa. It is pure when joined with the Kalās along with the Bindu, and [it is performed] with Keśava and the others. Here, the fifth [assignment], the Śrīkaṇṭha-mātṛkā, is prescribed for the limbs of the nyāsa. He who performs the Mātṛkā-nyāsa—either conjoined with the Rudras or alone—at the commencement of rites for the mantras, his mantras immediately attain perfection; his old age and defects go to destruction together. Now, I shall explain the Tattva [assignment] for those desiring it, by which, through the mere performance of the Tattva-nyāsa, the reality itself is produced.

*Oṃ maṃ namas parāya jīvātmane namaḥ* (Oṃ maṃ, salutation to the supreme one; salutation to the individual soul). *Oṃ bhaṃ namas parāya prāṇātmane namaḥ* (Oṃ bhaṃ, salutation to the supreme one; salutation to the vital breath). These two [syllables] are for all the limbs. *Oṃ baṃ namas parāya buddhyātmane namaḥ* (Oṃ baṃ, salutation to the supreme one; salutation to the intellect-soul). *Oṃ phaṃ namas parāya ahaṃkārātmane namaḥ* (Oṃ phaṃ, salutation to the supreme one; salutation to the ego-soul). *Oṃ paṃ namas parāya manātmane namaḥ* (Oṃ paṃ, salutation to the supreme one; salutation to the mind-soul). These three are for the heart.

*Oṃ naṃ namas parāya śabdātmane namaḥ* (Oṃ naṃ, salutation to the supreme one; salutation to the sound-soul). Thus, on the head. *Oṃ dhaṃ namas parāya sparśātmane namaḥ* (Oṃ dhaṃ, salutation to the supreme one; salutation to the touch-soul). Thus, on the mouth. *Oṃ daṃ namas parāya rūpātmane namaḥ* (Oṃ daṃ, salutation to the supreme one; salutation to the form-soul).

*Oṃ thaṃ namaḥ parāya rasātmane namaḥ*—thus at the heart. *Oṃ taṃ namaḥ parāya gandhātmane namaḥ*—thus at the genitals. *Oṃ ṇaṃ namaḥ parāya śrotrātmane namaḥ*—thus at the two ears. *Oṃ ḍhaṃ namaḥ parāya tvagātmane namaḥ*—thus on the skin. *Oṃ ḍaṃ namaḥ parāya cakṣurātmane namaḥ*—thus at the two eyes. *Oṃ ṭhaṃ namaḥ parāya jihvātmane namaḥ*—thus on the tongue. *Oṃ ṭaṃ namaḥ parāya ghrāṇātmane namaḥ*—thus at the nose. *Oṃ traṃ namaḥ*... [and so forth].

"Oṃ jhaṃ, salutation to the Supreme One; salutation to the self of speech"—thus on the speech. "Oṃ jhaṃ, salutation to the Supreme One; salutation to the self of the hands"—thus on the two hands. "Oṃ jaṃ, salutation to the Supreme One; salutation to the self of the anus"—thus on the anus. "Oṃ chaṃ, salutation to the Supreme One; salutation to the self of the feet"—thus on the two feet. "Oṃ caṃ, salutation to the Supreme One; salutation to the self of the generative organ"—thus on the generative organ. "Oṃ ṅaṃ, salutation to the Supreme One; salutation to the self of space"—thus on the head. "Oṃ ghaṃ, salutation to the Supreme One; salutation to the self of air"—thus on the mouth. "Oṃ gaṃ, salutation to the Supreme One; salutation to the self of fire."

"Oṃ Khaṃ, salutation to the Supreme One whose essence is water; salutation"—thus at the heart. "Oṃ Kaṃ, salutation to the Supreme One whose essence is earth; salutation"—thus at the feet. (5) "Oṃ Śaṃ, salutation to the Supreme One whose essence is the heart-lotus; salutation. "Oṃ Haṃ, salutation to the Supreme One whose essence is the lunar orb, to the sixteen-fold digit;

salutation. "Oṃ Saṃ, salutation to the Supreme One whose essence is the solar orb, to the twelve-fold digit; salutation. "Oṃ Raṃ, salutation to the Supreme One whose essence is the fire-orb, to the ten-fold..."

*Lā-ya-na-maḥ*. These four [syllables] are placed in the heart. *Oṃ ṣaṃ namaḥ parāya parameṣṭhyātmane vāsudevāya namaḥ*—thus on the head. *Oṃ yaṃ namaḥ parāya puruṣātmane saṃkarṣaṇāya namaḥ*—thus on the face. *Oṃ vaṃ namaḥ parāya viśvātmane pradyumnāya namaḥ*—thus in the heart. *Oṃ laṃ namaḥ parāya nivṛttyātmane aniruddhāya namaḥ*—thus in the secret place. *Oṃ kṣaṃ namaḥ parāya sarvātmane nārāyaṇāya namaḥ*—thus on the feet. *Oṃ kṣauṃ namaḥ parāya...*

"Obeisance to Nṛsiṃha, whose nature is the *yakāra*," thus one performs the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*). Regarding this, the wise who know the reality of ritual placement (*nyāsa-tattva-vidaḥ*) have declared that even for one who has not performed the worship, the placement of the principles (*tattva-nyāsa*) must be done again because it is the cause for attaining that [state]. He who performs the placement of the principles certainly becomes purified; the Blessed Lord, having entered through his own self, remains there.

Because all principles are served and everything is established within Him—this is the placement of the principles (*tattva-nyāsa*). Now I shall describe the supreme placement of the cage of His forms (*tan-mūrti-pañjara-nyāsa*), beyond which there is no other fruit.

For the accomplishment of that form [of the deity], [one should perform the placement of mantras]: *Oṃ aṃ oṃ śaṃ keśavāya dhātre namaḥ*—on the forehead. *Oṃ āṃ oṃ nārāyaṇāya aryamṇe namaḥ*—at the navel.

*Oṃ iṃ oṃ moṃ māṃ mādhavāya mitrāya namaḥ*—at the heart. *Oṃ iṃ oṃ bhaṃ yaṃ goviṃdāya varuṇāya namaḥ*—at the throat. *Oṃ uṃ oṃ gaṃ naṃ viṣṇave aṃśāya namaḥ*—on the right side. *Oṃ ūṃ oṃ baṃ maṃ madhusūdanāya bhagāya namaḥ*—on the right shoulder. *Oṃ eṃ oṃ taṃ rāṃ trivikramāya...*—[on the left side].

"Oṃ māyavivasvate namaḥ"—thus on the right shoulder. "Oṃ aiṃ oṃ vāṃ rāṃ vāmanāya indrāya namaḥ"—thus on the left side. "Oṃ oṃ oṃ suṃ māṃ śrīṃ dharāya pūṣṇe namaḥ"—thus on the left shoulder. "Oṃ auṃ oṃ deṃ yaṃ hṛṣīkeśāya parjanyāya namaḥ"—thus on the left shoulder-blade. "Oṃ aṃ oṃ vāṃ na padmanābhāya tvaṣṭre namaḥ"—thus on the back. "Oṃ aḥ oṃ yaṃ maṃ dāmodarāya viṣṇave namaḥ"—thus on the crown of the head. "Oṃ namo bhagavate vāsudevāya".

"One should place [the mantra] on the head"—thus has the *mūrtipaṃjara-nyāsa* been declared by the Supreme Lord: "By performing this nyāsa once, the practitioner becomes the unsurpassed embodiment of Rāma. This concludes the *mūrtipaṃjara-nyāsa*. Recite the mantra: *Oṃ, salutation to the one who possesses a crown, armlets, necklaces, makara-earrings, and holds a discus, conch, mace, and lotus in his hands; who wears yellow garments; whose chest is marked with the *śrīvatsa*; who is accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi;
and who radiates a pair of self-luminous lights with a brilliance equal to a thousand suns.* While reciting this, contemplate the pervasion of that supreme light throughout your own body.

One should place [the mantra] upon the head with the kirīṭa-mudrā; this is the kirīṭa-nyāsa. I shall now describe the indriya-nyāsa for the purification of the senses, so that the wise practitioner may attain joy through the instruction of the preceptor. *Oṃ digbhyo namaḥ*—thus on the two ears. *Oṃ vāyave namaḥ*—thus on the skin. *Oṃ ādityāya namaḥ*—thus on the two eyes.
*Oṃ varuṇāya namaḥ*—thus on the tongue. *Oṃ aśvibhyāṃ namaḥ*—thus on the nose. *Oṃ agnaye namaḥ*—thus on the organ of speech. *Oṃ indrāya namaḥ*—thus on the feet.
With "Oṃ viṣṇave namaḥ," [place] on the two feet; with "Oṃ mitrāya namaḥ," on the anus; with "Oṃ prajāpataye namaḥ," on the generative organ; with "Oṃ candramase namaḥ," on the mind;

with "Oṃ brahmaṇe namaḥ," on the intellect; with "Oṃ rudrāya namaḥ," on the ego; with "Oṃ kṣetrajñāya namaḥ," on consciousness; and with "Oṃ īśvarāya namaḥ," on the mind—this is the placement of the senses (*indriya-nyāsa*). I shall now declare the placement (*nyāsa*) of this mantra, which bestows all fruits. The wise say that recitation (*japa*) performed without this placement is as fruitless as a seed sown in barren soil. Brahmā is the seer (*ṛṣi*) of this mantra.

The Gāyatrī meter is said to belong to Śrī Rāma; the deity is proclaimed to be Vaiṣṇava, known as Dhāma. The first seed-syllable (*bīja*) is *namaḥ*, the power (*śakti*) is *rāmāya*, and the pin (*kīlaka*) is likewise [the same]. Because he is the Guru, the Seer (*ṛṣi*) should be borne on the head; because it consists of syllables, the meter (*chandas*) should reside in the tongue; and because it is to be understood by the intellect, the deity should always be established in the heart. The seed-syllable is most secret because it is the word of salutation (*namaḥ*) resting upon Mādhava; or else, the seed and power are in the breasts, and the pin is in the heart. This is its meaning: the Seers are the Brahmins...

"Oṃ *ṇena* maḥ" on the head; "Gāyatrī-chandasena maḥ" on the face; "Śrīrāmāya paramātmane namaḥ" on the heart; "Bījātmane namaḥ" on the private parts; "Śaktaye namaḥ" on the feet. This is the Nyāsa of the Seer (*ṛṣi*) and the rest. Then the limb-nyāsa (*aṅga-nyāsa*): "Oṃ rāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ" (on the heart); "Oṃ rīṃ śirase svāhā" (on the head); "Oṃ ruṃ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ" (on the tuft of hair); "Oṃ reiṃ kavacāya huṃ" (on the armor); "Oṃ rauṃ anāmikābhyāṃ namaḥ" (on the ring fingers); "Oṃ rauṃ kaniṣṭhakābhyāṃ namaḥ" (on the little fingers); "Oṃ raḥ karatalapṛṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ" (on the palms and backs of the hands). Alternatively, one may perform the nyāsa with the six syllables individually. Thus ends the finger-nyāsa.

The *sahṛdayādinyāsa* (the placement beginning with the heart) is as follows: the placement of the syllables of the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) upon the locations of the head, the space between the eyebrows, the heart, the navel, and the secret organ is called the *akṣaranyāsa* (syllable-placement). Thus, the *akṣaranyāsa* is performed: *rāṃ namaḥ* on the head; *rāṃ namaḥ* between the eyebrows; *māṃ namaḥ* on the heart; *yaṃ namaḥ* on the navel; *naṃ namaḥ* on the secret organ; *maṃ namaḥ* on the two feet. This is the *padanyāsa* (foot-placement). [Then the following placements are made]: *maṇḍūkāya namaḥ* on the *ādhāra*; *kālāgnirudrāya namaḥ* on the *svādhiṣṭhāna*; *kacchapāya namaḥ* on the navel; [and] *ādhāraśakti*... [on the base].
"Oṃ namas" at the heart; "Dharmāya namaḥ" on the right shoulder; "Jñānāya namaḥ" on the left shoulder; "Vairāgyāya namaḥ" at the base of the left foot;

"Aiśvaryāya namaḥ" at the base of the right foot; "Adharmāya namaḥ" on the face; "Ajñānāya namaḥ" at the base of the *liṅga*; "Avairāgyāya namaḥ" on the right side; "Anaiśvaryāya namaḥ" on the left side; and "To the infinite one (*Ananta*) endowed with seven coils and a thousand hoods, namaḥ" at the heart.

One should place [the elements] in the center of the lotus; in its center, upon the hood, [one should offer salutations]: "Obeisance to the root of bliss (ānanda-kanda); obeisance to the stalk of consciousness (saṃvit-nāla); obeisance to the stalk of consciousness; obeisance to the lotus of all principles (sarva-tattva-kamala); obeisance to the petals consisting of primordial nature (prakṛti); obeisance to the filaments consisting of transformation (vikāra); obeisance to the pericarp enriched with the fifty letters; Oṃ, obeisance to the solar disc (arka-maṇḍala) whose self consists of twelve kalās; Śaṃ, obeisance to the lunar disc (soma-maṇḍala) whose self consists of sixteen kalās; Maṃ, obeisance to the fiery disc (vahni-maṇḍala) whose self consists of ten kalās; Saṃ, Sa..."

"Obeisance to the Self whose nature is awakening through you (tvāyapravodha)," "Obeisance to the Self who is passion and primordial nature (raṃrajaseprakṛti)," "Obeisance to the Self (āṃātman)"—thus [he places these] on its south. "Obeisance to the Inner Self (aṃantarātman)"—thus on its west. "Obeisance to the Supreme Self (yaṃparamātman)"—thus on its north. "Obeisance to the Self of Knowledge (hnīṃjñānātman)"—thus on its east. In the center, he should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of all the mantras beginning with *praṇava* over each of the principles (*tattva*), as follows: "Obeisance to the Principle of Māyā," "Obeisance to the Principle of Time (kālātattva)," "Obeisance to the Principle of Knowledge (vidyātattva)," and "Obeisance to the Supreme Principle (paratattva). Then, he should place the nine Śaktis upon the petals starting from the east and in the center. Thus: to Vimalā... [and so forth].

Salutations to Utkarmiṇī; salutations to Jñānā; salutations to Kriyā; salutations to Yogā; salutations to Prahvī; salutations to Satyā; salutations to Īśānā; salutations to Anugrahā. Oṃ, salutations to the Blessed One, the Self of all beings, Vāsudeva; salutations to the Self who is the seat of the lotus of yoga, the union with the essence of all. Having thus meditated upon the mantra, which possesses the splendor of a thousand suns, in the center of that seat, one should bring the breath through the path of inhalation into the water and perform the placement (nyāsa). This is the pervasive placement (vyāpaka-nyāsa). Having performed the placement in this manner, one becomes directly Nārāyaṇa himself. [Fever...]
Abortionists and the like go to destruction; it cannot be otherwise. Likewise, *bhūtas*, *pretas*, *piśācas*, *brahmarākṣasas*, *kūṣmāṇḍas*, and *ḍākinīs* are not even capable of looking [upon this].

The wise man who performs this installation becomes Rāma himself in person. Indeed, there is nothing more purifying or meritorious than this. Thus ends the second chapter in the *Rāmārcanacandrikā*, composed by Ānandavana, disciple of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrī Mukundavana Śrīcaraṇa. Now, the meditation (*dhyāna*): In the beautiful city of Ayodhyā, within a jeweled pavilion...

In the center, one should meditate upon a beautiful jeweled lion-throne at the root of the wish-fulfilling tree (Kalpataru). In its midst is an eight-petaled lotus encrusted with various gems. Therein, one should meditate upon the one named Śrī Rāmacandra, who is beyond the Supreme (Rātpara), dark-complexioned by his inherent nature, the remover of the states of preservation, creation, and destruction, served by gods, asuras, lords of sages, and hosts of yogis. He has four arms, bearing the conch, discus, mace, sword, and lotus; he is adorned with a crown, necklaces, armlets, and jeweled earrings. One should contemplate the identity of the deity, the guru, and the mantra with one's own self—[the mantra] *gadāriśaṅkhābja*.

One who meditates upon the Lord of Dharaṇī (the Earth), the enemy of worldly existence, immediately attains liberation; so says all the Śruti. Having meditated thus, one should recite the mantra six thousand times day after day. O child, having become the Lord of Speech and Śrī, one becomes a poet within a year.

Having enjoyed all worldly pleasures, one shall go to the supreme state at the end. Alternatively, one should meditate on the God who is the beloved of Jānakī, who possesses the luster of a sapphire, seated upon that lion-throne in the Vīrāsana posture, bearing in his right hand the mudrā consisting of truth and knowledge, while his other [left] hand, which radiates light, rests upon the crown of his knee, and who is constantly engaged in expounding the divine [teachings].

One should meditate upon the Joy of the Raghus (*Raghunandana*), attended by sages such as Vasiṣṭha and Vāmadeva, with Sītā, who resembles gold, seated on his left side; she is the eternal bestower of desires, holding a red lotus and a lotus in her hands. To the west is Lakṣmaṇa, holding a parasol and a fly-whisk, while Bharata and Śatrughna stand at his sides, both holding palm-leaf fans. Having thus meditated, one should recite the mantra, which is the vessel for wisdom and fortune for those practitioners who recite it. For the wise who employ this method of meditation, this mantra yields fruit even without the performance of the *puraścaraṇa* rite. Thus [it is said] in the forthcoming *Mahāca...* (text fragment).
