In the pericarp of the lotus, the stainless one, who pervades all things, whose form is the embodiment of bliss, and who is the four-footed Brahman—the form of Rāma of wondrous deeds—is eternally served by yogis; therein lie the *siddhis* through the realization of "I am He. Thus says the Śruti: Now, there are these verses: Born from the letter ‘A’ is Saumitri (Lakṣmaṇa), the nourisher of the universe; Born from the letter ‘U’ is Śatrughna, whose nature is splendor (*tejas*); The son of the Earth (Bharata) is born from the letter ‘M’, whose nature is wisdom (*prajñā*); Rāma, whose nature is the half-measure (*ardhamātrā*), is Brahman, the singular embodiment of bliss. By the power of His command, Śrī Rāma [manifests] the world.

She who effects the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of all embodied beings is Sītā; she should be known as that which is designated as *Mūlaprakṛti* (Root Nature). The exponents of Brahman say that she is called *Prakṛti* because of her nature as *Praṇava*. Regarding this syllable *Oṃ*: "All this is this syllable. Its exposition is: what has been, what is becoming, and what will be—all this is the syllable *Oṃ*. And whatever else is beyond time, that too is within the syllable *Oṃ*. For all this is indeed Brahman; this Self is Brahman. This Self is four-footed. The waking state is its first foot: it is externally conscious, has seven limbs, and one face."

The first foot is Vaiśvānara, who has nineteen mouths, is the enjoyer of gross objects, and whose sphere is the waking state; he is internally conscious. The second foot is Taijasa, who has nineteen mouths, is the enjoyer of subtle objects, and whose sphere is the dreaming state. When one does not dream and desires no desire whatsoever, that is deep sleep (*suṣupta*). In the state of deep sleep, having become unified in the mass of consciousness (*prajñānaghana*), being blissful, consisting of bliss, and enjoying bliss, with the intellect as his sole mouth, he is Prājña—the third foot. He is the Lord of all, he is the All-knowing, he is the Inner Controller, and he is the source of all; for he is the origin and the dissolution of all beings.

They consider that [Self] to be neither inwardly conscious, nor outwardly conscious, nor conscious of both, nor conscious, nor unconscious, nor even the absence of consciousness; unseen, beyond conventional usage, ungraspable, without characteristics, unthinkable, indescribable, reachable through the realization of the oneness of the Self, the cessation of the phenomenal world, auspicious, and non-dual—the Fourth state (*turiya*). This Self is to be known as eternally luminous, devoid of knowledge and its effects, free from the bonds of one's own nature, always devoid of duality, of the nature of bliss, the sole substratum of all, pure existence alone, with all obstacles, darkness, and delusion dispelled. Thus he spoke, having reflected upon it.

Having established oneself as the Supreme Brahman, whose nature is consciousness—reciting "I am that Rāmacandra, the conscious Self," "Om, I am Rāmabhadra, the Supreme Light"—one should, through the mind, absorb the self into Brahman. Those who truly proclaim "I am the eternal Rāma" are indeed not wanderers in saṃsāra; of this there is no doubt. This is the Upaniṣad. "He who knows thus becomes liberated," said Yājñavalkya. This alone is supreme meditation; this alone is supreme recitation (japa); this alone is the supreme worship of Rāma, which cuts through worldly existence, [surpassing] even the horse-sacrifice.

"Even hundreds of thousands of Vājapeya sacrifices do not equal even a sixteenth part of a single yoga of meditation. Thus ends the section on meditation. Thereafter, having fashioned a square, a hexagon, and a triangle mandala using the water of the general *arghya*, one should stabilize it with the conch-mudrā. Then, worshipping with flowers and unbroken rice (*akṣata*), one should worship the Heart, Head, Crest, and Armor mantras in the southeast, southwest, northwest, and northeast respectively; the Eye mantra in the center; and the Weapon mantra in the directions starting from the east. Having washed the support (*ādhāra*) with the root mantra, [one should worship] "AṂ, to the Fire-mandala consisting of ten kalās, for the sake of Śrī Rāmā..."

Having established the support (*ādhāra*) consisting of the *arghyapātra* and the seat (*āsana*), one should worship the ten digits (*kalā*) of Fire in the eight directions starting from the east, as well as above and below. They are as follows: *ṣpaṃ* to Dhūmrā, 1; *raṃ* to Nīlaraktā, 2; *laṃ* to Kapilā, 3; *vaṃ* to Visphuliṅginī, 4; *śaṃ* to Jvālinī, 5; *ṣaṃ* to Niḥpatikā, 6; *saṃ* to Havyavāhinī, 7; *haṃ* to Kavyavāhinī, 8; *laṃ* to Raudrī, 9; and *kṣaṃ* to Saṃhāriṇī, 10—thus with "namaḥ" in every case. Having worshipped these digits upon the support, one should then purify the conch at its mouth.

"Obeisance to the vessel for the offering (arghapātra) of Śrī Rāma, whose self consists of twelve kalās belonging to the solar disc. Having thus placed the vessel upon its support, one should worship [the syllables] everywhere as follows: Kaṃ Bhaṃ Tāpinyai 1; Khaṃ Vaṃ Tāpinyai 2; Gaṃ Phaṃ Saṃ Dhinyai 3; Ghaṃ Paṃ Caudhinyai 4; Ṅaṃ Naṃ Kālinyai 5; Caṃ Dhaṃ Śoṣiṇyai 6; Chaṃ Daṃ Vareṇyai 7; Jaṃ Thaṃ Śrīkarṣaṇyai 8; Jhaṃ Taṃ Vaiṣṇavyai 9; Ñaṃ [Pṛ.
31b] Ṇaṃ Viṣṇuvidyāyai 10; Ṭaṃ Ṭhaṃ Jyotsnāyai 11; Ḍhaṃ Ṇaṃ Hiraṇyāyai namaḥ 12. Having worshipped these in the conch, one should then recite the Mātṛkās in reverse order.

Having filled that conch with water sanctified by the syllable *raṃ* and the word *śraddhā*, one should worship the Moon right there with the mantra: *oṃ somamaṇḍalāya ṣoḍaśakalātmane śrīrāmārghyāmṛtāya namaḥ*.

One should worship the sixteen digits (*kalās*) as follows: *aṃ* to Amṛtā, *āṃ* to Mānadā, *iṃ* to Tuṣṭi, *īṃ* to Puṣṭi, *uṃ* to Prīti, *ūṃ* to Rati, *ṛṃ* to Lajjā, *ṝṃ* to Śrī, *ḷṃ* to Svadhā, *ḹṃ* to Rātri, *eṃ* to Jyotsnā, *aiṃ* to Haṃsavatī, *auṃ* to Chāyā, *auṃ* to Pūraṇī, *aṃ* to Vāmā, and *aḥ* to Amā—*namaḥ* (obeisance) is added to each in every case. Having worshipped these with water, [the fire] emerges as a flame that is smoky, blue, red, tawny, and sparkling.

The ten digits (*kalās*) of Fire are: Kīcī, Havyavāhanikā, Kavyavāhanikā, Raudrī, Saṃhāriṇī, Tapinī, Tāpinī, Saṃdhinī, Bodhinī, and Kālinī. The digits of the Sun are declared by the wise to be twelve: Śoṣiṇī, Vareṇyā, Karṣaṇī, Vaiṣṇavī, Viṣṇuvidyā, Jyotsnā, Hiraṇyā, Amṛtā, Mānasī, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, and Prīti. The digits of the Moon are: Ratihnikā, Śrī, Svadhā, Rātri, Jyotsnā, and Haṃsā.
"The sixteen digits of the moon, which fill the shadow of the night, are present there"—thus is the collection of digits described in the *Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā*.

Then, reciting the mantra "Gaṅge," one should invoke the pure sacred waters (*tīrtha*) into that conch water; thereafter, one should worship them with [mantras] beginning with "Gaṅgā. Placing the palm of the hand upon the conch, one should mutter the six-syllabled mantra (*ṣaḍakṣara*). One should contemplate the sacred water as consisting of pure consciousness (*cinmaya*), having brought it forth by means of the *aṅkuśa-mudrā*. Then, having displayed the *dhenu-mudrā* from the sacred waters within the belly of the universe (*brahmāṇḍa*), one should [display] the conch and the mudrā.

One should display the *krama-mudrā* and the one called *garuḍa-mudrā*, and having rendered [the objects] supreme with effort, one should contemplate them as purified. O Dear One, by joining the two hands together, this is the *ācārātrika*; this mudrā is named *paramīkaraṇa* (the act of making supreme) and it grants all desires. One should sprinkle that [water) upon the head of the Deity, upon the articles of worship, and upon oneself. By means of inspection (*avekṣaṇa*), sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), gazing (*vīkṣaṇa*), striking (*tāḍana*), and likewise honoring (*arcana*), one should effect the purification of all things. Only when everything is purified does it become fit for worship and meaningful. Thus ends the consecration of the conch (*śaṅkha-pratiṣṭhā*). The vessels are made of copper...

Within the water, various wonderful lotuses created by magic appear for the purposes of worship and so forth. For the purpose of offering the *arghya* vessel, for the *madhuparka*, and likewise for the purpose of sipping (*ācamana*), one should place four vessels. One should first prepare a conch shell for oneself to the east. Then, having filled the *arghya*, *pādya*, and other vessels with auspicious water, one should place fragrances, flowers, barley, and unbroken rice (*akṣata*) into the *arghya* vessel. For the accomplishment of the *arghya*, one should also add the tips of *kuśa* grass, sesame seeds, *dūrvā* grass, and mustard seeds. Into the *pādya* vessel, one should first place *śyāmāka* grain.

One should employ *meva*, *arjuna*, *viṣṇukrāntā*, and *pādyasiddhi* for the preparation of the water for washing the feet (*pādya*). Likewise, O Sage, one should place nutmeg (*jātīphala*) in the vessel for sipping water (*ācamana*), as well as cloves (*lavaṅga*) and *kakola*, which are highly praised for that purpose. The honey-mixture (*madhuparka*) shall consist of curd, honey, and clarified butter. Alternatively, one may arrange the water for washing the feet, the respectful offering (*arghya*), and so forth, in a single vessel; for when the materials for all the ritual services (*upacāra*) are unavailable, the mental visualization (*bhāvanā*) alone is indeed sufficient. Aṭṭahāsa has declared that the vessel is complete with pure water alone. Thus concludes the arrangement of the vessels. Having thus arranged the vessels...

Then one should begin the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*). For it is thus: having meditated upon Rāghava, whose nature is consciousness, as being seated upon that throne—a beautiful lotus born from the bulb of Dharma (*dharmakaṇḍa*), with the stalk of knowledge (*jñānanāla*), the eight petals of the eightfold sovereign powers (*aiśvaryāṣṭaguṇa*), and the pericarp of supreme dispassion (*vairāgya*)—one should worship Him with sandalwood and other offerings, and with lamps fed by ghee. At the time of eating, having performed some recitation (*japa*), one should offer it [with the mantra]:

"O You, the protector of the most secret of secrets, accept this recitation performed by us. May success be mine, O God; by Your grace, I abide in You. [This is done] in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) located at the *svādhiṣṭhāna*.

One should kindle the fire in a triangle, which is the form of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*), and then offer the ego (*ahaṃtā*) and other elements into it with the *praṇava* (Om). Whatever worship, fire-offerings (*homa*), and so forth have been performed for the deity, may you be pleased by that; O Lord, make my mind pure. "I offer myself to You; You are my supreme refuge, O Supreme Lord"—having spoken thus, one should offer oneself as the light situated within the path of the breath. Having become one with That, consisting of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*sac-cid-ānanda*), one should remain for some time. This internal worship with mental flowers is considered the virtuous and auspicious *sāttvika* rite, free from the remains of offerings (*anirmālya*).

Because [external worship] is impure, does not grant liberation, and yields inauspicious results, one must certainly perform mental worship first with every effort, and only afterwards proceed with extensive material offerings. Then, having distinguished oneself as consisting of pure consciousness (cinmaya) by means of perfumes and other substances, one should worship with: *Oṃ ātmatattvāya namaḥ*, *Oṃ kalātattvāya namaḥ*, *Oṃ vidyātattvāya namaḥ*, *Oṃ śrīrāmatattvāya namaḥ*. Having thus worshipped, one should perform the external sacrifice. First, one should draw the King of Yantras, the embodiment of the Joy of the Raghus, which destroys the long-lasting sufferings arising from defects such as lust and anger.

Because it restrains [the senses], they call it a *yantra*; in this [yantra], Rāma is pleased when worshipped. It is declared that the *yantra* consists of mantra, and the deity is the essence of the mantra. Just as there is a distinction between the body and the self, so too is there a distinction between the mantra and the deity. Therefore, having drawn the king of *yantras* upon a pedestal, one should worship there—whether on gold, silver, copper, cloth, birch bark, or even on the ground. Without a *yantra*, the worship is not complete, and the deity does not become propitious. When Śrī Rāma is worshipped in the *yantra* along with Sītā, constrained by the *yantra*, he performs whatever is desired; for that is the power of the supreme mantra. [The rest of the verse begins: *tāpa...* (suffering...)

The Yantra-nāyaka, which bestows desires upon men and even liberation through its mere retention, as declared in the Nīlarudropaniṣad, is now described. Having drawn a frame of three lines, one should write the two *Tāra* (Oṃ) syllables in the middle.

Having written the seed-syllable (*bīja*) in the center of that, one should write the name of the practitioner (*sādhya*) below it, ending in the accusative case, and likewise above it, ending in the genitive case. One should write "Kuru" twice on its sides, and the goddess Rāmā within the spaces between the seed-syllables. The wise and pure-minded person should encircle all of this with the two *Praṇavas*. In the six corners, which possess long vowels, one should write the seed-syllable along with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*) and the others.

One should draw the serpent at the tip of the *ramā* (the syllable *hrīṃ*) on the corner side; having written the mantra and the fierce speech (*ugiraṃ*) within the intervals between the corners, one should draw three circles and an eight-petaled lotus.

One should write the vowels in the pericarp and the eight groups of consonants (*varga-aṣṭaka*) on the eight petals. Upon those [petals], one should write the eight-syllabled name of Nārāyaṇa, and in the pericarp, the *ramā*. Outside of that, one should draw a twelve-petaled [lotus] and likewise write the twelve-syllabled mantra: "Oṃ namo bhagavate vāsudevāya. One should write the letters from *a* to *kṣa* in the pericarps in a circular form. Outside of that, one should draw a sixteen-petaled [lotus].

One should inscribe the beauty of the filaments (keśara) joined with the armor (*varma*) and weapon (*astra*) mantras; on the petals (*dala*), the twelve-syllable mantra; and at their joints (*saṃdhi*), the mantras of Ṭhirañja and the others. Then, one should carefully inscribe the letters of the King of Mantras, joined with the nasal bindu, upon the thirty-two petals of the great lotus (*mahāpadma*). Therein, one should write the *anuṣṭubh* verse—or rather, the reading "ragho" [is used]; for even that which is not explicitly stated in the Śruti should be accepted if it is part of the traditional lineage (*sāṃpradāyika*). One should meditate there upon the eight Vasus, the eleven Rudras, and the twelve Ādityas.

One should draw the Dhātṛ and the Vaṣaṭkāra, and outside that, the Bhūgṛha (Earth-palace) provided with vajras and tridents, endowed with three *rerava*s, furnished with doors, adorned with the zodiac signs (*rāśi*) and so forth, and joined by the serpents (*phaṇin*). Ananta and Vāsuki are indeed the two Brahmins; Takṣaka, Kola, Padmaka, Mahāpadma, Śaṅkha, Pulika, and Oṣṭha are the clans (*kula*). Ananta and Kulika are declared to be of the fire-color (*vahni-varṇa*); each is adorned with a thousand hoods (*phaṇā*). Vāsuki and Śaṅkhapāla are Kṣatriyas, yellow in color; each has [a thousand] hoods.

Takṣaka and Mahāpadma, numbering seven hundred, are known as Vaiśyas; they are blue in color and possess five hundred high, excellent hoods. Padma and Karkoṭaka, numbering three hundred, are Śūdras and are white in color. Having thus drawn the maṇḍala, one should draw Nārasiṃha and Varāha in its cardinal and intermediate directions, as well as the two mantras. This yantra, which embodies all things, was practiced by the sages in former times; it is a supreme secret, difficult even for the Lord to fathom. Thus has the yantra been fully described. It should not...

One who possesses ordinary consciousness should not draw that [diagram] by means of his own intellect, following the path of the Guru’s vision; for all rites unspoken by the Guru will certainly be fruitless. O Rāma (p.

33b), previously in the *Tāpanīya-ṭīkā*, the Lord of Yantras was explained by us for those desiring the attainment of perfection (*siddhi*); thus ends the extraction of this King of Yantras as prescribed in the *Pūrva-Rāmatāpanīyopaniṣad*. Now, the pedestal (*pīṭha*) of Rāghava in this Great Wheel of Worship is described; first, one should worship that, and then the sequence of service is stated: "On one's own left side, obeisance to the venerable Gurus. Furthermore—

Having worshipped with "Salutation to the Gurus," "Salutation to the Higher and Lower Gurus," and "Salutation to the Gurus Beyond the Beyond," one should worship on one's own right side with "Salutation to Gaṇapati," "Salutation to Saṃsaravatī," "Duṃ, Salutation to Durgā," and "Kṣaṃ, Salutation to Kṣetrapāla. Then, having worshipped "Salutation to Vāstupuruṣa" in the center of the sacrificial hall, and subsequently worshipping "Oṃ Maṃ, Salutation to Mṛdbhṛkā" in the center of the pedestal, and then worshipping "Salutation to Kālāgnirudra," "Salutation to Kūrma," and "Salutation to Ādhāraśakti" one above the other, [one should worship] "Oṃ, Salutation to Ratnadvīpa."

Having worshipped with: *oṃ ratnamaṇḍapāya namaḥ*, *oṃ kalpavṛkṣebhyaḥ namaḥ*, *oṃ ratnavedikāyai namaḥ*, *oṃ ratnasiṃhāsanāya namaḥ*, one should worship the four principles beginning with Dharma at the feet of the pedestal starting from the southeast (Agni). Likewise, one should worship the principles beginning with Adharma on the sides of the pedestal starting from the east. Then, one should worship the lotus of bliss (*ānandakamalanaroruha*) in the pericarp (*karṇikā*), as well as the filaments, the petals, and the pericarp itself. One should worship the syllable *Tārā* (Oṃ), the sun, the moon, the fire, the three circles, the three qualities beginning with Sattva, and then the fourfold self (*ātmacatuṣṭaya*) and the principle of Māyā.

One should worship *latatattva* (the principle of the vine), *vidyātattva* (the principle of knowledge), and the supreme [Ātmatattva] one by one; thereafter, one should worship the nine Śaktis: Vimalā, Utkarṣiṇī, Jñānā, Kriyā, and Yogā as the fifth, then Prahvī, Satyā, Īśānā, and the ninth, Anugrahā. One should worship them in the eight petals starting from the east and in the pericarp (*karṇikā*) in due order, using their respective names joined with the dative case and the word "namaḥ. Afterward, the knower of mantras should worship in the pericarp with the *pīṭha-mantra*, first uttering the syllable *Oṃ* and then saying the word "namaḥ," followed by the word "Bhagavate" and then the word "Viṣṇave."

Then, having offered [the mantra] "Obeisance to Vāsudeva, the self of all beings," one should again offer a handful of flowers with this [mantra] joined with the root [syllables]: "Obeisance to the self who is the seat of yoga through union with the self of all.

(pṛ0 34a) When the seat has been thus worshipped, one should invoke the Lord and worship Him. The specific details regarding the placement of mantras (*nyāsa*) during the worship of the seat should be observed. This concludes the worship of the seat. One should contemplate Rāma, whose form is consciousness, situated in the lotus of the heart, as having arrived via the path of the breath within the handful of flowers. Having brought Him into the image with the *pādukā* mudrā, one should worship Him with a focused mind and display the seventeen mudrās. The invocation is complete.
Likewise, Agastya has said: "The *āvāhanī*, *sthāpanī*, *sannidhīkaraṇī*, *susannirodhinī*, *saṃmukhīkaraṇī*, *sakalīkaraṇī*, and likewise the *mahāmudrā*;
the conch, discus, mace, lotus, *dhenu*, *kaustubha*, and *gāruḍa* [mudrās]; those called *śrīvatsa* and *vanamālā*; and one should display the *yonimudrā*.

By means of these seventeen mudrās, the wise who constantly worship Rāma delight the Lord of the Immortals; they cause him to melt with affection, O best of Brahmins, and thereby obtain their prayers."

O Sage, these are the seventeen mudrās. The *kusumāñjali* (flower-offering) mudrā, formed by joining the hands from the *mūlādhāra* to the *dvādaśānta*, which has been purified by the splendors residing in the three places (*tri-sthāna*), is the mudrā for invocation (*āvāhanī*) during the ritual of worshipping the deity in images and other forms. This same mudrā, when turned face-downward, is again recommended for the rite of installation (*sthāpana*). In the ritual of worshipping the deity, the mudrā named *sannidhīkaraṇī* consists of both hands made into fists with the thumbs raised. The *sannirodhinī* mudrā is formed by placing the thumbs inside the palms. The *saṃmukhī* mudrā consists of two upturned fists facing each other.

The ritual placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) by means of the five limbs themselves constitutes the *sakalīkaraṇa* (the rite of making [the deity] complete). (5) When the two hands are extended with the thumbs interlocked, it is called the *mahāmudrā*; it is to be performed until the deficiency or excess is completed. (6) With the little finger, ring finger, and middle finger placed inside, and the other fingers (index and thumb) in front, hidden at the base of the thumbs and bent into a bud-like shape with both hands—this is the *śaṅkhamudrā*, used in the worship of the gods. (7) One should, however, wrap [the hands] with the fingers in a reversed manner, touching them face-to-face. (8)

O Sage, this forming of a circle with effort is declared to be the *cakra-mudrā* (9). Next is the *gada-mudrā*: with the fingers joined facing one another, the middle fingers raised, and the two fists [formed] from the eight [fingers], O ascetic, by properly drawing the tips of the fingers together in a circular fashion, this becomes the *padma-mudrā* (10–11). Next is the *dhenu-mudrā*: the ring fingers, the little fingers, the index fingers, and the middle fingers are joined facing one another (12). Then follows that known as the *kaustubha-mudrā*, where the little fingers are joined to one another...

This is the Śrīvatsa-mudrā; from this [position], the Vanamālā-mudrā is formed by the little finger, ring finger, and middle finger [forming a fist], with the index fingers raised high and rotated over the head; with the two index fingers [pointing upward], the gods [are invoked]. This is declared to be the Yoni-mudrā, produced by the two hands joined together. When the two index fingers and the thumb are placed inside, and the pair of ring fingers are situated at the base of the middle fingers, with the tips of the thumbs resting there—this is praised for worship. Thus ends the description of the mudrās. For the Śāligrāma and Lord Sūrya, there is invocation but no dismissal; [worship] is always performed upon the Śāligrāma stone and so forth.

Having first uttered the root mantra *sannihito hariḥ*, one should likewise offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) with the mantra: *tathā rāmāya yantrine ca sāyudhāya savāhanāya saparivārāya svaśaktiyuktāya puṣpāñjaliṃ parikalpayāmi namaḥ*.

One should offer this for every handful of flowers during all the ritual services (*upacāra*), beginning with the water for the feet (*pādya*). First, having offered a handful of flowers, thereafter perform the worship of the feet (*pādārcana*). Then, as appropriate, offer the water for the feet (*pādya*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), the water for sipping (*ācamana*), and the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*). Having offered the unguent (*abhyañjana*) and the ointment (*udvartana*), one should perform the great bath (*mahāsnāna*). After offering the garment for the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), one should cause Hari to be fanned (*tīrājayet*). The bath should be performed with the *Puruṣasūkta* and pure [water].

One should consecrate [the deity] by sprinkling it one hundred, one thousand, ten thousand, or as many times as possible, with conch-water, and separately with milk, curd, clarified butter, honey, and sugar; likewise with coconut water, palm fruit juice, various fragrant substances, scented water, water from the *aiṃkava* plant, and fragrant water produced from plantain, jackfruit, and mango. Having filled the excellent conch with that same water along with flowers, one should offer incense at intervals with black agallochum (*kṛṣṇāguru*) smoke. Then, [it becomes] pure...

One who desires a kingdom should, with single-minded devotion, bathe Him with water alone for a full year every day with great care, for the sake of attaining royal success; by bathing Him in this very manner, one becomes a king, and not otherwise. Having offered water for sipping (ācamanīya), one should cause two garments to be put on [the deity]. One should again offer water for sipping, a sacred thread (upavīta), and a seat. Having brought and established Hari with the *pādukā-mudrā*, one should adorn Him with suitable ornaments resting upon *tulasī* leaves. Then, with the root mantra, one should offer sandalwood paste and eight handfuls of flowers. On His left side, one should place Sītā along with Her attendants.

One should worship her with the mantra “*Śrīṃ sītāyai svāhā*,” which resembles a *caṇaka* (chickpea). Then, one should worship Lakṣmaṇa at the tip of the eastern spoke in the southern corner with the mantra: “*Oṃ laṃ lakṣmaṇāya namaḥ*. Thus, according to the Śruti, it takes the form of a triangle. On the left side of the triangle, from the right-hand petal, one should worship the bow with “*Oṃ śaṃ śarṅgāya namaḥ*” and the arrows with “*Oṃ śaṃ śarebhyo namostu*. Having then obtained permission for worship, one should worship the outer limbs (*bahir-aṅga*). This concludes the primary worship (*pradhāna-pūjā*). [Then]: “*Oṃ rāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*.”

*Oṃ rīṃ śiraḥ svāhā; oṃ rūṃ śikhāyai namaḥ; oṃ reiṃ kavacāya namaḥ; oṃ rauṃ netratrayāya namaḥ; oṃ raḥ astrāya namaḥ.* This shall be the first circuit in the hexagon, performed with the limbs (*aṅga*) beginning with the heart. One should worship [the goddesses] starting from the southeast, holding the gestures of granting boons (*varada*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*). They possess the luster of crystal, the moon, and sapphire, and are dark-complexioned women with grain and oblations in their hands. Then, having washed one's hands and offered fragrance to Rāma, one should take a handful of flowers with the thumb, index finger, and middle finger of the right hand, and place it in the center of the conch.
Saying, "I shall offer water," one should devotedly present water for refuge from the serpent of saṃsāra.

Having uttered, "This is the worship of the first enclosure (āvaraṇa)," and having sprinkled that water, one should offer a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali). After washing the hands, one should perform the worship of the second enclosure, the fourth enclosure, the fifth enclosure, the sixth enclosure, the seventh enclosure, the eighth enclosure, the ninth enclosure, and the tenth enclosure; thus one should perform the enclosures (āvaraṇa), as well as the display of each respective mudrā, such as the conch and others.

Thus is the worship of the first enclosure: Oṃ āṃ, obeisance to the Ātman (Self). Oṃ niṃ, obeisance to Nivṛtti. Oṃ aṃ, obeisance to the Antarātman (Inner Self). Oṃ praḥ, obeisance to Pratiṣṭhā. Oṃ paḥ, obeisance to the Paramātman (Supreme Self). Oṃ viṃ, obeisance to Vidyā. Oṃ jñāṃ, obeisance to the Jñānātman (Knowledge-Self). Oṃ śāṃ, obeisance to Śānti. In the second [enclosure], starting with the Ātman and so forth, there are eight deities at the base of the lotus; just as in the garden, so too are these Śaktis, holding lotuses in their hands. Thus is the second [enclosure]. Oṃ vāṃ, obeisance to Vāsudeva. Oṃ śrīṃ, obeisance to Śrī. Oṃ śaṃ, obeisance to Saṃkarṣaṇa.

Oṃ śāṃ śāntyai namaḥ; Oṃ praṃ pradyumnāya namaḥ; Oṃ prīṃ prītyai namaḥ; Oṃ aṃ aniruddhāya namaḥ; Oṃ raṃ ratyai namaḥ. On the third [layer], there are Vāsudeva and the others on the eight petals in the same manner. Rāma is remembered as holding a sword (ca), a shield (pa), a bow (ga), and an arrow (śa) in his four hands. Pradyumna, the Lord, holds a discus (ca), a conch (śa), a mace (pa), and a lotus (ga) in his fourth hand. The lotuses in their right lower hands are, in order from the front: a white lotus, a golden lotus, a dūrvā grass lotus, and an indranīla gem lotus. These deities have complexions like crystal, gold, dūrvā grass, and sapphire respectively, and they stand upon a golden eight-petaled lotus with dark blue filaments.

"Yādayaḥ"—this is the third [set]. Oṃ haṃ, obeisance to Hanumān. Oṃ suṃ, obeisance to Sugrīva. Oṃ bhaṃ, obeisance to Bharata. Oṃ viṃ, obeisance to Vibhīṣaṇa. Laṃ, obeisance to Lakṣmaṇa. Oṃ aṃ, obeisance to Aṅgada. Oṃ śaṃ, obeisance to Śatrughna. Oṃ jāṃ, obeisance to Jāmbavanta. On the fourth [layer], starting from the east on the tips of the petals, the wise ones should perform the worship of the gods in front of the deities at the tips of their respective bows, beginning with the Son of the Wind (Hanumān) and the others in sequence. Having uttered "Prācī" (the East) as prescribed, the worship of the gods should be performed; they are golden-hued and dark-blue in sequence.

He was causing Hanumān to recite an excellent and beautiful manuscript before the Lord; Bharata and Śatrughna held chowries at His sides; the son of Sumitrā (Lakṣmaṇa) held a fan with his hands joined in *añjali*; and other devotees were likewise present. Because of his great affection, Lakṣmaṇa is mentioned again. He is like Śeṣa bearing the parasol of a thousand hoods; the meaning is that he is addressed again by the name "Lakṣmaṇa. *Oṃ sṛṃ sṛṣṭaye namaḥ* | *Oṃ naṃ jayantāya namaḥ* | *Oṃ viṃ vijayāya namaḥ* | *Oṃ sauṃ saurāṣṭrāya namaḥ* | *Oṃ rāṃ rāṣṭravardhanāya namaḥ* | *Oṃ aṃ akopāya namaḥ* | *Oṃ dhaṃ dharmāya...* [Page 36a]

*Pālāyanāya namaḥ*. *Oṃ suṃ sumantāya namaḥ*. One should place [the mantras] on the second eight petals in the eastern direction and so forth, with palms joined in reverence, for those who advise on the science of inquiry (*anvīkṣikī*). Thus ends the fifth [section]. *Oṃ vaṃ vasiṣṭhāya namaḥ*. *Oṃ vāṃ vāmadevāya namaḥ*. *Oṃ jāṃ jāvālyāya namaḥ*. *Oṃ gauṃ gautamāya namaḥ*. *Oṃ bhaṃ bhāradvājāya namaḥ*. *Oṃ kau kaumikāya namaḥ*. *Oṃ vāṃ vālmīkāya namaḥ*. *Oṃ nāṃ nāradāya namaḥ*. *Oṃ saṃ sanakāya namaḥ*. *Oṃ saṃ sanandāya namaḥ*.

Oṃ *saṃ* salutation to Sanātana; Oṃ *saṃ* salutation to Sanatkumāra. One should worship all twelve sages, who hold water-pots (*kamaṇḍalu*) and recite mantras, in the order of the petals starting from the east: Thus is the sixth [set]: Oṃ *nīṃ* salutation to Nīla; Oṃ *naṃ* salutation to Nala; Oṃ *suṃ* salutation to Suṣeṇa;

Oṃ *maiṃ* salutation to Mainda; Oṃ *saṃ* salutation to Maṃrabha; Oṃ *dviṃ* salutation to Dvivida; Oṃ *caṃ* salutation to Candana; Oṃ *gaṃ* salutation to Gavākṣa; Oṃ *kiṃ* salutation to Kīrīṭa; Oṃ *kuṃ* salutation to Kuṇḍala.

Oṃ namaḥ; Oṃ śrīṃ, obeisance to Śrīvatsa; Oṃ kauṃ, obeisance to Kaustubha; Oṃ paṃ, obeisance to Padma. One should worship these sixteen lotuses in the order starting from the eastern direction with palms joined in reverence. This is the seventh [section]. Oṃ dhuṃ, obeisance to Dhruva; Oṃ dhaṃ, obeisance to Dhara; Oṃ sauṃ, obeisance to Soma; Oṃ aṃ, obeisance to Apa; Oṃ aṃ, obeisance to Anila; Oṃ aṃ, obeisance to Anala; Oṃ praṃ, obeisance to Pratyūṣa; Oṃ praṃ, obeisance to Prabhāsa; Oṃ vīṃ, obeisance to Vīrabhadra; Oṃ śaṃ, obeisance to Śambhu; Oṃ giṃ, obeisance to Giriśa.
Oṃ sraṃ, salutation to Ekapada; Oṃ straṃ, salutation to Ahirbudhnya; Oṃ kaṃ, salutation to Kapālī; Oṃ diṃ, salutation to Dikpati; Oṃ sthāṃ, salutation to Sthāṇu;

Oṃ bhaṃ, salutation to Bharga; Oṃ vaṃ, salutation to Varuṇa; Oṃ sūṃ, salutation to Sūrya; Oṃ veṃ, salutation to Veda; Oṃ bhāṃ, salutation to Bhānu; Oṃ iṃ, salutation to Indra; Oṃ riṃ, salutation to Ravi; Oṃ gaṃ, salutation to Gabhastin; Oṃ yaṃ, salutation to Yama; Oṃ hiṃ, salutation to Hiraṇyaretas; Oṃ diṃ, salutation to Divākara; Oṃ miṃ, salutation to Mitra; Oṃ viṃ, salutation to Viṣṇu.

Oṃ dhāṃ, obeisance to Dhātṛ. The eighth enclosure, consisting of thirty-two petals, begins with Dhruva and others. Dhruva, Dhara, Soma, Āpa, Anila, Anala, Pratyūṣa, and Prabhāsa—these are proclaimed as the eight Vasus. The sequence of weapons belonging to the Vasus is: a trident, a sword, a staff, a lotus, a chisel, a bow, and a mallet. Vīrabhadra, Śambhu, Girīśa, Mahāpaśu, Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Pinākī, Aparājita, Bhuvanādhīśvara, and Kapālī, the lord of the quarters.

Sthāṇu, Bhaga, and the illustrious Bhagavān—these are remembered as the eleven Rudras. [Their respective weapons are: the *sallarka*, the *marara*, the trident (*śūla*), the *śikhara*, the *yamadaṃṣṭraka*, the black serpent, the *pināka* bow, the *aghora* missile, the goad (*aṅkuśa*), and the *khaṭvāṅga*;

these are the supreme weapons held by Sthāṇu, and Śiva has thus declared these to be the weapons of the Rudras in their proper order. Varuṇa, Sūrya, Vedāṅga, Bhānu, Indra, Ravi, Gabhasti, Yama, Svarṇaretas, Divākara, Mitra, and Viṣṇu—these are declared to be the Ādityas, beginning from the first.

One should know the weapons of the twelve Ādityas in their respective order: the noose (māt), the mallet (pāśantu), the hammer (mudgara), the spear (śaṃṣa), the arrowhead (śalya), the horn (śṛṅga), the sword (kṛpāṇaka), the mace (gadā), the staff (daṇḍa), the thunderbolt (vajra), the lotus (abja), and likewise the serpent (sarpa) and the Sudarśana discus.
Thus ends the eighth [section]. Oṃ laṃ, salutation to Indra, the lord of the gods, together with his weapon, his vehicle, his retinue, and endowed with his own power.

Oṃ raṃ, salutation to Agni, the lord of splendor. Oṃ yaṃ, salutation to Yama, the lord of the departed spirits. Oṃ kṣaṃ, salutation to Nirṛti, the lord of splendor. Oṃ vaṃ, salutation to Varuṇa... [the lord of waters].

*Oṃ lāṃ namo 'gnaye jvalanādhipataye* (Salutation to Agni, the lord of fire). *Oṃ yaṃ namo vāyave prāṇādhipataye* (Salutation to Vāyu, the lord of breath). *Oṃ saṃ namo somāya nakṣatrādhipataye* (Salutation to Soma, the lord of the constellations). *Oṃ haṃ nama īśānāya vidyādhipataye* (Salutation to Īśāna, the lord of knowledge). Thus, in the eight directions starting from the east. *Oṃ āṃ namo brahmaṇe lokādhipataye* (Salutation to Brahmā, the lord of the world). Thus, between the east and the northeast. *Oṃ hrīṃ namo viṣṇave bhūtādhipataye* (Salutation to Viṣṇu, the lord of beings). Thus, between the southwest and the west. With *Indrāya* and so forth in the earthly abode (*airbhūgṛha*), there shall be the ninth enclosure (*navamāvaraṇa*). This is the ninth. *Oṃ vaṃjraṃ namas* (Salutation to the thunderbolt). *Oṃ śaktiṃ namas* (Salutation to the spear). *Oṃ daṇḍaṃ namas* (Salutation to the staff). *Oṃ khaṅgaṃ namas* (Salutation to the sword).

Oṃ, salutation to the noose; Oṃ, salutation to the goad; Oṃ, salutation to the mace; Oṃ, salutation to the trident; Oṃ, salutation to the thunderbolt; Oṃ, salutation to the curved weapon—one should worship these in the second earth-pavilion. Thus ends the tenth [section]. In the hexagon, the first enclosure (āvṛti) begins from the southeast with the limbs (aṅgas) in sequence; the second with the deities beginning with the Self (Ātman) and so forth; likewise, the third on the eight petals with Vāsudeva and the others. The fourth is with the sons of Vāyu and others, starting from the southeast petal and proceeding in order. The fifth enclosure is with Sṛṣṭi and the others on the second set of eight petals; the sixth is on the twelve petals.

The seventh [concentric circle] on the sixteen-petaled lotus should be known as consisting of Siṣṭa and others; the eighth, on the thirty-two petals, is to be known by Nīla and others, along with Kapi and Yuga. In the outer earthen enclosure (bhūgṛha), the ninth enclosure consists of Indra and others. The tenth, auspicious enclosure, consists of their weapons, headed by the thunderbolt (vajra). O best of practitioners, this worship of the ten enclosures should be performed by an excellent adept (sādhaka) who is capable of it. If one is unable to perform the ritual worship (ārādhanā), he should offer the means of worship (arcanasādhana). He who is not even able to give that should perform the visualization of the worship. O best of sages, for one who does not know even a single part of this, there is no liberation from the ocean of worldly existence. One should recite it.

Thus, in no other way, the wise one who, with devotion and effort, personally prepares all the requisites and performs the rite shall obtain the complete fruit. *Oṃ, salutations to the attendants of Śrī Rāma.* In the third earth-chamber (*bhūgṛha*), having offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) to the Nāgas outside of that, one should present the offerings of incense and so forth to the Blessed Lord together with his retinue. This is the worship of the enclosures (*āvaraṇapūjā*).

Then, while sounding the bell and making the sounds of "jayas," one should offer [the oblation]. Having worshipped the place of incense, with the ring finger and thumb joined, [one recites]: "The essence born from the tree, rich in fragrance, fragrant..."

"O Supreme One, most excellent among all the gods, please accept this incense. Having thus made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) and offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), one should recite the *Yaśas* hymn. Furthermore, in the *Pariśiṣṭa* (p. 37b), it is said: "One should waft the limbs with incense using a fan; during all the lustration rites (*nīrājana*), one should chant the names of Viṣṇu. One should perform the recitation (*japa*) of the *Yopam*, proclaim auspiciousness (*kalyāṇa*), as well as the *Maṅgaladyos* and the praise of the Seed of the Universe (*jagadbīja*). [The deity holds] a staff in his left lotus-hand and a single arrow in his right hand at the rear.

I worship the dark-complexioned Rāma, who eternally bears his beloved quiver upon his left shoulder, whose body is joined with Jānakī and Lakṣmaṇa, and who destroys the mental anguish of those who take refuge in him. He who offers guggulu resin smeared with clarified butter to the descendant of Raghu shall have no fear of birth, death, old age, and the like. This is the incense offering. Then, having worshipped Rāmacandra with an *ārārtika* lamp consisting of many wicks arranged in an uneven pattern, one should offer it with the middle finger of the left hand.

"A great lamp, brilliantly shining, dispelling darkness on all sides; having worshipped it, one should offer it to Lord Rāmacandra with the left and middle fingers. 'This great lamp, brilliantly shining, dispelling darkness on all sides—may this light-lamp, both external and internal, be accepted. Saying 'Salutations to the Lord of Lamps,' one should then offer a handful of flowers. Having fumigated and worshipped him with musical instruments, one should perform the *nīrājana* ceremony over the Lord's head. One should meditate upon the King as holding an arrow and a bow, seated upon a lotus posture, wearing yellow garments, and [possessing] a new..."

One should recite "Śrī Rāma, Japa" and so forth, while meditating on Rāmabhadra—who has three eyes, who is serene, whose eyes are fixed upon the lotus-face of Sītā seated on his lap, who resembles a dark rain-cloud, who is radiant with various ornaments, and who bears a great mass of matted locks. For the food offering (naivedya), a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, bell-metal, Palāśa leaves, or a lotus leaf is dear to Viṣṇu.
One should daily offer to Śrī Hari food endowed with all qualities—eatables, chewables, lickables, and suckables—and by casting Tulasī [into the water], one obtains infinite merit.

Having sprinkled [the food] seven times, one should consecrate it while displaying the *dhenu-cakra* and *astra* [mudrās], touching [it] with the thumb of the left hand. Having transformed the water into the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), one should offer it to the Supreme Lord. "O Knower of Food, please enjoy this auspicious rice-mess, along with meat, fish, and vegetables; with soups, syrups, and delicacies; with white, nectar-like fruits and various eatables that are pleasant to the taste; with abundant ghee, well-fried and pleasing to the eyes; with mustard, cardamom, and black pepper as a savory garnish; and with a variety of leafy greens."

The mantra for the offering: Seated comfortably with Brahmā, Īśa (Śiva), and the other [guardians] of the quarters, being respectfully fanned by Lakṣmī—who holds a conch and a lotus in her hands—the Lord of Śrī eats the food of six flavors from a pure vessel adorned with gold, making the row of guests laugh with his playful jests and smiles. He who is the thought-gem, the wish-fulfilling tree, the source of all opulence, and the ornament of all ornaments in the three worlds—having offered the golden ladle with curds, honey, and salt, and having honored the vision [of the deity], he partakes. Nivedana-mantra: May the Lord of Śrī eat, being respectfully fanned by Lakṣmī—who holds a conch and a lotus in her hands—as he sits comfortably with Brahmā, Īśa, and the others of the quarters; laughing at the row of guests with faces smiling in playful sport, he enjoys the six flavors in a pure vessel adorned with gold. He who is the thought-gem, the wish-fulfilling tree, the source of all power, and the ornament of all ornaments in the three worlds, having honored the sight with the golden ladle and offerings of curds, honey, and salt... [he partakes].

One should recite "Rājyo Rāmacandra," "Dinakara-kara-ugra-ratna-dīpāvalibhiḥ," "Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Govinda-Devetyādi," and so forth; thereafter, having performed the *japa* according to one's capacity, one should offer it to Hari with the mantra "Guhyātiguhye. Then, assuming the forms of Gajānana (Ganesha), Āditya (the Sun), Pañcāsya (Śiva), Śakti, and Siṃhāsya (Narasimha), and being honored by all, one should satisfy the Soul of All (Sarvātmā) for the sake of the two-fold welfare. Having properly established the fire in a well-cleansed sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) that has been duly prepared, one must certainly perform the oblations (*homa*). Thus end the services up to the food offering (*naivedya*). [In a sacrificial pit or altar] duly prepared according to the rules... in the fourfold...

Having brought the blazing Āhavaniya, Gārhapatya, and ordinary fires into the *rasnaka* (enclosure), one should abandon the flesh-eating (*kravyād*) portion in the southwest with the *astra-mantra*. One should then re-establish the divine portion in front with the *mūla-mantra*. This rite known as *agnyādhāna* (establishment of the fire) is required for the daily *homa*. It is held that the inspection is performed with the *mūla-mantra*, the sprinkling with the *śara-mantra*, the striking with *darbha* grasses, and the lustration with the *varma-mantra*. Then, having performed the *anvādhāna*, having sprinkled water around and strewn [the grass] according to rule, and having restrained the breaths, one should meditate upon Lakṣmī’s Lord (Viṣṇu) along with his limbs, weapons, and retinue.

Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*)—"I shall offer the expenditure of cooked food, substances, and water"—and remaining silent, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and sprinkle the *praṇītā* water with the root mantra. One should then perform the purification (*utpavana*) of the *pavitra* according to the rites of one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra*. [The mantras for the limbs of the fire-god are as follows: To the thousand-rayed one, the heart: *namaḥ*. To the auspicious and full one, the head: *svāhā*. To the rising person, the tuft (*śikhā*): *vaṣaṭ*. To the smoke-pervading one, the armor (*kavaca*): *haṃ*. To the seven-tongued one, the three eyes: *vauṣaṭ*. To the wielder of the bow, the weapon (*astra*): *phaṭ*. *Oṃ raṃ phaṭ*. *Oṃ vaisvānara jātaveda ihāvaha lohitākṣa sarvakarma...* [etc.]

*Maṇisādhaya svāhā*. Having thus invoked [the deity] and cast the fuel-sticks (*samidh*), one should kindle the all-pervading Fire with: *Oṃ citiṃ galad-vṛta-varūpa capa capa sarve śāpaya svāhā*. One should address the ignited Fire, the Jātavedas, the powerful one, golden-hued, like fire itself, kindled, facing in all directions: *Oṃ, may the rites beginning with the impregnation (*garbhādhāna*) of Agni—the progenitor of the entire world—be accomplished, svāhā*. [The mudrā: Having made the two hands equal at the base of the wrist, with the fingers extended and the middle fingers joined together, place the two thumbs in the middle of them.

One should cast [the oblation] with this mudrā called Saptajihvā (Seven-Tongued) and display it to Jātavedas. The seven tongues of the Fire-god are Hiraṇyā, Gaganā, Raktā, Kṛṣṇā, Pītā, Śvetā, and Bhāsvarā; they bestow all accomplishments and are meritorious. On the seat of the eight-formed Lord, one should first offer food and drink along with the limbs [of the ritual], and thereafter, O King, one should worship the Fire-golden-seeded (Hiraṇyaretas) according to the rules, together with Indra and the others. [The names of the fires are: Jātavedas, Saptajihva, Havyavāhana, Aśvodaraja, Vaiśvānara, Kaumāratejas, and Viśvadeva.

The forms of the twice-born [Brahmins] and the fires should be established with the syllable *vaṃ* at their mouths; in the center of the fire, one should prepare a pure seat and a circle for worship. One should invoke the Lord Rāmacandra together with his retinue.

Having performed the ritual placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*) upon this, one should display the mudrās as before. One should worship the Lord, along with the fire, with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps. If the sacrificial ladle (*sruva*) is unavailable, one should offer the oblation using the "deer-mudrā" (*mṛgamudrā*). Alternatively, one may use a leaf of the betel vine (*nāgavallī*) or a leaf of basil (*tulasī*). First, one should perform the two portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*) and then offer the oblation soaked in clarified butter.

One should protect this [offering] by enveloping it with the *kavaca* (armor) mantra and shielding it with the *astra* (weapon) mantra. Having sprinkled it with water and consecrated it (*abhimantrita*) with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), the wise one should offer oblations. Having recited the Lord of Mantras (*mantra-īśa*) together with the seed-syllable of the Power (*śakti-bīja*) as the "mouth of the fire" (*agnimukha*), one should then utter *svāhā*. The offering of the oblation at the end of the mantra constitutes its dedication; this applies to all oblations. Thus, at the beginning of the sacrifice, one should offer sixteen oblations along with the *śakti*. Then, one oblation each should be offered to the limbs of the God who is afflicted by arrows. There are thirty-two door-deities beginning with Gaṇeśa, forty-eight pedestal deities (*pīṭhadeva*) beginning with Maṇḍūka, and one hundred and eighteen [others].

The gods become the heart and so forth; one hundred and ninety-eight gods are proclaimed [as the recipients]. Having offered oblations to Gaṇeśa, Savitṛ, Maheśa, and Hrī, one should then offer the oblation of *brahmārpaṇa*. [The prayer is: "Whatever was done by me previously, through the authority of life-force (*prāṇa*), intellect (*buddhi*), body, and duty (*dharma*); in the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep; through mind, speech, and action; through the authority of mind, speech, and action in the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep; and whatever was remembered by the two hands, the two feet, the belly, and the organ of generation—"

"May everything be an offering unto Brahman. Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, hāḥ! This is salutation to Brahman. Having uttered the root mantra, saying "To the one with [his] limbs and weapons, svāhā; this salutation to Śrī Rāma," and having performed the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), he should perform the sweeping (*parisamūhana*). He should apply the *tryāyuṣa* mark on his forehead with the mantra beginning "That which Agni... He should fill the full vessel (*pūrṇapātra*) with water consecrated seven times and sprinkle himself with it, along with *kāśa*, *dūrvā*, and *tulasī* leaves. Having scattered a handful of flowers, being filled with devotion, he should offer the measure of food to the mouth of the consumer of oblations (the Fire).

One should offer an oblation to the Lord of the Thirty (Indra) with the mantra *udvāsya vahnim*, and to the Yoginīs of the Nakhayoga. Thus, in the daily homa (*nityahoma*), there are two hundred and twenty oblations;

for the limbs (*aṅgas*) and the three locations, there are three oblations each. This is the daily homa. Having offered the oblation of sacrificial food (*havis*) soaked in clarified butter (*ājya*) according to one-tenth of the number of recitations (*japa*), one should satisfy the Lord with water mixed with perfumes and flowers using the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*) according to one-tenth of that amount, saying: "I satisfy [the deity] along with his limbs" (*sāṅgaṃ gaṃ tarpayāmi*). Then, with those waters consecrated seven times according to one-tenth of that amount, one should bathe oneself.

One should sprinkle [the deity] with *durvā* grass and *tulasī* leaves. Having thus performed the libation (*tarpaṇa*) and the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), one should meditate upon Śrī Rāma as having assumed the form of the Lord of Restraint (*saṃyama-mūrti*) and arrived at the pedestal.

Then, from the primary portion intended for the Lord, one should set aside a portion of the vessel and the food offering (*naivedya*). Then, saying: "To Viṣvaksena, who is the embodiment of all gods, the Supreme, the Most Excellent, and who is joined by the army of Śrī Rāma," one should offer the water used for bathing (*tīrtha*) to the left of Rāmacandra.

This should be a hundredth or a thousandth part; otherwise, it shall be fruitless. One should likewise offer it to Gaṇeśa as Vakra-tuṇḍa and to the Sun as Caṇḍāṃśu. Having uttered [these names], [one should perform the offering].

"To the Caṇḍālī, to Śivā, and to Caṇḍeśvara"—thus the offering of the *bali* is made. Having said "Great Grace" (*mahāprasāda*), the wise should receive it with cupped hands; especially the food offering (*naivedya*), the foot-wash water, the scrapings from the base of the vessel, and the remains of the garland.

I bow to the Supreme Śrī Rāmacandra, who dwells in the pericarp of the lotus, laughing and joyfully caressing with his own hands the servants standing before him—headed by Viṣvaksena—who are eager and looking upon their master with the thought that they themselves are receiving [the offerings]. He speaks with words that delight them. Furthermore... [the text continues].

In the *Pariśiṣṭa*, it is stated: "The offering (*naivedya*) of Viṣṇu is remembered as pure by the gods, Siddhas, and sages; having eaten the offering of another deity, one should perform the *Candrāyaṇa* penance. Furthermore: "Leaves, flowers, fruits, and water that have been offered to Śiva (*śivanirmālya*) become entirely pure through contact with the *śāligrāma* stone. Such is the acceptance of the grace (*prasāda*). Having given water for rinsing the mouth (*gaṇḍūṣika*), one should then give water for sipping (*ācamana*).

Then, after rubbing the hands, one should offer camphor and ornaments such as earrings, and display the ten mudrās beginning with the conch (*śaṅkha*). Likewise, one should place the bow and arrow at the tips of the fingers of the left hand.

Having drawn that bow to the right, it is released with the index finger. One should offer betel nut (*lavaṇa*), *gaja*, *jātī*, *kaṅkola*, the powder of *kramuka* and *khādira*, camphor, *supuṭī* leaves, and betel leaf. Likewise, one should show a mirror, provide an umbrella and chowries, and perform a grand lustration (*nīrājana*) with auspicious and sacred *śāka-tulasī*.

Having recited Vedic mantras, one should then offer a handful of flowers; one should mutter prayers and bow to the Lord, saying, "Be gracious, O Blessed One. This [deity] is always to be meditated upon as the destroyer of humiliation and the granter of desired objects.

I worship your lotus feet, O Great Being, which are the abode of ultimate truth, bowed to by Śiva and Brahmā, the refuge for all, the remover of the distress of servants, and the boat for those seeking liberation from the ocean of worldly existence.

Having abandoned the royal splendor that is so difficult to relinquish and desired even by the gods, you went to the forest at the word of your righteous and noble elder; you pursued the illusory deer that appeared before you—O Great Being, I worship your lotus feet.

O Śrī Rāmacandra, O Bull among the Raghus, O Best of Kings, O Lord of Kings, O Rama, O Leader of the Raghus, O Lord of the Raghus, O Sovereign of Sovereigns, O Delight of the Raghus, O Rāmabhadra, today I am your servant.

I have gone for refuge to that pair of lotus feet of the Lord of the Raghus, which are honored by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, and whose stainless fame even now the assembly of kings sings as being as pervasive as the lords of the quarters, Indra and the bull. Homage to Rāma, the god who is devoted to Brahmanas, whose intellect is unshaken, who is the foremost among those whose verses rise upward, and upon whose shoulders the earth has been placed. I bow to that Sītā, in whose mind dwells Rāma—who is dark like the petal of a blue lotus, beautiful, and lotus-eyed—and who [is supported] by her two arms, two feet, and two knees.

A prostration with the mind, speech, and body, resembling a mountain peak, is declared to be the eight-limbed (*aṣṭāṅga*) salutation. By touching the ground with both knees, both arms, and the head before Viṣṇu, one attains the merit of deeds performed in the past.
One should give one cow to Vināyaka, two to the Sun, seventy to the Rudras, four to Keśava, and half of that as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for Śiva.

Then, one should fan the divine Śrī Rāma with fans and other articles; for his praise, the great mantras praised in the scriptures and those bestowing the nectar of immortality are recommended. Then Bharadvāja and Yājñavalkya [addressed] him...

He said: "O Blessed One, tell me which mantras please Śrī Rāma and by which he reveals his own Self. Yājñavalkya replied: "Instructed thus by Śrī Rāma, Brahmā again offered salutations with this sacrificial verse (*yāgāthā*) and praised the Supreme Lord, while meditating in his mind upon Mahāviṣṇu, the sustainer of the universe, Nārāyaṇa, the one free from ailment, the perfect bliss, pure consciousness, whose nature is the supreme light: 'Om! He who is indeed Śrī Rāmacandra is the Blessed Lord, the non-dual Supreme Bliss-Self; he is the full Brahman, the reality of Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ—to him alone [be salutation]... "

Salutations again and again to Him who is the one undivided essence, the soul of Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Suvah. (2) Oṃ! Salutations again and again to that very Lord Rāmacandra, who is Brahman-bliss, and by whom Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Suvah are enveloped. (4) Salutations again and again to that very Tāraka-Brahman, who is to be known as identical with all from the beginning, and who is Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Suvah. (4) Salutations again and again to that very one who is all the Vedas with their limbs (Aṅgas), their branches (Śākhās), and the Purāṇas, and who is Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Suvah. (6) Salutations again and again to that very one who is the five fires, and who is Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Suvah. (7) Salutations again and again to those seven sacrificial utterances (Vyāhṛtis), and who is Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Suvah. (8)

Salutations, salutations to Him alone who is the *sruk* (ladle), *bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svar*. 8. Salutations, salutations to Him alone who is the individual soul (*jīvātman*), *bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svar*. 9. Salutations, salutations to Him alone who is the inner self of all beings (*sarvabhūtāntarātman*), *bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svar*. 10.

Salutations, salutations to Him alone who is the Self (*ātman*) [manifesting as] the incarnations such as Kūrma and others, *bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svar*. 11. Salutations, salutations to Him alone who is the *praṇava*, *bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svar*. 12. Salutations, salutations to Him alone who is the self of the fourfold internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇacatuṣṭaya*), *bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svar*. 13. Salutations, salutations to Him alone who is the five great elements (*pañcamahābhūtāni*), *bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svar*.

To that which is downward-turned *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svar*, to it indeed be salutation after salutation. 15 To that which is downward-turned Manu, *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svar*, to it indeed be salutation after salutation. 16 To that which is downward-turned Yama, *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svar*, to it indeed be salutation after salutation. 17 To that which is downward-turned Antaka, *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svar*, to it indeed be salutation after salutation. 18 To that which is downward-turned Mṛtyu, *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svar*, to it indeed be salutation after salutation.

19 To that which is downward-turned Amṛta, *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svar*, to it indeed be salutation after salutation. 20 To that which is downward-turned Avidyā, *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svar*, to it indeed be salutation after salutation. 21 To that which is downward-turned Sarasvatī, *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svar*, to it indeed be salutation after salutation. 22

Salutations again and again to the Nyāla-lakṣmī who is Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ; salutations again and again to him. (23) Salutations again and again to the Nyā-gaurī who is Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ; salutations again and again to her. (24) Salutations again and again to the Nyā-jātakī who is Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ; salutations again and again to her. (25) Salutations again and again to the Nyā who is the three worlds—Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ; salutations again and again to her. (26) Salutations again and again to the Nyā who is the Sun—Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ;

salutations again and again to him. (28) Salutations again and again to the Nyā who is the stars—Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ; salutations again and again to her. (29) Salutations again and again to the Nyā who is the eight Vasus—Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ; salutations again and again to her. (30) And also to the Nyā who is... [the rest of the text follows].

Salutations, salutations to Him who is the eight world-protectors, Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ; salutations to Him alone. (31) And salutations to the other nine planets, Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ; salutations to Him alone. (32) And salutations to the other eleven Rudras, Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ; salutations to Him alone. (33) And salutations to the other twelve guardians of the directions, Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ; salutations to Him alone. (34) And salutations to whatever has been and whatever will be, Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ; salutations to Him alone. (35) And salutations to Him who pervades all directions of the cosmic egg, who is the Virāj, Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ; salutations to Him alone. And salutations to Hiraṇyagarbha, Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ; salutations to Him alone.

Salutations, salutations! (37) To that Mahādeva who is *bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ*, to him alone be salutations, salutations! (38) To that Maheśvara who is *bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ*, to him alone be salutations, salutations!

(39) To that Ukāra who is *bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ*, to him alone be salutations, salutations! (40) To that Ukāra who is *bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ*, to him alone be salutations, salutations! (40) "O Madhusūdana, this servant has committed offenses against you day and night; forgive me for them all. Having recited this mantra, one should prostrate and offer this prayer. Hari, the All-pervading Lord, forgives thousands of offenses. This alone is the way to [attain] Kṛṣṇa.

A prostration performed ten times is equal to the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of ten horse-sacrifices; one who performs ten horse-sacrifices returns to rebirth, but one who prostrates before Kṛṣṇa is for the sake of no further birth.
Whatever transgression one has committed through body, speech, mind, senses, intellect, or soul, following one's own nature, one should offer all of that to the Supreme Nārāyaṇa.

Whether good or bad, whatever action has been performed by me, O Lord Viṣṇu, accept all of that as my supreme worship. Thus, one should offer water from a conch-shell into the right hand of the Deity.

May the Lord, who possesses the forms of Gaṇeśa, the five-faced one (Śiva), Śakti, and Siṃha, and who is the delight of all souls through His equanimity, be pleased with me—thus is the offering of action. Even though there is no difference [between us], I nevertheless bow to You. Who am I? You are the ocean; the wave is not the ocean, nor is the ocean merely the wave. He whose pure and firm intellect is such that he thinks "I am He" and "He is I," and which is not destroyed by actions due to the severance of the sense of agency—even in adverse circumstances—he is indeed Sattva. "I am Sattva, and You are I; we are both the support of Being-Consciousness. May the delusion regarding the difference between us perish through Your Command.

"Since [the world] is vast, let there be the offering of oneself to You in that very same way. Adorned with the garlands, perfumes, garments, ornaments, and unguents used by You, we shall chant Your mantra as servants who eat the remnants (ucchiṣṭa-bhojin). O Lord, protect me, who have sought refuge, from the ocean of the house of death. When thus entreated, He who is a portion of Deva (Viṣṇu) says, "It is a great favor," and with supreme affection, He duly honors himself with the remnants of those scents, flowers, and so forth. Thus is the taking of the crest-lock (āśikhā-grahaṇa). Having meditated upon Rāma, one should chant the mantra until it resides in the heart. This is the most secret...

O Rāghava, one should offer this with the secret mantra: "O Lord of Ramā, whatever has been worshipped by me—though devoid of devotion, devoid of ritual action, and devoid of mantra—may that be complete for You, O Rāma. Having thus offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) and withdrawn the attendants (*āvaraṇas*) from Hari, one should pray: "O Lord of Rest, enter into my own food which has been purified through devotion. Then, having offered water for the feet (*pādya*), one should dismiss Hari along with His limbs. Having performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and the *ṛṅga* [ritual], and having made the dismissal gesture (*visarjanī-mudrā*), one should recite this mantra: "I am Rāma, I am not another. Thus is the dismissal. [One should contemplate] the Self constantly...

"Those who sport with Rāma, having honored Him, have no evil deed whatsoever, nor do they face calamities arising from sin"—so says the Śruti. Thus ends the third chapter in the *Śrīrāmārcanacandrikā*, composed by Ānandavana, disciple of the feet of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrī Mukundavana.

On the sixth day, during the division of the day, one should perform the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*): the sacrifice to the gods (*daiva*) is performed by means of oblation (*homa*); that to the spirits (*bhūta*) is by the offering of sacrificial food (*bali*); that to the ancestors (*pitṛ*) is by the gift of food to Brahmins; and that to the ancestors is also by the ancestral rite (*paitra*).

The *nṛyajña* (sacrifice to men) is fourfold: by giving food, or by providing water, or by honoring guests, or by performing funeral rites (*śrāddha*). The *brahmayajña* (sacrifice to Brahman) is performed through the chanting of the *Vedas*, the recitation of the *Purāṇas*, or by offering salutations and praise. Having thus performed these six parts, one should spend the eighth portion on the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas*. Among those, one should especially read the *Śrīmad Bhāgavata* with great reverence. Those by whom this *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* has not been heard, and by whom the Ancient Person (*Puruṣa*) has not been worshipped—by them, O gods on earth, this [scripture] has been stolen from their mouths.

The birth of those men who have not heard the life-story of the Lord, which extends to hundreds of millions of verses, is in vain; for each single syllable is meritorious and destroys even great sins. (Page 42a) In the dialogue between Śiva and Rāghava in the Padma Purāṇa: "Even if one has internalized the Vedas and knows the meaning of all the scriptures, if a person has not heard the Purāṇas, his vision does not truly reach [the truth]. I consider the meaning of the Purāṇas to be superior to the meaning of the Vedas. By treating the Purāṇa otherwise, one attains the womb of an animal; the river of stories flows toward Vaikuṇṭha without effort."

The virtuous take refuge in the Blessed One; let us enjoy the great festival of the Lord of Sacrifice in the three-fold path. Even the world of the Lord of Asuras is not to be served [by those who follow this].

Thus ends the procedure for the seventh part of the day in the narration of Hari’s stories. Having performed the twilight worship in the eighth part, and likewise having offered the Agnihotra according to the prescribed rite, one should then complete the oblation.

Such is the duty of the eighth part. Having performed the six-limbed ritual placement (*nyāsa*) preceded by breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), and having worshipped and performed the lustration (*nīrājana*) once, one should pray to the Lord of Jānakī.

"O Valīvāsā, understand the path of the master; come, O Rāghava, to the bedchamber with Sītā. Upon the Tilaka-pillow on the excellent couch, whose surface is variegated by the marks of the Lord of Serpents and which serves as a canopy for his own royal umbrella—there, honored by Śrī Sītā who acts as the crest-jewel of her noble lineage, and provided with soft head-covers and the like, the King, the illustrious Lord of Kośala, eternally reclines, bestowing the fruit of immeasurable merit. Thus ends the evening and morning worship of the bed by the twice-born and others, according to the Śruti.

Now, the *ktaśayana* (lying down after eating) is described as being equal to the *agnihotra* sacrifice for the satisfaction of Rāma, O dear one. Having become pure with washed feet, one should eat auspicious food with clarified butter. Indeed, unasked food (*ayācita*) is superior to fasting; food obtained without cooking (*apākita*) is superior to unasked food; and the *nakta* meal is superior even to that for the sake of the Discus-wielding Lord. Therefore, for the satisfaction of the Supreme Lord, a Brahmin devoted to Viṣṇu should especially be intent upon the *nakta* vow to remove the sins of the day. Upon seeing the food, he should bow to it, saying, "May this be for us," and should recite the *Gāyatrī* mantra at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), saying, "Thou art splendor."

One should reverently sprinkle the offered food with water while reciting the mantras beginning with "satyaṃ tvartena. Then, one should eat the food after it has been consecrated seven times with the King of Mantras, saying: "To Dharmarāja, to Citra, and to Citragupta, Svāhā! By this, one becomes radiant, fortunate, prosperous, healthy, and long-lived. "Food is Brahmā, its essence is Viṣṇu, and the eater is the god Maheśvara; he who eats knowing this is not tainted by the faults of food. "You move within all beings, in their secret cave, facing in every direction. You are the sacrifice, you are the exclamation Vaṣaṭ, and you are the supreme abode of Viṣṇu. You..."

Having used [these], and being adorned with garlands, incense, garments, ornaments, and unguents, we—the servants who eat the remnants—may conquer that Māyā of yours. Reciting thus, "Thou art the nectar that carries across," the wise man should consume the water from the Lord’s holy feet (*śrītīrtha*) mixed with *tulasī* before the fire. In the center, toward the directions of Indra, Varuṇa, the Moon, and Yama, as well as the intermediate points, he should place the ear-rings representing the *Anvāhāryapacana*, *Āhavanīya*, *Gārhapatya*, *Sabhya*, and *Āvasathya* fires. With the mantra "Oṃ, he makes it a household; svāhā to Prāṇa," and "To Hiraṇya, svāhā," he should perform the *Prāṇāgnihotra*.

From the ring finger and the thumb in succession, saying "To Anvāhāryapacana, Svāhā," the wise one should offer the second oblation with the red-colored *sruva* ladle using the pair of the little finger and the thumb.

Saying "To Vyāna, to Āhavanīya, Svāhā," he should offer the third oblation with the black-colored *sruc* ladle using the pair of the middle finger and the thumb. Saying "To Udāna, to Sabhya, Svāhā," he should likewise offer the fourth oblation with the bright-colored *sruc* ladle using the pair of the index finger and the thumb. Saying "To Samāna, to Āvasathya, Svāhā," [he should offer the fifth oblation] with the bright-colored *sruc*.

One should offer the fifth oblation with all the fingers. One who daily eats the remains of the food offering (naivedya) mixed especially with *tulasī* and the water from the feet of Viṣṇu, the Enemy of Tripura, obtains the merit of ten million sacrifices. One should not eat what is forbidden, nor even ghee that is not purified. Likewise, in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, it is said: during both twilights, while reciting prayers, while eating, when one is blind, during ancestral rites (*pitṛkārya*), and likewise before a deity, after voiding urine or excrement, in the presence of elders, when giving a gift, and especially when performing obeisance—[one should remain silent].

A person who eats while sitting on a clean seat attains heaven. One should not eat with hands other than those [usually used], nor drink from anything other than a vessel. Having set aside the right hand, one should place the water-pot on the left. That food which is brought without being placed in a vessel becomes unfit for consumption, as does that which is brought by a woman who has drunk liquor. Once satisfied, one should place the remainder of the food on the ground for the satisfaction of the destitute. "May this gift given by me stand inexhaustible for the sake of the wretched ones who dwell anywhere, their souls seized by hunger and thirst. One should cover the vessel with water from a sacred site (*tīrtha*), saying, "You are the repository of nectar," and should offer half of the remainder to the portion of the earth.

Having sipped water properly for the satisfaction of the ancestors who have fallen into misfortune, one should pour water upon the big toe of the right foot with the mantra: "The Person the size of a thumb resides within the thumb;

the Lord of the entire world, the Master, the Consumer of all, may He grant us life. Then, being content with truth and surrounded by disciples, one should recite the mantras of Annapati (the Lord of Food), beginning with "O Lord of Food, bestow food upon me," and so forth: "May Agastya, Agni, and Vānala consume this food; may they digest this food entirely along with me, and may there be happiness arising from its digestion."

"May Viṣṇu, the Lord who is the primary being within all the senses and the body, grant me freedom from disease and eternal life; by that truth, may this remaining food become a source of health for me. Then, having eaten, he should chew betel leaf through the grace of the Lord of Jānakī, and together with his dear and disciplined disciples, he should chant the divine and auspicious name of the Blessed One. Thus concludes the Prāṇāgnihotra.

Having performed the purification rite with earth, washed his feet, and sipped water twice while remembering the Lord of the Universe, the King of Kośala, the illustrious Śrī Rāma, he should partake of the warm [food].

Drinking the nectar-like words that flow like streams of glory, and having wiped his pair of feet with a cloth, one should lie down upon the bed and sleep immediately. He who constantly remembers Rāma, Skanda, Hanumān, Aja (Rāma), and Vṛkodara (Bhīma) while lying on the bed does not see bad dreams. Having remembered the *Mūla-mantra*, one should recite the *Rāma-rakṣā* for the pacification of obstacles. By means of the verse beginning with "gurvarthe" (Oṃ gurvarthe...), a woman may sleep happily without distraction. He who approaches his wife only during her fertile period (*ṛtu*) and remains devoted solely to his own wife is to be known as a perpetual celibate (*brahmacārī*). He is indeed a knower of Brahman.

The sixteenth night of the lunar fortnight is the time for the *āśrama* (the householder stage); among those sixteen nights, four are highly recommended for the giving away of a daughter. Among these, one should avoid the even-numbered nights and specifically the asterisms of *Candramas*, *Sanduṣya*, *Maghā*, and *Mūla*. Being pure, one should approach his wife during an asterism named after a male deity, especially so that she may give birth to a son who accomplishes the goals of human existence (*puruṣārtha*). By following the path laid down in the scriptures composed by sages such as Manu, one is not bound by the snares of artificial desires and attains the state of Śrī Rāmacandra.

Thus ends the procedure for retiring to bed; thus ends the duty for the first watch of the night. May there be salutation to Śrī Rāmacandra. Now, the *puraścaraṇa* (preliminary rite) of this King of Mantras is described.

Without which, a practitioner of mantras (*mantrī*) would not achieve success even in hundreds of years. Having received the excellent mantra from a guru—who is pleased by devotion, faith, and the offering of desired gifts—the wise one, observing fixed vows and remaining pure, should daily worship as before and recite [the mantra] six thousand times, one thousand times, or one hundred and eight times. Thus propitiated...

When Rāma awakens one's devotion, then—having performed the *puraścaraṇa* either at the beginning or the end [of the period]—the knower of the Self, having restrained himself internally and externally according to his capacity, should perform everything like the *puraścaraṇa*, with the exception of the fire-oblation (*homa*). Thus is the preliminary rite; thereafter, having made a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), he should diligently perform the *puraścaraṇa*. For a long time, without interruption, with self-restraint and firm vows, on a mountain peak, in the midst of water, on the shore of the salt ocean, on a riverbank, at the root of a holy fig tree (*aśvattha*), or in a beautiful grove of *bilva* trees...

It is recommended [to beg] in places facing east or north, in temples of Śiva, in areas free from bulls and the like, in groves of Aśvattha, Bilva, and Tulasī, amidst other flowering trees, in cow-pens, at holy fords (tīrthas), and in sacred fields. Thus, alms should be sought from those who follow Vedic conduct, who are pure, prosperous, and born of noble families. Or, one may eat the food of a Brahmin (agrajanman) who consumes only sacrificial offerings, vegetables, barley-meal (yāvaka), roots, fruits, or whatever is obtained there—such as the root, fruit, milk, or curd mentioned in the Gautamīya.

"Alms-food, rice-gruel, flour-cakes, vegetables, roots, and the eight kinds of grain—these are said by the wise to be the food for the practitioner. Such are the rules regarding what may be eaten. One should avoid salt, sugar, alkaline substances, honey, meat, and other [forbidden] flavors. One should also avoid black gram, mung bean, lentils, and the like, as well as *kodrava* and chickpeas. One should avoid speaking untruthfully, eating the food of others, worshipping another deity, eating at improper times, and likewise eating at night or from an unworthy person. One should avoid women, *śūdras*, outcasts (*patita*), those who have fallen from their vows (*vrātya*), atheists, and foul speech. One should avoid speaking untruthfully, speaking deceitfully, and speaking harshly; one should not speak even when it is the truth [if it is harmful]. *pṛ0 44a)* [End of page 44a] (Note: The text provided contains a mix of Sanskrit and Prakrit/Pali-like forms, such as *bhikṣānna-sakta-daḥ-sākam-dāṣṭa-vidham*. The translation reflects the intended meaning of the ritual and dietary restrictions common in Tantric and Śaiva traditions.)

In the performance of recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and other rites, he should always remain free from desire through speech, mind, and action; he should avoid listening to songs, poetry, and the like, as well as constantly looking at women and such objects.

One should completely avoid betel, the application of perfumes, the wearing of flowers, sexual intercourse, conversation concerning it, and social gatherings centered upon it. One should also avoid deceit, honey, oil massage, eating food that has not been offered, and actions performed without a formal resolve, as well as massages and the like. Abandoning bathing with hot water and the use of fragrant *āmalaka* and similar substances, one should purify the head and body internally and externally with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*). These are the things to be avoided. One should bathe with *pañcagavya* and with pure *āmalaka*, and perform the ritual bath while reciting the mantras declared in the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, and *Purāṇas*. One should bathe at dawn.

If one is unable [to bathe] at the three daily junctures (*triṣavaṇa*), one may otherwise perform it once; such are the rules for bathing. Having made a circle divided into nine squares, one should draw the form of a tortoise (*kūrma*).

One should place pairs of vowels in order in the eight directions starting from the east (*indra*), and the consonant groups (*varṇas*) beginning with *ka* in the remaining spaces, ending with *kṣa* in the center as the lord of the vessel (*sthālādhipa*). That square where the first syllable of the name [of the person] is located on the head of the tortoise is the "illuminator" (*dīpaka*). The two squares on its sides are the two hands; below them are the belly and the feet. The remaining square becomes the tail, and the letter *si* is at the mouth.

Wisdom is supreme when situated at the head; however, in the great belly of afflictions, one may encounter suffering. If it is at the feet, there will be poverty; likewise, if at the tail, there will be pain through imprisonment and the like.

One seeking liberation should place it in the mouth; for subjugation (*ābhicārika*), in the south; one desiring prosperity (*śrī*) should be in the west; and in the north, this [wisdom] becomes the bestower of peace. In the northeast (*īśāna*), there is the destruction of enemies; in the southeast (*āgneya*), it is the illuminator of enemies; in the southwest (*naiṛta*), there is the crushing of enemies; and in the northwest (*vāyavya*), there is escape. Whether in a village or in a forest, wherever one looks, or by a river—[the same applies].

One who desires the success of all undertakings should not perform recitation (*japa*) without knowing the *Kūrma-cakra*; for one who performs it without such knowledge, there is no fruit from the recitation, and it leads to all manner of misfortune. Thus ends the section on the *Kūrma-cakra*. A wise person should prepare a seat upon a superior *kuśa* grass mat or a deerskin, arranged in the order of the *Svastika* and other postures; then, free from distraction, he should sit upon it according to his purpose.
