For the rite of paralyzing (*staṃbhana*), an elephant hide is used; likewise, for killing (*māraṇa*), a buffalo hide; for driving away (*uccāṭana*), a sheepskin; and for the rite of subjugation (*vaśya*), a sword-skin. A cloth seat causes disease, while a seat of *vetra* grass brings great prosperity. Silk (*kauśeya*) [brings] power (*pau*...).

A seat made of straw causes the destruction of one's work; a blanket is difficult to release from; a bamboo seat brings poverty; a wooden seat brings misfortune; sitting on the bare ground results in the accumulation of suffering; and sitting on a stone results in the arising of pain. Sitting on grass takes away one's reputation; these are the common [faults] regarding the seat during recitation (*japa*). As for the rosaries (*akṣamālā*) for a householder, they should consist of twelve types of beads: rudrākṣa, śaṅkha, lotus seeds, putrajīvaka, pearls, crystal, gems, gold, coral, kusha grass, and bamboo joints. Counting with the fingers yields a single merit, while counting with a cord yields eightfold merit.

A rosary made of *putrajīva* seeds is tenfold [in merit], one of conch shells is a hundredfold, one of coral or precious gems (*maṇiratna*) is a thousandfold, and one of crystal is said to be ten-thousandfold. One of pearls is declared to be a hundred-thousandfold, one of lotus seeds (*padmākṣa*) is ten-hundred-thousandfold, and one of gold is said to be ten-millionfold. A rosary of *kuśa*-grass knots yields a hundred-millionfold, while one of *rudrākṣa* beads yields an infinite result.
A rosary fashioned from beads of *lasīkā* wood grants the fruits of all desired objects for all rites; it should consist of one hundred and eight or fifty [beads].

The rosary should be made with twenty-seven beads plus four [additional ones] for general purposes; one seeking liberation should recite with twenty-five, one seeking wealth with thirty, and one seeking nourishment with twenty-seven. For malevolent rites (abhicāra), it should be made with fifteen. In the case of the Mātṛkā, it should consist of the letters in direct and reverse order, excluding the *visarga* and including *kṣa*. It may also be made with the eight groups of consonants (*aṣṭavarga*). Among these, the "womb" (*yonimālā*) is auspicious. It should be shaped like a cow's tail, having a single neck and including the *meru* bead. One should join mouth to mouth and attach tail to tail. When obtained...

On page 45a): Having fashioned the rosary for the accomplishment of that rite with threads of various colors such as red and so forth, one should then begin the consecration (saṃskāra). One should wash it with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) while reciting the *Sadyojāta* mantra, and purify it with pure water while reciting the *Vāmadeva* mantra. One should fumigate it with incense while reciting the *Aghora* mantra, and anoint it while reciting the *Puruṣa* mantra. One should consecrate each bead individually one hundred times with the fifth mantra alone; likewise, one should consecrate the central bead (*meru*) with that same fifth mantra. One should recite the very same mantra by which the rosary was installed. A wise person should not perform the recitation of another mantra [for this purpose].

One should never touch [the beads] with the fingers; one should not allow them to fall from the hand. One should know that the thumb grants liberation, the index finger destroys enemies, the middle finger leads to the attainment of wealth, and the ring finger is for rites of pacification (*śāntika*). The little finger is to be used for attracting (*karṣaṇa*) and bestows success in the act of recitation (*japa*). Any rite performed without the thumb becomes fruitless.

One should not touch the thread with the index finger, nor should one shake it or wave it about. One should perform the circumambulation starting from the base of the ring finger, moving clockwise around the middle joint of the thumb.

One should recite [the mantra] nine times in succession, from the middle finger down to the root (the little finger), across the ten joints: Oṃ sadyojātaṃ prapadyāmi sadyojātāya vai namaḥ | bhave bhave nātibhave bhajasva māṃ bhavodbhavāya namaḥ || 1 Oṃ vāmadevāya namo jyeṣṭhāya namaḥ śreṣṭhāya namo rudrāya namaḥ kālāya namaḥ kalavikaraṇāya namo balavikaraṇāya namo balāya namo balapramathanāya namaḥ sarvabhūtadamanāya namo mano-nmanāya namaḥ || 2 [The offering of] arghya...

"From the fierce ones, from the terrible ones, from those more terrible than the terrible—O Śarva, salutations be unto you from all your forms! Oṃ, we know that Puruṣa, we meditate upon Mahādeva; may Rudra impel us. "Oṃ, Īśāna is the lord of all sciences, the lord of all beings, the overlord of Brahman, the overlord of the Veda; may Brahman be auspicious to me, Sadāśiva! This is the characteristic of the rosary for recitation (*japa*); the repetition of syllables in *japa* may be loud, whispered, or mental, and performed with high, low, or circumflex (*svarita*) accents.

One should recite the mantra with speech using clear words and syllables; that is the *vācika* (vocal) sacrifice. Reciting the mantra hundreds of times while moving the lips slightly so that it is somewhat audible is known as *upāṃśu* (whispered) recitation. When one recites the sequence of syllables consisting of letters, vowels, and words within the mind, while recollecting their meaning, that is remembered as *mānasa* (mental) recitation. Whispered recitation is ten times more effective than vocal recitation, while mental recitation is remembered as being a thousand times more effective than whispered recitation. Mantras established in the state of *paśu* consist solely of the form of letters. In the *sauṣupta* (deep sleep) state...

Those who recite [the mantra] with devotion attain lordship; the Lord of Mantras belongs to one who has risen from the ninefold [state]. O Sage, one should know that the single [mantra] consists of a recitation of one hundred thousand repetitions according to the prescribed rule.

One should contemplate the syllables of the mantra as being strung upon a thread like jewels. She alone reveals the supreme, most excellent, and expanded Supreme Nectar—the true nature of the Self—even without worship or fire-offerings (homa).
There is no fault in mental recitation at all times and in all places. O best of the twice-born, one intent on recitation obtains the fruit of all sacrifices; indeed, of all sacrifices...

The sacrifice of recitation (*japa-yajña*) is praised; because it involves no injury to living beings, it yields great fruit. "Among sacrifices, I am the sacrifice of recitation," said the Blessed Lord Hari. As long as our ritual sacrifices (*karma-yajña*) remain unkindled, they do not equal even a sixteenth part of the sacrifice of recitation. Through recitation, the deities are constantly praised and become propitious; being pleased, they bestow abundant enjoyments and eternal liberation. For those desiring spiritual perfection, the sacrifice should be mental; for those desiring nourishment, it should be whispered (*upāṃśu*); or it may be performed aloud.

Recitation (*japa*) is praised as being of two kinds: *cikitsita* (therapeutic) and *māraṇa* (destructive). In the *Mantradevaprakāśikā*, it is stated that recitation is recommended in the presence of the Sun, Fire, Guru, Indra, the Moon, Water, Brahmins, and Cows;

one should recite facing them directly. Concentration of the mind on the syllables of the mantra, silence, reflection on the meaning of the mantra, freedom from distraction, and absence of anger are the causes for the perfection of recitation. One should never recite while wearing a turban, a bodice, at night, with disheveled hair, covered in dirt, without the ritual ring (*pavitra*) on the hand, while speaking incoherently, or while unclothed.

Having placed both hands over the head and covered it, or being distracted by anxiety, angry, bewildered, afflicted by hunger, fasting, walking, or rising [from sleep], one should not recite [the mantra] while on a street, in an inauspicious place, or in the midst of darkness. Likewise, with feet hidden by shoes, or while lying down or on a bed, one should not recite; nor should one extend the feet or sit in the *kukkuṭāsana* (cock-fighting posture).

Upon seeing, speaking to, or hearing outcasts (*antyaja*), or upon injury, the passing of wind, or yawning, one should abandon the recitation. Having encountered these [conditions], one should perform *ācamana* and six rounds of *prāṇāyāma*.

Having performed the *gaka* (the ritual purification), one should recite the mantra correctly until the appearance of the sun and other celestial bodies. Upon seeing a cat, a cock, a crane, a dog, a Śūdra, a donkey, or a monkey, one should perform *ācamana* (ritual sipping of water) and then carry out the rite; having touched them, bathing is prescribed.

Whether impure or pure, whether walking, standing, or even sleeping, the wise man who has the mantra as his sole refuge should always practice it with the mind alone. Recitation at home is said to be standard; in a cow-pen it is remembered as being a hundredfold; likewise in a beautiful garden, it is said to be a thousandfold. On a mountain it is ten thousandfold, and by a river it is ten times that; they say it is ten millionfold in a temple, and infinite in a sacred place (*śiva-sthāna*).

If one is capable, one should perform all of this in the presence of the deity; if incapable, one should recite according to one's ability. Whether desiring liberation or not a devotee, one remains within the scope of the injunctions. As it is stated in the Śrīmad Bhāgavata: "One should perform ritual actions as long as one does not become detached, or until faith arises in hearing My stories and so forth. This Rāma-mantra is especially effective when consecrated. Such is the characteristic of the recitation (*japa*). One should constantly recite the Supreme Person (*Puruṣottama*) with self-restraint three times a day, worshipping Him without distraction, until ten lakhs have been completed. [Then follows] the libation (*tarpaṇa*).

Having worshipped with water as before, accompanied by flowers, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), and other offerings, using a pure practitioner who has performed ten parts (*daśāṃśa*) of the ritual according to the prescribed method; then, having invoked Rāma into the fire as previously described, one should worship Him with bilva fruits, flowers, and leaves. One should offer lotuses mixed with the three sweets (*madhuratraya*), or sesame seeds, or any one of these. Thereafter, one should feed the Brahmins. Worship performed at the three times of day, daily recitation (*japa*), libation (*tarpaṇa*), burnt offering (*homa*), feeding the Brahmins, and eating—this is called *puraścaraṇa* for a mantra received from a guru, once it has been made propitious according to the rules.

(p. 46b) This seat of the five [elements] (pañcāṅgāsanam) is prescribed for the sake of accomplishment (siddhi). Even for those free from desire, direct realization (sākṣātkāra) shall occur through this alone; however, for those with desire, the attainment of worldly objects is the result. If it is not so, then all of that is fruitless. The wise man who performs this Pañcāgama before the [deity] conquers the world through knowledge, sovereignty, sons, and other blessings. At the beginning, the middle, and the end, he should feed many Brahmins out of devotion, dedicating it to the Garden (Rāma), day by day according to his capacity. When the Brahmins have been well-fed, that rite becomes complete in its limbs (sāṅga) and fruitful. In this cycle of existence (saṃsāra), which abounds in suffering, if one desires—

One should worship Rāma with devotion through the five-limbed adoration (*pañcāṅgopāsana*) for the sake of one’s own happiness. This five-limbed adoration performed with devotion is called *puraścaraṇa*. This is the best among the methods of the wise and is the cause for cutting asunder the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*). "O ascetic, there is no dharma like this, no austerity like this, and no means for attaining desired goals like this. If one is unable to perform the fire-oblation (*homa*), the worship (*pūjā*), or the libation (*tarpaṇa*), then the *puraścaraṇa* may be accomplished, O noble one, by reciting the mantra that many times [as required] and by honoring Brahmins. If any limb [of the ritual] is omitted...

If [a limb] were to be omitted, a recitation (japa) twice that number must be performed for the sake of accomplishing the ancillaries (aṅgas). If one is unable to do that, one should perform it with devotion; whichever limb is omitted, by that much one will fail to obtain the desired result. If any rite should be deficient in its limbs, it cannot be a means for achieving the desired goal. To achieve the perfection of having all limbs complete, one should feed Brahmins for the sake of all goals. By the mere propitiation of Brahmins, even a rite lacking limbs attains completeness. Alternatively: "From the japa, the fire-oblation (homa) should be one-tenth; from that, the libation (tarpaṇa) one-tenth; the sprinkling (mārjana) one-tenth of that; and the feeding one-tenth of that. Thus [is the procedure]. This is the additional [instruction] regarding the Drāviḍa [tradition].

When the king of mantras has been thus perfected, one should then accomplish the ritual applications (*prayoga*). These are: *granthana* (stringing), *vidarbha* (interlacing), *saṃpuṭa* (enclosing), *rodhana* (obstructing), *yoga*, and *pallava*; these six are to be known as being for the six types of rites. One should know that *granthana* is the method of placing the letters of the name [of the target] between the letters of the mantra according to rule; it is highly recommended for rites of pacification (*śāntika*). One should write the letters of the name of the person to be acted upon situated between pairs of the mantra’s letters; this is to be understood by practitioners as *vidarbha*, used for rites of subjugation (*vaśya*). That which has the name at the beginning, the end, and in the middle is known as *saṃpuṭa*.

(p. 47a) "This is to be known as *saṃstambhana* (paralysis/stilling), so it is said by those who know the mantras. At the beginning or at the end, the name should be placed; that is the method for its obstruction (*rodhana*). This is declared to be praised in the procedures for *vidveṣaṇa* (enmity). In the case of *uccāṭana* (expulsion), the name should be at the end of the mantra; this is considered the proper application. In *māraṇa* (killing), the mantra should be at the end of the name; this is considered the 'sprout' (*pallava*) method. Thus, having fully understood the knowledge of the six 'sprouts' and the arising of the principles (*tattva*), one should perform the rites as is appropriate. One should perform *stambhana* when the earth-principle (*kṣmātattva*) arises, and *śāntika* (pacification) through the water-principle (*ambhas-tattva*). *Vaśya* (subjugation) and *ākarṣaṇa* (attraction) occur when the fire-principle (*tejas-tattva*) arises. [In] *uccāṭana*...

One should know that killing (*māraṇa*) occurs in the principles of air (*vāyu*) and space (*vyoman*). That principle is known to be doubled by the letters situated in the *vidu* (the triangle). This is the knowledge of the principles (*tatvajñāna*).

For rites such as pacification (*śāntika*), one should employ sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) shaped like a lotus: a four-cornered (*catur-asra*), a triangular (*tri-asra*), a crescent-shaped (*ardha-candra*), a circular (*vṛtta*), a six-cornered (*ṣaḍ-asraka*), and an eight-cornered (*aṣṭāsra*) one. Regarding the fires: pacification (*śāntika*) and the auspicious nourishment (*pauṣṭika*) should be performed in a common (*laukika*) fire; subjugation (*stambhana*) is said to be in a fire from a *vaṭa* tree; and killing (*māraṇa*) in a fire from a cremation ground (*śmaśāna*). Enmity (*vidveṣa*) is in a fire from a *vibhītaka* tree. These are considered the foremost among the six ritual acts (*ṣatkarma*). These are the fires. [The measurement of] the finger... [text ends].

One should recite [the mantra] with the ring fingers in rites of expulsion; one should recite with the thumb and middle fingers for the sake of achieving attraction (*ākṛṣṭi*); through the union of the index finger and the thumb, there shall be enmity (*vidveṣa*) and eradication (*uccāṭana*);

and one should recite with the little finger and the thumb in the rite of killing (*māraṇa*). This is the knowledge of recitation (*japa-jñāna*). In the winter season, one should perform propitiatory recitation (*pauṣṭika*) from sunrise until the end of the first watch (*yāma*).

During the cold season (*śiśira*), one should perform the recitation for killing during the first two watches of the night. In the spring, one should recite from after the first watch until midday; therein, the work of attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*) of the desired object should be performed with mantras. In the summer... [text fragment ends].

One who is deluded by the third fever [should perform] the rite of causing hatred; thereafter, until the sun has set, one should effect expulsion (*uccāṭana*) at the onset of the rainy season. At midnight, with speech restrained, one should mutter the mantra for the sake of the quarters, as Vasiṣṭha has said: "In whatever season the auspicious accomplishment of mantras is to be performed, it should be done in the forenoon for subjugation and nourishment; at midday for the destruction of affection; in the afternoon for expulsion; likewise at twilight for killing;
and at midnight for pacification; and after this, all rites [may be performed]. This is the knowledge of seasons. Subjugation (*vaśya*) occurs when facing the east.

(Page 47b) One should know that the rite of sorcery (*ābhicārika*) is in the south, wealth (*dhana*) in the west, and pacification (*śāntika*) in the north. Furthermore, attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*) is in the southwest (*nairṛta*), killing (*māraṇa*) likewise in the southwest, expulsion (*uccāṭana*) in the northwest (*vāyavya*), and the bestower of liberation (*mokṣadāyaka*) in the northeast (*īśāna*). Such is the rule for the directions. Regarding the lunar days (*tithi*): the second, third, and fifth days of the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*), when conjoined with Mercury, Jupiter, or Venus, are prescribed by the wise for rites of pacification (*śāntika*). Likewise, the seventh, sixth, thirteenth, fourth, and ninth days, when conjoined with the Moon, Jupiter, or Venus, are determined by the wise for rites of prosperity (*pauṣṭika*). Also, the eighth, ninth, tenth, and eleventh days [are similarly used].

When joined with Venus or Saturn, these [days] are auspicious for the rite of enmity (*vidveṣa*). Therefore, the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, Saturday, and likewise the eighth day are praised for *uccāṭana* (eradication), as spoken by Śaṅkara.

The new moon, the eighth day of the dark fortnight, and similarly the fourteenth day, when joined with Sunday, its son (Saturday), or Mars, are commended for killing (*māraṇa*), paralyzing (*stambhana*), recitation (*japa*), and fire-offerings (*homa*). This is the determination of the lunar days (*tithi-nirṇaya*). Having performed one hundred thousand or half that number of recitations, or a tenth part thereof, and having offered oblations with white lotuses or bilva fruits according to the desired goal, whatever is wished for is attained.

If one offers oblations into the fire with flowers of the *aiśvaryya* tree, one shall attain sovereignty; by offering *pālāśa* flowers, one becomes wise and a knower of the Vedas. By offering either *dūrvā* grass or *guḍūcī* stalks, or even unbroken grains (*akṣata*) individually, one becomes free from disease, long-lived, and a treasury of austerity. One desiring health should eat food consecrated with mantras; by drinking water purified by the *sumedhā* mantra, one becomes a poet. By the immediate homa of medicines prescribed for a disease, one is liberated from that ailment at once. And by offering *jātī* flowers sprinkled thoroughly with sandalwood water into the fire...

One should bring even a king under one's control by meditating on Rāma as the God of Love (Manmatha) and remembering Sītā as Rati. In all rites for subjugation, such as recitation (*japa*) and fire-oblations (*homa*), one obtains the desired wealth by offering fresh red lotuses. By properly offering blue lotuses, one may indeed subjugate the entire world. Having worshipped Rāma according to the rules, the practitioner who knows the ritual application, having offered blue lotuses into a blazing fire, may properly subjugate the entire world. Having worshipped Rāma according to the rules, the practitioner who knows the ritual application, [should offer] with a vessel joined with a stream of honey...

By sacrificing with *yava* seeds, one certainly attains sovereignty over all and freedom from enmity; of this there is no doubt. By offering *vilva* blossoms, *kumuda* lilies, and even *vilva* leaves, the practitioner of the mantra (*mantrasādhaka*) obtains prosperity before long. O Sage, having propitiated Rāma in the orb of the moon for a year—reciting the mantra with undistracted mind from sunrise until sunset—the fruit that results for him is auspicious and difficult even for the gods to attain. One who desires royal power and the enjoyment of pleasures should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times with undistracted mind, and perform a fire sacrifice (*homa*) with lotuses or *vilva* blossoms consisting of one-twelfth of that number. This should be done on the shore of the ocean or in a cow-pen.

One who has performed one hundred thousand recitations (*lakṣajāpa*) while observing the milk-vow (*payobrata*) shall become a treasury of knowledge by offering oblations of milk-rice (*pāyasa*) mixed with clarified butter (*ājya*). He whose sovereignty has been exhausted should subsist on vegetables and, standing within water, perform one hundred thousand recitations and offer oblations with *bilva* flowers in the tenth part (*daśāṃśa*) of that number; then his own sovereignty will surely return to him, there is no doubt. Having fasted and worshipped Rāma while staying within the waters of the Gaṅgā or other such rivers, one should perform one hundred thousand recitations and offer oblations in the tenth part of that number using lotuses, sesame seeds, or *bilva* blossoms mixed with the three sweets (*madhuratra*). Even one of meager fortune shall obtain a kingdom, prosperity, and the service of others.

If one desires the wishes of others, one should remain in the water during the month of Māgha, subsisting on roots, tubers, and fruits; one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times and perform a fire sacrifice with milk-rice (pāyasa) ten thousand times for the sake of obtaining sons and grandsons, O Nirmala. The remainder is generally for the beloved wife. O Prajāpati, even the son and grandson of one who beholds Śrī Rāma become powerful. When a minister is overcome and insulted by powerful enemies, he should then recite the name of the enemy ending in "hata" (slain), while meditating on the descendant of Raghu as enraged like another fire of cosmic destruction, with his bow drawn and arrows ready.
Having thus meditated upon the great hero Rāma, who stands upon the chariot of Indra on the battlefield, destroying all enemies with showers of sharp arrows from his circle of arms;

and [upon Lakṣmaṇa and the other great heroes] who, raising trees and rocks with their hands, roar with fierce *huṃkāras*, *bhobhokāras*, and great shouts, running about in battle toward Rāvaṇa—the practitioner of the mantra, remaining without food, should again offer oblations with *śālmalī* flowers ten times the number [of the recitation]. Even if he is possessed of supreme sovereignty and prosperity, no enemy shall remain; [he shall destroy] the foe, Rāvaṇa.

Having meditated thus and having visualized himself as the scion of Raghu, one should effortlessly accomplish all that [previously described]. Contemplating the Lord of the Raghus while remaining without food and dwelling in water, one should recite the mantra over a quantity of sesame seeds ten times the number of recitations and offer them as oblations; this will paralyze the host of enemies. Having placed the seed-syllable of Vāyu (Yaṃ) at the end and visualizing the enemy—distressed by the search for Sītā—one causes even a mountain-like foe to wander about visibly before long. Furthermore, there are many other applications of the syllable "Sī" within this King of Mantras. Moreover: [Page 48b] ...having meditated thus and having visualized himself as the scion of Raghu, one should effortlessly accomplish all that [previously described]. Contemplating the Lord of the Raghus while remaining without food and dwelling in water, one should recite the mantra over a quantity of sesame seeds ten times the number of recitations and offer them as oblations; this will paralyze the host of enemies. Having placed the seed-syllable of Vāyu (Yaṃ) at the end and visualizing the enemy—distressed by the search for Sītā—one causes even a mountain-like foe to wander about visibly before long. Furthermore, there are many other applications of the syllable "Sī" within this King of Mantras. Moreover: [The text continues with further ritual applications. (Note: The provided source text contains repetitive and fragmented Sanskrit verses regarding specific tantric rituals involving the visualization of Rāma, the recitation of mantras, the use of seed-syllables (*bīja*), and the performance of *japa* and *homa* to achieve various effects such as paralyzing enemies or causing them to wander.)

For those who perform ritual applications (*prayoga*), no other world exists; for them, the very accomplishment of the application is the fruit, and nothing else shall come to pass. For devotees free from desire who engage in rites such as recitation (*japa*) and fire-oblations (*homa*), liberation alone is their fruit; there is nothing whatsoever here in this world for them. "O Wise One, take up the Brahma-weapon (*brahmāstra*) and release these two, Śaśāda and Umā. This mantra does not grant liberation; let it not be employed for killing and the like. Thus ends the section on the means of ritual application. Now, therefore, I shall fully explain various yantras for practitioners (*mantriṇaḥ*) which bestow various goals, O Rāma.

In the *Brahmasaṃhitā* of the *Pañcarātra*, which is distinct from the various other scriptures, the Lord of the Age (Kalki) has declared as follows: "Having drawn a hexagonal wheel (*cakra*) joined with vowels and consonants, one should write the syllables of the mantra in the corners; outside of that, an eight-petaled lotus, upon whose petals one should inscribe the root mantra joined with the *praṇava* (Oṃ), repeating it again and again. Then, another twelve-spoked lotus, upon whose petals one should inscribe the *trailokyamohana* seed-syllable (*bīja*) conjoined with the name. In the pericarp (*karṇikā*), one should write the name interspersed with the *tāra* (Oṃ) and the mantra."
By Mahāsudarśana, this supreme wheel was fashioned: its exterior is like the hollow of the earth, adorned with eight vajras, auspicious with four spokes, and joined at the tips with hooks.
On an auspicious day, one should draw it upon birch bark with yellow orpiment and other substances; having drawn it, one should place it on the head or on the right arm of the mantra-practitioner.

As long as that [wheel] remains worn, no misfortune exists for him. He shall not be overcome by diseases, nor by snakes, nor by thieves, nor by enemies, nor by elephants, nor by mantras, nor by other minor [obstacles].

By the mere sight of that practitioner (*mantrin*), all living beings—including women—become submissive. Kings, regional lords (*maṇḍalika*), vassals, and royal ministers [will be won over]. There shall be an abundance of wealth and grain, and he attains all his desires. "O son, you must not speak of this King of Yantras (*yantrarāja*) to anyone who is not a disciple, nor to one whose penance is deficient, nor to one who is not peaceful, nor to a stranger. It should be given to a disciple who is devoted to mantras, endowed with faith and devotion, and who bestows [benefits] upon others; otherwise, one will fall into hell. Such is its meaning. One should draw a six-cornered wheel (*ṣaṭkoṇa-cakra*) on a parasol...

One should draw a pair of triangles with the preeminent *raṃ* syllable. Then, in the directions of Indra (East), Agni (Southeast), Nairṛti (Southwest), Varuṇa (West), Vāyu (Northwest), Īśāna (Northeast), and in the center, one should place six *ḍamaru* [drum] symbols. This is declared to be a hexagon joined with petals and filaments; outside of this is an eight-petaled lotus. In the various corners, starting from the East, the mantra for the six corners is: *oṃ rāmāya hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. Then follows: *śrīṃ śrīṃ rāmāya hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*, or *rāṃ rāmāya svāhā phaṭ*.

Having written the mantra syllables in their proper order—*svāhā*, *rāṃ rāmāya svāhā*, and *vaṣaṭ*—one should then draw two circular lines. Outside of that, one should draw an eight-petalled lotus, and outside of that, an eight-pointed lotus provided with filaments and sixteen filaments. Upon the petals, one should write the root mantra, *oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya*, as well as upon the desired beautiful petals. Then, one should write each syllable enclosed by the *praṇava* (Oṃ), such that it is situated between two *praṇavas*. Furthermore, [the worship]...

First, one should draw a hexagon as before, accompanied by the syllables of the mantra. Then, from the tip of each corner, one should draw two curved lines. Next, one should draw a twelve-spoked lotus with twelve petals, and upon those petals, one should write the *trailokyamohana* seed-syllable *klīm*, joined with the [practitioner's] name. That seed-syllable, together with the name of the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), should be written on every petal. Then, within the pericarp (*karṇikā*), one should write; in the center of the original hexagon, one should draw two circular lines. Like the pericarp, within that [central space], [one should place] the name of the object to be accomplished.

One should write [the name] interwoven with the Tārā-mantra. How so? Interwoven with the nine syllables of the mantra beginning with "Tārā. First, two mantra-syllables; next, each single syllable of the name of the person for whom the rite is performed (*sādhya*);

again, two mantra-syllables; thereafter, one should continue writing until the end of the name's syllables is reached. This is indeed the interweaving. And thus it is said: "When two mantra-syllables are placed at every single syllable of the name to be accomplished, that is called the supreme 'interwoven' (*vidarbha*) form, which brings about all protection. Thus, in a rite of pacification (*śāntika*), having first written the entire mantra, immediately after the weapon-mantra (*astra*), the name of the person for whom the rite is performed...

One should write the mantra in its entirety once more; this is called "encasement" (*saṃpuṭa*). Likewise, having first written the mantra and then the object of attainment (*sādhya*) immediately after it, and again at the end, there is the "mantra-encasement" for rites of pacification (*śānti*). For subjugation (*vaśya*), one should write the first syllable of the mantra, then the first syllable of the name, then the second syllable of the mantra, then the second syllable of the name, and so on until the completion, like a garland woven with various flowers. This is "interlaced" (*granthita*); likewise, each individual object of attainment—

This [method] is known for the rites of subjugation and attraction (*vaśyākṛṣṭi*): the syllables of the name are enclosed within the garland of the mantra-syllables and strung together. Regarding the "swallowed" (*grasta*) method: first, having written the entire mantra, one then writes the remaining letters of the name; then, having written the entire mantra again, one writes the remaining letters of the name once more, and then writes the entire mantra again. Thus it is said: "The wise practitioner should place the mantra at the beginning, middle, and end; with the name occurring in the middle of each, it is called 'swallowed' (*grasta*)."

Regarding this very *rodhitika*, some say that the *yoga* is as follows: having first written the most excellent mantra, one should afterwards write all the syllables of the name (*nāmākṣara*). Others say that one should first write the complete name and afterwards write the complete mantra. And so it is stated there: "If the *ratna* is indicated therein, it is remembered as *pallava*.

The application (*viniyoga*) of these two is likewise declared; for instance, the wise employ them in rites of pacification (*śāntika*), prosperity (*pauṣṭika*), divine [rites], purification through atonement (*prāyaścitta-viśodhana*), enchantment (*mohana*), and illumination (*dīpana*).

(p. 50a) "For killing, for destroying poison, for subduing *grahas* and spirits, for expulsion (*uccāṭana*), and for causing enmity (*vidveṣa*), one shall explain the *pallava* [method]. Here, in all these cases, having written the name of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*) joined with the mantra, one should place one's own name within it, ending in the dative case (*caturthyanta*), followed by the word *brahmaṃ*, and then the word signifying *pallava* in the accusative case (*dvitīyānta*). One should repeat [the mantra] twice, saying "make my body [so-and-so]. This is the traditional method (*sāṃpradāyika*). Having thus written it in the pericarp (*karṇikā*) according to another application, one should encircle it; thus he says: "This is encircled by the Mahāsudarśana," meaning this yantra is encircled by the Mahāsudarśana mantra, the Great Discus of Sudarśana (*sudarśanamahācakra*).

One should draw this supreme wheel, which is an excellent *yantra*, encircled by the following mantra: *rājadhagadhagāntakaduṣṭabhayaṃkaracchindabhindabhindavidārayavidārayaparamantrān grasagrāsabhakṣabhakṣabhūtāni śasaya trāsaya trāsaya huṃ phaṭ svāhā*. The meaning is as follows: it is a "earth-enclosure" (*pṛthivī-sampuṭa*), meaning that on the outside there is a square earth-mandala (*pṛthivī-maṇḍala*) forming an enclosure; within that, one should draw eight intersecting triangles (an eight-pointed star) joined with eight instances of the letter *cha*. Then, two lines should be drawn on the exterior.

Having drawn [the hexagon], one should then make a four-cornered [figure]. In its corners, one should draw the goads (*aṅkuśa*) and nooses (*pāśa*), marked with *kroṃ* and *āliṃ*. One who desires that goal and has won over the presiding deity should write this wheel on birch bark (*bhūrjapatra*) on an auspicious day using yellow pigment (*rocanā*) and other substances—namely, substances such as *rocanā*, saffron (*kuṅkuma*), sandalwood (*candana*), and camphor (*karpūra*). On a day with favorable stars and flowers, one should write it. This is what is meant: first, one should draw a six-cornered wheel; thereafter, two circular lines.
Then, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus; each petal is joined with two filaments. Then, two circular lines at the tips of the eight petals; then a hexagon, likewise with two lines.

Then a twelve-petaled lotus, again with two lines in the same manner. Then an eight-spoked wheel (*cakra*), likewise with two lines. As in the first case, within the lower circular mandala called the *karṇikā* (pericarp), one should write the mantra accompanied by the name of the person for whom the rite is intended (*sādhya*). One should write the syllables of the mantra upon the six corners. Then, on the eight petals, [one should write] the eight-syllabled Nārāyaṇa mantra.

Having divided the mantra, one should write the sixteen vowels in numerical order upon the filaments of the lotus situated within the half-moon. Then, between the two subsequent lines, one should write the letters from *ka* to *kṣa*. Furthermore, in the six corners, one should write the syllables of the root mantra. Then, between the two subsequent circular lines, one should perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breaths) with the following: "Oṃ! May the vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) of this person [Name] be here; may the life-force (*jīva*) of this person remain here; may all the senses, speech, mind, and vital breaths of this person come here. For the well-being of the skin, eyes, ears, and nose, may there be happiness; may there be well-being for a long time; may it be sweet, Svāhā! Thus is the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā*.

One should write the *ṣṭā* mantra; its specific details should be learned from the mouth of the Guru and others. It is said that [the syllable] dear to Kṛṣṇa is to be written, and then on the twelve petals, the *trailokyamohana* seed-syllable (*bīja*) together with the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Then, between two circular lines, one should write the *sudarśana* mantra. In the eight triangles, one should write the letter *cha* in each corner. Then, outside [that], in the four corners, one should write the *pāśa*, *aṅkuśa*, and *anivīja* mantras in each corner. Having written thus, one should wear [it]; the rest is clear in meaning. In all these cases, the three... [is to be applied].

The specific details regarding the duration of retention (*dhāraṇa*), the *muhūrta*, and so forth, as taught in the section on mantras, are now being stated. Thus, on an auspicious day, under a favorable lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), and in a good location free from impurities, the preceptor (*ācārya*) together with his disciple—or, in his absence, the disciple alone—should sit facing north or east, bow to the Guru, the Lord of the Universe, and then draw the yantra. Regarding the specific times for different desires, it is said: one should draw [the yantra] for subjugation (*vaśya*) and attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*); for nourishment (*puṣṭi*), it is prescribed during the two [periods] beginning with that; for causing enmity (*vidveṣaṇa*), it is traditionally taught for [the period of] Ārdrā; and for killing (*māraṇa*), it is declared for the [period of] Prākta.

The eradication of grass [or enemies] occurs; likewise, the specific type of pen is also subject to one's desire. Thus, one should write the yantra with a pen made of *darvā* wood for subjugation (*vaśya*); for attraction (*ākṛṣṭi*), it should be made of *karañja*; and for killing (*māraṇa*), it should be made of *pināsmitā*. For the rite of paralysis (*staṃbhakarma*), it is known that a pen from the *rājavṛkṣa* or *uruvūka* is used. For rites of pacification (*śāntika*) and nourishment (*pauṣṭika*), as well as for the desire for long life and knowledge, a pen of *sārpyā* is used. For the suppression of cattle, for speech, for paralysis, for causing delusion, and for driving away [enemies], a pen made of stone is recommended. [A pen] made of donkey [bone] is for harsh [rites].

On page 51a): For the purpose of subduing enemies through hatred, for great eradication (*uccāṭana*), and for the destruction of the banner-bearer, one should certainly accomplish [the rite] as correctly described by the Lord of Milk (Kṣīroda). Likewise, having written [the mantra], one should accomplish everything—fever, torment, grief, and the slaying of enemies—with a yellow cloth; it is not otherwise. Furthermore, regarding the different substances: with various materials such as moonstone, sandalwood, and *rocanā* (yellow pigment), combined with *uśīra* and milk, there is no need for hesitation here. For the purpose of subjugation (*vaśya*), one uses *nāgeṃdra-mada* (elephant ichor) and *rocanā*. For minor rites such as striking and eradication, one uses poison, *dhattūra*, funeral ashes, and soot.

One should accomplish the ritual acts (*kārmāṇi*). The extraction (*sāraṇa*) is said to occur through the combination of poison, the juice of *arka*, and *guñjā*. Having carefully inscribed this king of diagrams (*yantrarāja*) beginning with the Lord of Mantras (*maṃtreśa*), one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, having meditated upon the God who is the Teacher of the World. Then, having encased it in the three metals (*triloha*), one should perform the worship. Having received it held in the hand of the deity, the best of practitioners should accomplish his goal; [wearing it] on the hand, the neck, or the crest-lock, he should remain as if the deity were present—this is the specific instruction; the rest is easy to understand. Now, for the second diagram: one should draw a hexagon in the center with the name preceded by the *praṇava* (Om), and write it on the outside.

One should write the mantra-syllables in the corners; one who deludes the universe should write this in the outer corner of the Māhendra-maṇḍala on a leaf of the *kapāla* tree. One should heat it with blood drawn from the ring finger or with the fire of the *dirāgni*. In seven days, even a woman like Rambhā will come under one's control. The meaning of this is as follows: "The name together with the *praṇava* in the center" means that one should write the name of the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) between two *praṇavas* in the middle of the two circular lines previously drawn. One should write this outside the hexagon. One should write the *prāṇa* (the vital breath) outside; [it is] joined...

One should draw two circular lines called *kāreṇakarṇikā*. In the corners, one should write the mantra-syllables: *rāṃ rāmāya huṃ phaṭ*, or alternatively, the six syllables *rāṃ rāmāya svāhā* (*vaṣaṭ*) in the six corners in due order. Between every two corners, one should write the "Universal Enchanter" (*viśvamohana*): *oṃ śrīṃ drāṃ śrīṃ dāsarathāya sītāvallabhāya trailokyamohanāya namaḥ*; this mantra should be written as far as possible. Then, one should draw two circular lines, writing either *klīṃ* or the "Enchanter of the World" (*jaganmohana*).

On page 51b): One should write the seed-syllable; outside the Māhendra-maṇḍala, in the outer part, one should draw an eight-spoked wheel. One should write the letter *cha* in all the spokes. Regarding the phrase "one should write this on the cheek," the meaning is that one should write this yantra on a human skull. As for which substances [to use], he says: with blood arising from the ring finger—that is, with the blood issuing from the finger situated next to the little finger—one should write it. One should measure [the area] with fire from *khadira* wood and meditate upon the target. One should recite the mantra eight thousand times over seven days using *khadira* fuel.

One should heat it with a well-kindled fire of *khadira* wood; the remainder is clear. Now, for the third [method]: this other machine (*yantra*) is encircled by the seed-syllable of illusion (*māyābīja*). Having written it continuously with the seed-syllable *hrīṃ*, he says that it becomes effective at dawn. Having written it according to the rule on birch bark—that is, having written it on a birch leaf as prescribed by the scriptures—one should draw the form of the target (*sādhya*).

In the pericarp situated in the center of the hexagon, one should write the form of the person to be acted upon—whether male or female—complete with limbs such as hands and feet, encapsulated by the mantra. Having prepared the stone...

Having prepared the previously mentioned *yantra* for piercing, one should perform the digging and depositing upon the ground where the corpse is to be burned. To the question "Where?", he says: "At twilight, one should pierce the child.

The meaning is that by doing so at the very time of sunset, one attains strength and conquers the opposing side, as if becoming a child oneself. It brings about the attraction of the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*);

the meaning is that one should effect the bringing of the desired object from its actual location into one's own vicinity. Furthermore, O Sage, one should write the name joined with the fourth and second syllables in the middle, and extract [the syllables] in the corners.

Outside the *Ṛṇānvin* [mantra], having drawn the circle of Varuṇa (*vāruṇamaṇḍala*) all around, one should place the water from jars such as those of the Gaṅgā and other rivers upon it. At its opening, one should arrange a divine lamp filled with *kapilā* ghee. Having invoked the Lord of Devas into the midst of the lamp according to the prescribed rule by means of the mantra, one should perceive there the *māla-mantra* and the form of the Blessed One clearly. Whatever has been touched, whether past or future, the practitioner (*mantrin*) speaks; a young maiden sees it quickly, unless she is devoid of *mumukṣā* (the desire for liberation). The meaning of this is: O Sage, one should write the name joined with the second vowel in the middle; that [name] is encapsulated by the syllable "RĀM."

On page 52a): One should draw within the pericarp of a six-cornered [figure] named the "Abode of Meditation" (Dhyānavasthāna). "O Sage" is the address; one should extract and write the six syllables—*rā-mā-yā-huṃ-svā-hā*—in the six corners. Outside the six-cornered figure, one should draw the Varuṇa-maṇḍala, a bow-shaped maṇḍala outside the hexagon. The seed-syllable *vaṃ*, representing Varuṇa, should be written all around it without interruption. Then, having drawn the four-cornered maṇḍala known as the Bhūpura, which is common to all and joined with the noose (*pāśa*), the goad (*aṅkuśa*), and the earth-seed-syllable (*la*), [one should apply] lac-dye...

One should surround [the area] with the waters of the Gaṅgā and other rivers. Having filled a pitcher with the water of the Gaṅgā and other rivers, one should place that machine (yantra) within that pitcher-water. At its mouth, one should arrange a lamp filled with the ghee of a tawny cow (*kapilā*); the meaning is that one should prepare a vessel (*śarāva*) filled with the ghee of a tawny cow and place it at the mouth of that pitcher. Having invoked the Lord of Devas with the mantra, one should invoke the Lord of Devas—known as Śrī Rāma, who resides in the lamp—into the midst of the lamp according to the prescribed rule. Its meaning is as follows: [He is] the Supreme... of Śrī Rāma.

The deity is Ātmā; the seed-syllable (*bīja*) is *Rā*; the power (*śakti*) is *Svāhā*. Regarding the syllables, the sages are proclaimed as Brahmā, Bhṛgu, Bharadvāja, Viśvāmitra, Gautama, Pulastya, and Vāmadeva. Likewise, the meters (*chandas*) are stated by the wise in their proper sequence: Gāyatrī, Uṣṇih, Anuṣṭubh, Bṛhatī, Paṅkti, Triṣṭubh, and Jagatī. According to the order of the deities and syllables, the presiding deities are Paramātman, Hara, Durgā, Sūrya, Skanda, and Pitāmaha (Brahmā); these are the seven deities of the *Vītihotra* [mantra].

The first [vowel] is of the color black; the second should be white; the third has a luster like fire; the fourth has a greenish luster; the fifth is tawny; the sixth has a luster like yellow; and the seventh should be blue—these colors have been proclaimed. Of the first four vowels, the acute (udātta) is declared, and the fifth vowel is the circumflex (svarita); the sixth vowel is the grave (anudātta), and the seventh vowel is the acute. O sinless one, these accents have been described by me; now [follows] the application of the breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) and so forth.

Having performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) with the *saṃkīrtana* mantra, and having performed the purification of the hands (*kara-śuddhi*) with "Svāhā," one should place the five syllables of the mantra "Rāmāya huṃ phaṭ" upon the head, the crest-lock, the armor, and the eyes.

With "Svāhā astrāya phaṭ," one should place the weapon (*astra*) in the directions. This is the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*). Then, having displayed the mudrās of the bow and arrows of Yoga, and having turned [the hand] upward with the *praṇava* (Oṃ), and having made it firm with the *vyāhṛtis*, one should then meditate upon Śrī Rāma: dark as the petal of a blue lotus, adorned with a crown of matted locks, and yellow-clad...

One should meditate upon the God who holds the boon (Varada), adorned with divine earrings, and on Lakṣmaṇa to his right, who has the luster of gold and wears a crown. On the left side, one should meditate upon the Supreme Goddess Prakṛti, the source of the universe—Sītā—with limbs as fair as the Campaka flower, adorned with white garments and all ornaments, possessing two arms and red earrings. Having meditated thus and performed the recitation (*japa*) three hundred thousand times, one should offer oblations with *aśoka* flowers. By this rite, the mantra becomes perfected. Then, having invoked the God residing in the lotus of one's own heart by means of the *āvāhana-mudrā*, one should establish Him within a lamp placed in a shallow bowl upon the mouth of a well-consecrated water-pot.

Having displayed the *nasannidhīkaraṇa* and other mudrās and performed the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*), one should show the six mudrās of the bow of Yoga; then, on both sides, Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, followed by the eight *gaṇas*, then the Guru, Gaṇapati, Durgā, and Kṣetrapāla, then the eight world-protectors (*lokapālas*), and in front, the devotees such as Viṣvaksena, Garuḍa, and Nārada, and thereafter Hanuman, Sugrīva, and the others—one should invoke them. Having worshipped this assembly with the sixteen types of offerings (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*), and having worshipped a youth or a maiden in front, one asks: "Who stands in the midst of the lamps?"

"Having said 'Śye', one should show the lamp; there the practitioner (mantrī) should clearly perceive the form of the Blessed One. This and the following is easy to understand. Now, for the fifth yantra:

having written the name within the pericarp (karṇikā), embedded with the third syllable, and having written the remaining [syllables] in the other spaces, one should then encircle it. An earthen mandala should be drawn carefully on the outside at night; one should deposit this in the hollow of a *niśija* tree. "Stambhana of the mouth, stambhana of the neck, and stambhana of the tongue from the Bhadra-dantī"—this is its meaning. "Embedded within the pericarp" refers to the sixth...

The meaning is that one should write two circular lines situated within the hexagon, with the third syllable of the name of the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*)—that is, the mantra-name—enclosed within them. Having written this, one should write the remaining six syllables, *oṃ rāmāya hūṃ phaṭ*, in the six corners. Then, one should surround it with other [syllables], and subsequently encircle it with the two syllables *svāhā*. Outside of that, one who is diligent should draw a four-cornered earthly mandala (*pārthiva-maṇḍala*) together with the noose (*pāśa*), the goad (*aṅkuśa*), and the seed-syllable of the earth (*nivīja*). One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with effort.

Having performed the preliminary rites (*sādikam*) and established protection for oneself, one should draw the yantra. For one who is capable of performing a rite for a specific desire (*kāmyakarma*), there is the possibility of being overcome by gods and other beings; likewise, for one who is capable of the desired rite, his enemy may become a friend if he is auspicious, or [the opposite] from the contrary. Thus, when a crisis has arisen that cannot be avoided by other means, one should perform the ritual action with full attention. At what time? During the night, after the first half-yāma and before the fourth yāma. Having prepared the yantra and performed the consecration of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*), one should worship...

Having performed the *japa* [of the mantra] one thousand times with *akṣaya* beads and having consecrated it (*abhimantrita*), one should place this yantra inside the hollow of a *pruñja* tree or within the belly of a *palāśa* wood-apple fruit; the rest is easy to understand. Two yantras are described in the *Agastisaṃhitā*; the worship of these two is praised for all the Rāma-mantras. First, one should draw a hexagon, then eight petals, and then a square, endowed with all characteristics, clearly manifest, and pleasing to all. Within that as well, very clearly, one should inscribe the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) together with the ritual action (*karman*).

One should again write that seed-syllable (*bīja*), which has the god of love (*manmatha*) placed upon it; then, O daughter, one should repeat the *satya* and the other seed-syllables. One should again encircle that very same [seed-syllable] with the ten-syllable mantra.

One should write the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) in order within the corners starting from the southeast corner. Likewise, one should then write "hrīṃ śrīṃ" twice on the cheeks of the corners. The "huṃ" seed-syllable should be at the tip of each petal, and the vowels should be at the tips of the filaments. There are forty-seven letters of the garland-mantra (*mālāmantra*); these letters are to be placed in the seven petals—six, six, five, and eight—in the petals starting from the east.

O ascetic, one should encircle all of this with the *kādi* [consonants]; one should draw the seed-syllables of Narasiṃha and Varāha in the cardinal and intermediate directions. With the syllable *Hūṃ*, one should place them in the four-cornered earth-house in the eastern direction.

By properly worshipping this yantra, one attains enjoyment and liberation. Having drawn this yantra and fashioned it into a pill, one should wear it. One without a son obtains sons; one without wealth shall obtain wealth. What need is there for much speaking here? This yantra bestows all success upon men; it has been fully described as removing sins through its wearing. The meaning of this is: a yantra, beginning with the hexagon and ending with the earth [the square], which is enchanting.

In the center of that yantra, one should write the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Śrī Rāma, which contains the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and the ritual action (*karma*), exactly as it was previously described. Having encircled all of that with the syllables of the Manmatha-mantra, one should surround it with the remaining mantra-syllables. Again, one should surround it with the ten-syllable mantra, and again with the Manmatha-mantra; according to the *Vasiṣṭha-kalpa*, the surrounding with the ten-syllable mantra occurs outside the eight petals. The rest is clear. This is the sixth [method]. Then, one should draw [the diagram] starting from the hexagon and ending with the earth-element as before; then, one should write the *Tāra* (Om) in the middle of its six-spoked hexagon.

Following the sequence of the *svapikrama*, one should write the syllables of the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) at the joints, the *aṅga-mantras* in the petals, and the letters of the vowels on the filaments. As before, the *mālā-mantra* should be written in order upon the petals. Having encircled it with the ten-syllable mantra, one should write the consonants beginning with 'ka' in the cardinal and intermediate directions using the seed-syllables of Narasiṃha and Varāha. One should worship the *saṅgāvaraṇa* (the assembly of attendants) within this yantra. Having drawn it on gold, silver, or birch bark, one should perform the worship; the wise should know that the fruit of this yantra is as previously described. Of this...

The meaning is as follows: in the center of the pericarp of the four-petaled lotus is a hexagon; in its center is the *praṇava* (Oṃ); in the six corners of the hexagon are the six syllables of the mantra; in the middle of those [syllables] is a hexagon; in its center is the *praṇava*; in the six corners are the six mantra-syllables: *rāṃ rīṃ rūṃraiṃ rauṃ raḥ*. At the junctions of the corners starting from the southeast are the *aṅga*-mantras; on the "cheeks" (*gaṇḍa*) of the corners are *klīṃ* and *hrīṃ*. On the filaments (*kiñjalka*) of the eight-petaled lotus are the vowels. On its eight petals, in order starting from the east, are forty-seven beads of the *mālā-mantra*, numbering six on each of the first seven petals, and five on the eighth.

On page 54a): Having surrounded [the diagram] on the outside with the ten-syllable mantra *oṃ kṣetrahūṃ jānakīvallabhāya svāhā*, one should write the letters from *va* to *kṣa* in the cardinal and intermediate directions, as well as the two seed-mantras of Nṛsiṃha and Varāha, *oṃ auṃ* and *huṃ*. The rest is clear. Thus ends the seventh yantra. What was stated in the *Mahatī Saṃhitā* is now set forth: Agastya said— "I shall describe the yantra of Rāmabhadra known as the *Kavaca* (Armor). By wearing it, mortals attain all perfections (*siddhis*); all sins are destroyed, calamities go to their destruction, and ghosts, spirits, piśācas, and the like flee."

By the mere sight of this yantra, mantras attain stability, enemies become friends, the planets become propitious, and kings become servants. What more need be said? Through this yantra of Rāmabhadra known as the *Vajrapañjara*, which is adorned with two rows and twenty-one compartments, one should place the supreme wheel and write the armor (*kavaca*). One should arrange the twelve syllables at the beginning and end of the [sections] for the subjugation [of obstacles] and so forth, proceeding in both direct and reverse order.

One should join the names of Rāghava and the others with salutations in the order of the syllables. The application of the mantra in all its parts should be as follows: "May it go to my head" (me śiraḥ yātu), and so on. In the eleventh house, one should write the name of the Sadhya joined with the vocative case-ending (*āheta*). Then follow the syllable of one's own name, the syllable of the weapon (*astra*), the word *Nārasiṃha*, and then the syllables of Lakṣmī, the noose (*pāśa*), and the goad (*aṅkuśa*), ending with the nature of *Phaṭ*. The twelve-syllabled mantra of Rāmabhadra is said to end with *Svāhā*. One should properly write this on a golden leaf, a silver leaf, or on birch bark (*bhūrja*), or else on copper.
One should wear it, rolled up in a leaf, for as long as one lives; however, on gold or silver it lasts twenty years, on birch-bark twelve years, and on a copper plate half of that.

This is the specific manner of writing: the yantra is established with power. One should draw six verses beginning with "etāṃ rāmabalopetām" in a circular shape around the exterior of the yantra. It pacifies all evils, destroys all calamities, and bestows longevity, health, sovereignty, and the increase of sons and grandsons. Through this, one attains all desires—so says Viṣṇu.

The meaning of the passage beginning with "I shall explain" and ending with "known as the *vallapañjara*" is as follows: Above the three vertical lines of the southern [section], twelve lines are drawn from east to west, resulting in twenty-two squares.

By means of a line drawn through the middle of the final two squares, it is adorned with two rows of twenty-one [squares] each. One should place the supreme wheel there and write the *Śrī Rāma-kavaca*. For example, among the syllables of the twelve-syllable mantra, one by one, [one writes]: "Obeisance to Rāghava; may my head be protected. Thus [it continues].

One should write the various words of the *jita* mantra, each one encapsulated within another, in a single square, moving clockwise. Thus, in the next row, there is the instruction for ten words in direct order (*ānulomyena*). Then, in the row below that, there is the instruction for the ten upper words in reverse order (*prātilomyena*), likewise encapsulated by the syllables of the mantra in an inverted manner. In the eleventh square, two syllables are filled; then, in the middle of the protection for such-and-such a person, one should write the two syllables "kuru kuru" on both sides in reverse order. Thus—

The application of the twenty-one squares: they show that very mantra consisting of twelve syllables with the words beginning with *sva* and ending with *sauvarṇi*; the power of the yantra is firmly established therein, as is clear from the word *ambhaḥ*. Therein, the portion beginning with *yāvajjīvam* and ending with *tāmrapatre* is common to all yantras. One should write the six verses beginning with *etām* so that there is a circular space outside the yantra. As for the remainder: "He who has no gurus and no sequence of initiation rituals—if he recites the Rāmarakṣā, one should offer him a leaf of *Tulasī*."

Because Agastya has stated that "even by a hundred other initiations (*dīkṣā*) this fruit is not obtained," there is nothing equal to the *Rāmarakṣā*; and the meaning indicated by the word "and" (*ca*) regarding the sequence of circumambulation should be understood as stated in another text. One should place the life-force (*jīva*) of the *Haṃsa* yantra in the center of the self, below the seed-syllable. One should write "Haṃsaḥ So'ham" for the vital breath (*prāṇa*) in the northeast according to the sequence of steps. One should place [the syllables] at the eyes of Indra (the east) on the sides, and likewise at the ears. A specific rule is remembered for the eight-petaled lotus and others: the writing of the *Gāyatrī*. [The mantra: "We know the King of Yantras; we meditate upon the Bestower of Boons."

From the mantra-gāyatrī, "tanno yatraḥ pracodayāt," one should write the syllables in groups of three on each petal. In the space of the letter *va* (of *bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ*), one should write the *pratiṣṭhā* [syllable] which bestows life-force (*prāṇadā*). According to the *Prayogasāra*:

"One should never wear a yantra that touches the ground, touches a conch, is soiled, is associated with faded flower offerings (*nirmālya*), is burnt, stepped over, or torn. This is the general procedure for all yantras. Thus ends the eighth yantra.
[This concludes the section from] the *Śrīrāmārcana* composed by Ānandavana, disciple of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrī Mukundavana.

The Fourth Chapter of the *Candrikā*. Now, the rites for the months beginning with Caitra are revealed, as taught by Nārada and others for the sake of the spiritual accomplishment of a devotee of Rāma. On the third day of the bright fortnight of Madhu (Caitra), one should worship the Lord, the Beloved of Jānakī, with royal offerings and cause Him to be swung on a swing throughout the month in the Kali age. By seeing the God, the Supreme Lord, well-worshipped while swinging and facing southward, even once, one is liberated from all sins. Those who behold Kṛṣṇa mounted upon the swing during the months of Madhu and Mādhava are released from thousands of offenses; they are truly liberated here.

For those who perform a vigil (jāgara) before the Lord as He is mounted upon the swing, the attainment of the fruit of all merit shall occur at every moment. Thus ends the Dolotsava in the *Garuḍa Purāṇa*.

On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, the supreme vow (vrata) which was proclaimed for the great [day] associated with Agasti should be performed. This is called Śrī Rāmanavamī; it is said to be superior to ten million solar eclipses. On that day of great merit, whatever action is performed with devotion directed toward Rāma, that becomes eternally inexhaustible. Fasting, keeping a vigil, and offering libations (tarpaṇa) directed toward Hari [bring the same result].

On that day, those desiring to attain Brahman must perform [the rites]; for it is said, "Rāma alone is the Supreme Brahman; therefore, pleasing Rāma" and so forth. Now, it is considered whether this is a daily (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), or optional (*kāmya*) vow. It cannot be an optional vow, as it is prescribed even for those free from desire (*niṣkāma*). Indeed, even those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), the best of gods, and especially Indra himself, never abandon the Śrī Rāmanavamī vow. Because it is observed constantly, this is primarily a daily (*nitya*) duty; it is not heard of as being merely occasional (*naimittika*), since it is performed as long as one lives.

[Page 55b] Its status as something to be cultivated (bhāvyatva) is always meaningful, and not otherwise. O Brahmin, in former times, on the ninth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Caitra, the Supreme Lord Rāghava, who is indeed the absolute Brahman itself, manifested. On that day, the vow of fasting must certainly be observed; therefore, the Śrī Rāmanavamī vow is indeed obligatory (nitya). It is not non-obligatory because it is directly perceived [in scripture], nor because no specific fruit is mentioned. [Objection: "One obtains that fruit which is repeatedly gained by performing great gifts at Kurukṣetra during a solar eclipse," and so forth. [Reply: This is not so. Because there is an absence of the defining characteristics of an obligatory rite (nitya-lakṣaṇābhāvataḥ), its status as obligatory is established through the mention of the fruit. Alternatively, its obligatoriness is established by the very fact that no fruit is mentioned [for non-performance].

In this regard, [the observance] is not optional (*anādi*) because it contradicts the *agnihotra* and other rites; nor is it occasional (*antyā*), for there is a clear scriptural declaration of grave sin for its non-performance. It is stated: "On the day of Śrī Rāma-navamī, the mortal of deluded intellect who does not observe the fast is cooked in the *Kumbhīpāka* hells. And: "But he of deluded intellect who, out of ignorance, eats on the day of Rāma-navamī, is cooked in the terrible *Kumbhīpāka* hells—of this there is no doubt," and so forth.

Therefore, since the destruction of sin is established as a constant result of its acceptance, one should perform the fast on Rāma-navamī without sloth. One does not enter a mother's womb again, and Rāma himself shall become [one's own self].

"Therefore, by means of every soul and in every way, those who perform the Navamī vow are liberated from all sins and go to the eternal Brahman. Thus, O Lord of the Earth, for the sake of destroying sin and attaining liberation, [the vow is established]. Through the principle of "separateness of connection" (*saṃyoga-pṛthaktva*), there is no contradiction between the fruit and the obligatory nature; for even in the case of obligatory sacrifices such as the *Darśa*, their obligatory character is heard in scripture. However, the fruit such as the destruction of sin would not be of the nature of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*); rather, the fruit would arise from the purpose. In the case of preparatory acts (*saṃskāra-karma*) and subsidiary acts, the fruit is understood through the purpose; but in the case of a primary injunction (*pratijñā*), it would not be so, because if a fruit were present, it would subvert the injunction, since that [act] possesses the nature of a preparatory act and a subsidiary act.

In this context, a substance is held to be the object of refinement (*saṃskārya*) when it has utility for a ritual action, both in its past and future states. However, the person (*puruṣa*) is neither already employed [in the ritual] according to the scripture, nor will he be employed here; furthermore, there is no hearing of any subordinate element (*aṅga*) belonging to the primary act (*pradhāna*).

Since it is established that the primary act is connected with the fruit and its subordinate elements are those suitable for it, the status of being a substance subordinate to the ritual—like the *juhū* ladle and so forth—is not possible here. Moreover, the cause for that [subordination], namely "being for the sake of another" (*parārthatva*), is simply not applicable in this case. But how can there be an injunction for injunctions that lack explanatory passages (*arthavāda*)? [If one were to claim both meanings,] there would result a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*) due to its having two distinct purposes.

(p. 56a) It is argued that two such meanings are not tenable, as in the case of sacrifices like the *Rātrisatra*. Therefore, because it serves the purpose of liberation through the destruction of the stream of defects, those who know the truth should understand it from the scriptures reinforced by logic. Thus ends the section on the obligatory nature of the Navamī of Rāma’s birth. The Navamī is considered to be of two kinds: the pure (*śuddhā*) and the pierced (*viddhā*). Even the pure Navamī is threefold—equal, deficient, and excessive. Furthermore, through the conjunction and disjunction with lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), it becomes sixfold. Likewise, the pierced Navamī is also sixfold due to the distinctions of equal conjunctions with the asterisms. Thus, the Navamī is divided into twelve types; therein lies the determination.

He who was born on the ninth lunar day of the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra through the conjunction with the pure Punarvasu asterisk, which bestows great fruit—he Rāma is Hari himself. That lunar day joined with the Punarvasu asterisk grants all desires; even if the conjunction with the Punarvasu asterisk is seen only for a moment, that lunar day on the ninth of the bright fortnight of Caitra grants all desires. It is proclaimed as Śrī Rāmanavamī, superior to ten million solar eclipses. If the ninth of the bright fortnight of Caitra is joined with Punarvasu, and it occurs at the time of midday, it becomes most exceedingly meritorious when the Sun has entered Aries and the Ascendant is Cancer.

On the day called *ṭaka*, another Supreme Person appeared from the entirety of Kausalyā; thus, because of the inclusion of the ninth lunar day (*navamī*) along with the eighth (*aṣṭamī*), it is said that "having performed the entire *navamī* vow with one's whole being. By the word "by all," it is revealed that everyone has the qualification for this. If the [ninth] day is conjoined with the [eighth] (*viddha*), how should the vow be observed? Because of the scriptural prohibition regarding the *navamī* being conjoined with the eighth, those devoted to Viṣṇu must avoid the *navamī* when it is pierced by the eighth. It is stated: "The fast on the ninth day should be on the tenth day itself by the other [method]. This is specifically so for the devotees of Viṣṇu. Therefore, in that case...

Regarding the phrase "by the Vaiṣṇavas": if there is an increase in the duration of the *daśamī* (the tenth lunar day), it must be avoided by the wise Vaiṣṇavas; however, for all others, the observance (*vrata*) is determined to take place on that very [tenth] day. By the explicit word "on the *daśamī* itself," one should not let the *daśamī* pass by. Having thus decided through deliberation, one should perform the *navamī* vow. This is the determination regarding the Śrī Rāma-Janma-navamī. From the statement "by the Vaiṣṇavas," their defining characteristics are now stated:

those who worship the twelve-syllable mantra, or the eight-syllable, or any other, along with its *saṅga*, *samudra*, *sannyāsa*, *sṛṣṭi*, *chandas*, and *devatā*, together with the rules for initiation (*dīkṣā*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and the *yantra*—they should be known as Vaiṣṇavas.

O Brahmins, those who always delight in Viṣṇu, who have received the initiation according to the prescribed rites, and who worship the King of Mantras along with its three Yantras, endowed with a thousand syllables, distinguished by the divisions of the Root-mantra (Mūla-vyūha) and so forth, and who meditate upon the five-fold form of the Lord—they are known as Mahāvaiṣṇavas and are exceedingly dear to Mahāviṣṇu. He whose mind does not waver from the dharma of his own caste, who maintains equanimity toward himself, friends, and enemies, and who neither harms nor causes harm to anyone—such a person is indeed the foremost among Vaiṣṇavas; thus it is said in the Padma Purāṇa. Even when faced with the temptations of the three worlds, those whose memory of the Lord is unshakable do not waver from the lotus feet of the Blessed One.

"Even for half a blink of an eye, [one should not look upon] those who are foremost among the Vaiṣṇavas"—thus it is stated in the *Bhāgavata*. This is the defining characteristic of a Vaiṣṇava. Furthermore, regarding the rule "not looking at the body," one should observe the logic in the *Ekādaśīmāhātmya* concerning the obligatory nature of this rite: "Ornaments, flowers, clothing, perfumes, incense, and ointments—these would defile one during a fast, as would collyrium for virtuous women; betel for those who abstain from it, and eating for those who abstain from food. The fourfold types of fasting have been proclaimed by sages such as Manu: (1) the three-night fast and others where one uses betel; (2) the non-eating on Ekādaśī and other days; (3) abstaining from betel; and (4) abstaining from food at the end of the fortnight.

It has been declared that one should subsist on a single meal, or eat only at night, or by begging, or on sacrificial food (*haviṣya*), or even on milk, roots, and fruits; or else, a child, an elderly person, or one who is ill may perform these quickly. One who eats only at night (*naktabhojī*) should practice six duties: eating sacrificial food, bathing, truthfulness, moderation in diet, tending the sacred fire, and sleeping on the ground. There are eight substitutes for broken vows: water, roots, fruit, milk, sacrificial food, the desire of a Brāhmaṇa, the word of a teacher, and medicine. Thus says Agastya regarding the very sharp substitute; it is described here for the sake of convenience, applying them properly in due order.

For those who possess wealth, worship may be performed with Rāma-mantras consisting of more than six syllables; however, it is said that among all Rāma-mantras, the six-syllabled mantra is the king of mantras and is the saving Brahman—therefore, its worship is highly praised.

Alternatively, one should perform the initiation according to the *Puruṣasūkta* and other Vedic hymns; in the absence of Vedic rites, it shall certainly be done with name-mantras. On the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra, having subdued the senses and having first cleansed his teeth, he should bathe according to the prescribed rule in a river, a pond, a well, a lake, or a spring. Then, while remembering Rāghava, he should perform the Sandhyā prayers and other duties.

Having returned to his home, the best of Brahmins should perform the *aupāsana* and other rites. He should invite a Brahmin who is self-controlled, a householder, always devoted to the Vedas and Shastras, intent on the worship of Śrī Rāma, of good character, free from hypocrisy, knowledgeable in the ritual rules, and whose sole means of practice is the Rāma-mantra. Having invited him with devotion and worshipped him, he should request him as follows: "O best of the twice-born, I shall perform the gift of the image of Śrī Rāma; please be my preceptor (*ācārya*) therein, being well-pleased. You alone are Śrī Rāma. Having said this, he should bathe that Brahmin with ghee. Then, after having himself anointed with oil, he should bathe while meditating on Rāghava in his heart.

Wearing white garments and bearing white perfumes and garlands, being honored and adorned, and having performed his midday rites, he should afterwards feed the preceptor extensively with pure (sāttvika) foods; he himself should likewise eat while remembering Rāma in his heart. On the ninth day, O Rāghava, by means of a single meal as an ancillary act, one should offer the dedication with this mantra: "O beloved of Ikṣvāku, Daṃśa, and Tilaka, may you be pleased; O beloved of Bhava! Then, together with the preceptor, having restrained the senses, he should spend the remainder of the day listening to the divine stories of Rāma; at night, he should observe the evening twilight (saṃdhyā).

One should perform the rites while recollecting Kriyārāma; together with the preceptor (ācārya), sleeping on the ground at night, with senses subdued, one should likewise dwell alone in a secluded place with the mind offered to Śrī Rāma. If capable of acting as the preceptor, one may eat oneself and sleep comfortably. Thus concludes the ritual for the eighth day. Then, having risen in the morning, bathed, and performed the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā), one should quickly complete all the morning duties. One should fast on the ninth day, saying: "O Raghava, by these eight watches (yāmas) [of fasting], may you be pleased; O Hari, protect me from saṃsāra. Thus he spoke.

The mantra for the offering of the oblation (*nivedana*): Then, O sinless one, having become composed in mind and accompanied by learned scholars, one should begin the construction of the sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇḍapa*) in the northern part of one’s own house. It should have four doors, be richly adorned with banners, possess a beautiful canopy and excellent archways, be delightful, very lofty, and well-decorated with flowers and other ornaments. The eastern door should be adorned with the conch, the discus, and Hanumān; the southern door with Garuḍa, the bow, and the arrow; the western door with the mace, the sword, and the armlet (*aṅgada*); and the northern door with the lotus, the *svastika*, and the blue sapphire. In the center, [it should be] four cubits...

(Page 57b) [The site] should be elevated, provided with a pedestal, and spacious; it should be well-endowed with dance, song, and instrumental music. There, one should have the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha-vācana*) performed by learned men of tranquil minds. Then, one should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) and meditate upon Rāma alone: "On this ninth day of Rāma (Rāmanavamī), intent on the worship of Rāma, having fasted for eight watches of the night and having worshipped according to the rules, I shall, with my own effort, give this golden image of Rāma to a wise devotee of Rāma for the sake of pleasing Śrī Rāma. May Rāma, being pleased, quickly take away my many sins accumulated through various births."

"Let them be very large"—this threefold resolve is declared for those who are capable, less capable, or utterly incapable [of making a large image]; it describes the fashioning of the form. Then, O great sage, one should fashion a golden image of Rāma weighing one *pala*, divine and two-armed, with Jānakī seated upon his left side. She holds the *jñānamudrā* in her right hand, while with her left hand she remains embracing the Goddess from below. He shines upon a throne fashioned from two *laṭṭu* measures of silver. For that illustrious person who is incapable [of this], [the image should be made] according to his wealth, weighing half a *pala* or even less than that.

O Sage, if one lacks even that much power through supernatural means (*ṛddhi*), O descendant of Raghu, one should have [the image] made of silver, or even fashioned from iron, stone, or wood. Alternatively, one may draw it on a cloth, depicting Hari seated on the lap of his distressed mother—his limbs tender, his eyes wide, and his luster like sapphire—with Daśaratha on his right side intent on searching for his son, Lakṣmaṇa behind him with a bright umbrella of golden radiance, Bharata and Śatrughna at his sides both holding palm-leaf fans, and Hanumān in front, desiring the grace of Rāma; [all this] without stinginess regarding wealth.
