One should diligently fashion an image; however, if one lacks the means, one should not fail to perform the ritual out of delusion, for one who does not do so does not obtain its fruit—the Lord of the Gods declares this. Thus ends the description of the image. Having seated [the deity] upon the seat and performed the array of ritual placements (nyāsa), one should worship the conch in front with perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice, and other offerings. One should carefully worship the water-pot situated in the left portion, as well as the articles of worship; and with devotion, while reciting the mantra, one should sprinkle oneself and the vessel. This is the consecration of the conch. Then, having drawn the *sarvatobhadra* diagram...

On the ground, one should place a beautiful vessel filled with water from sacred fords (*tīrtha*) in the center; it should be auspicious, its interior adorned with jewels, and provided with mango sprouts and flowers. Having established and worshipped it, one should draw a hexagon within vessels made of gold, silver, or copper. In their absence, having placed a bilva-wood pedestal upon the jar, the wise man should then place a pair of uncut, beautiful cloths over it, and having established a divine lion-throne (*siṃhāsana*) there, he should worship it with:
*oṃ namo bhagavate viṣṇave sarvabhūtātmane vāsudevāya sarvātmasaṃyogayogapīṭhātmane namaḥ*.

With this mantra, one should again offer a handful of flowers. Thus ends the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭha*). One should then offer the *arghya*, *pādya*, and so forth, as well as the bath with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*). For images made of clay and the like, there should be an ablution; one should also offer garments and the sacred thread (*upavīta*). Thus ends the bath. Then, having established the deity upon that pedestal, one should perform the worship according to the prescribed rule: invocation (*āvāhana*), installation (*sthāpana*), bringing into proximity (*sannidhāpana*), firm confinement (*sannirodhana*), and the veiling (*avaguṇṭhana*) with the respective mudrās. Having prayed to the Lord with devotion, one should offer ornaments variegated with various jewels.

One should diligently offer incense mixed with camphor, sandalwood, and fragrant substances, along with agallochum (agaru) and saffron. One should worship with white water-lilies (kahlāra), ketakī, jasmine (jātī), punnāga, and other flowers;

with jasmine (caṃdaka), lotuses (śatapatra), and other sweet-smelling, most enchanting blossoms; with mango sprouts and flowers, dūrvā grass, tulasī leaves, tender bilva leaves, and likewise with aśoka flowers. [Thinking: "The Mother of Rāma is this very world, whose essence is Rāma; therefore, I shall worship you, O Mother of the World! Salutations to you! i.

One should worship the father with the mantra: "Obeisance to Daśaratha, who is honored for his triple skill. This concludes the worship of the ancestors (*pitṛ-pūjana*). Then, having requested permission from the Lord of Devas, one should worship the attendants.

First, in the six corners of the hexagon, one should worship the six [limbs] beginning with the Heart in their proper order; this is the first enclosure (*prathamāvaraṇa*). [Then] Hanumān, Masugrīva, Bharata, Vibhīṣaṇa, Lakṣmaṇa, Aṅgada, Śatrughna, and Jāmbavanta in the petals and so forth; this is the second enclosure. [Then] Dhṛti, Jayanta, Vijaya, Surāṣṭra, Rāṣṭravardhana, Akopa, the one named Dharmapāla, and Sumanta in the middle of the petals; this is the third enclosure. Da...

On page 58b): One should worship the guardians of the world (lokapālas) with the fourth [syllable], and their weapons before them, using name-mantras in the dative case for the purpose of salutation. Fifth, while ringing the bell, one should offer incense and lamps to Him. With devotion, one should present the food offering (naivedya) consisting of various kinds of eatables and the like according to the prescribed rite. Then, having offered water for sipping (ācamana), excellent betel-leaf, and the great lustration ceremony (mahānīrājana), one should prostrate. Then, having praised Him with hymns or reciting the mantra, one should spend the watch of the night (yāma) together with devotees of Rāma, listening to and reciting His majesty as well as the stories of Rāma, while constantly remembering Rāma. Thus ends the first [chapter].

One should perform the duties of the watch (yāma-kṛtya) with a conch-vessel as a seat, remaining vigilant throughout the night. When the second watch has arrived at midday, one should contemplate one's own birth. When the five planets are in their exaltations, Jupiter and the Moon are present, on the lunar day of the tenth (daśamī), in the sign of Cancer (Karkaṭaka-lagna), and when the Sun has entered Aries (Meṣa) in conjunction with the Punarvasu nakṣatra—then all the Palāśa fuel-sticks are consumed by the fire. From the friction of the araṇi wood, the Sun arises as a unique, unprecedented, and great light that bestows sovereign power. Thinking thus, one should blow the musical instruments and offer the Arghya water to the Lord of the Universe, filling the vessel with fruit, flowers, and water.

"Taking the supreme conch shell, joined with *aśoka* flowers, *bhūta* flowers, and *tulasī* leaves—for the sake of slaying the ten-headed Rāvaṇa, for the establishment of Dharma, for the destruction of the Dānavas, for the death of the Daityas, and for the protection of the virtuous—Rāma himself, who is Hari, has been born. O sinless one, accept this *arghya* offered by me together with my brothers.

Thus is the *arghya* mantra. Having again offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), the wise man, alert and diligent, should worship according to the rules with devotion day and night, and pass the time. Then, having risen in the morning, he should perform his bath.

O Sage, having completed the rites beginning with *dhyāna* according to the rules, one should worship Rāma as before. Then, the knower of mantras performs the *homa* with the root mantra in the previously mentioned lotus-shaped fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) or on the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), according to the prescribed ritual in a common fire. Thereafter, while remembering Rāma with undistracted mind, he offers one hundred and eight oblations of milk-rice (*pāyasa*) mixed with clarified butter.

Then, O Sage, having fully satisfied the preceptor with devotion, one should honor him with two earrings set with fine gems, various finger-rings, perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains (*akṣata*), garments, and diverse beautiful ornaments.

Then, remembering Rāma and reciting this mantra, he should give [the gift]: "O Raghava, I am Rāma; may this golden image of Rāma, well-adorned and covered with a pair of variegated cloths, be given for the pleasure of Śrī Rāma. O Raghava, may you be pleased. This is the mantra for the gift of the image. Having performed this rite, he should then give land as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), and to others according to the rules, cows, gold, and so forth, according to his capacity. He should also give a pair of garments and grain as they are available from the beginning. Then, together with the Brahmins, he should eat and give them a sacrificial fee.

In that regard, the vow of breaking the fast (*pāraṇā*) is as follows: "By this breaking of the fast which I have performed, you are pleased; grant me devotion toward yourself. Having thus made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) for the breaking of the fast, a person is certainly liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*) and obtains the fruit of gifts such as the *tulāpuruṣa*. He is certainly freed from the sins accumulated over many births. What more need be said here? Liberation stands within his very hand. Whatever is obtained by performing the *tulāpuruṣa* gift and other rites many times at the highly meritorious Kurukṣetra during a solar eclipse, [is attained by this].

O sage of excellent vows, by this gift of food, a mortal obtains that very fruit; such is the ritual for the tenth day. Even one who possesses nothing, having fasted on the ninth day with self-restraint and having formed a circle (gaṇa) with devoted Rāma-bhakts, should worship Rāma according to the rules with devotion, while remembering Him with a focused mind. O sage, chanting the Rāma-mantra joined with Māyā (the syllable Hrīṃ) and Anaṅga (the syllable Klīṃ), or the single-syllabled mantra according to the rules, having performed all the ritual placements (nyāsa) with upliftment, he should duly perform the morning twilight (saṃdhyā) rites and the midday and other rituals, and should give gifts of cows, land, sesame seeds, and gold.

Accordingly, one endowed with faith should perform the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*) along with learned devotees of Śrī Rāmacandra and Brāhmaṇas, according to one's capacity. He who performs this with devotion is liberated from all sins. One should cast the clay images into the Gaṅgā, or place them within the house. Such is the vow; that which is prescribed for the capable is the vow, and for the incapable, it is the concluding rite (*udyāpana*). That too should be performed according to one's ability, following the entire path always. O Sage, by fasting on even a single Śrī Rāmanavamī with devotion, a person becomes one who has accomplished his purpose, freed from all sins.

[Page 59b] It is said that he is liberated; by the word "api" (also/even), the completion of the ten-fold power is indicated, and thus the concluding rite (*udyāpana*) for the vow is also indicated. For one who is capable year after year, the fulfillment is achieved through the vow alone; for him there is no further concluding rite, for nothing other than the vow itself is required. For the sake of completing every vow, one should perform the *rāma-vrata* together with one's wife. Its fulfillment is not accomplished by anything else, as it is like the ocean; by this alone is its completion attained. Thus ends the section on the concluding rite for the capable practitioner.

In the *Tapa Ityagasaṃhitā*, the ninth Jayantī vow concerning the birth of Rāma is concluded. On the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*) of the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra, the festival of giving (*dānotsava*) should be performed every year, as prescribed by Baudhāyana and others. In that rite, on one's own auspicious lunar days, the offering of the *damana* plant should be made to Agni and the other deities. These deities to be worshipped at the sacred sites (*tīrthas*) are: Agni, Viriñci (Brahmā), Girijā (Pārvatī), Gaṇeśa, Phaṇī (Śeṣa), Viśākha (Kārttikeya), Dinakṛt (the Sun), Maheśa (Śiva), Durgā, Antaka (Yama), Viśva (Viṣṇu), Harihara (Harihara), Sarva (Śiva), and Śaśin (the Moon). O Lord, for the sake of ensuring the non-omission of ritual acts and for the attainment of knowledge, whatever has been ordained here, may no obstacle arise.

"O Viṣṇu, Lord of the Vedas, Protector of the Kurus, full of compassion, you are in every way and at all times my supreme refuge. O Lord of the World, I shall please you with a fast, so that desire, anger, and the other enemies may be subdued by this vow. O Lord of Gods, from this day until the day of the Vaiśvadeva [the twelfth], protection must be provided for all this world by you, O Lord of the World.

Having thus petitioned the God, and having prostrated before the feet of the Guru, he should then bathe in the morning, worship the Lord of Gods according to the rules, and proceed to the well-adorned temple of the Lord on the eleventh day, taking [the offerings] in due order.

One should worship the three [trees] with sandalwood and other offerings, praying: "I shall perform the worship for the sake of Rāma. Having thus prayed, one should bow to him. After sprinkling [the site] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and washing it with water, one should worship in sequence upon the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) at the foot of an *aśoka* tree with perfumes and other offerings. One should worship the *aśoka*, as well as Kāla and Vasanta-kāma, with this [mantra]: "Oṃ, salutation to you, O Aśoka, destroyer of the sorrow of women's desire; eternally remove the manifestation of grief and produce joy! With this, one should worship the *aśoka* that destroys sorrow with flowers. "Oṃ, from the beginning of creation until the end of time, you are the form of Time, the Great..."

"Salutation to that one whose nature is Time (Kāla), who is 'la', who calculates (kalate), and who is indeed 'ya', the All; with this [mantra], one should worship Kāla, who is imperishable and whose nature is calculation (kalanā). "Salutation to you, O Vasanta (Spring), the beloved of trees, shrubs, and creepers; salutation to you, who possess a thousand faces and can assume any form at will (kāmarūpa). With this mantra, one should worship the one who possesses a form of desire (kāmarūpin) using the flowers of spring. "Oṃ! Salutation to you, who are drenched by the tears of Rati arising from the ashes of Kāma, and who utterly delude the sages, Gandharvas, and gods. Having taken up the sacred Damana flower, one should worship [him] with this immortal mantra. "Oṃ! Salutation to the one who has five arrows and who causes the delight of the world."

To the Lord of the World, the Sacrifice of Desire (Manmatha), who is beloved by Rati and Priya, one should perform the subduing [of the flower] with this supreme mantra. Having separated that Damana flower from the Manmatha [plant], one should worship Manmatha with one portion according to the path of devotion, accompanied by his retinue. "Obeisance to Kāma" (*kāmāyanamaḥ*)—this mantra begins with the *praṇava* (OM). With this mantra, one should worship Damana with perfumes and flowers. Covering it with a washed new cloth and placing it upon a new mat, one should bring it to one's own home amidst the sounds of bells, the *Puruṣasūkta*, and other hymns. Thus is the bringing to the house; [it should be performed] in the manner to be described hereafter.

Or one may endure the mental [disturbances]; at night, in front of Rāmacandra, one should fashion an auspicious eight-petaled lotus, clearly filled with white, black, red, and yellow colors. Having made a square outside that, one should fill it with yellow color. Outside of that, there should be three circular mandalas with white, yellow, and other colors. Outside of that, there should be a square filled with red color; this is the Sarvatobhadra diagram which fulfills all desires—one should draw it. Having filled a jar with holy water and adorned it with gold and jewels, having placed it auspiciously there in front of Rāma, one should worship the Amṛtamantra therein. One should hang a canopy known as "five-colored" above.

With a focused mind, one should perform a great worship; that is the consecration (*adhivāsana*) for the sake of worshipping the God of gods, Viṣṇu, the Lord of Lakṣmī, the Sovereign. The invocation mantra is: "O Damana, come here, grant your presence; salutations! Then one should worship with: "Oṃ klīṃ, salutations to Kāmadeva; Oṃ hrīṃ, let there be salutations to Rati. And in the various directions: "Salutations again and again to Smaraśarīra and Anaṅga; Oṃ to Manmatha and Rāma; klīṃ to Vasanta-sakha; to Smara, to the one with the sugarcane bow, and to the one whose arrows are flowers. Then: "Oṃ, we know that form which belongs to Kāmadeva; may our intellect be directed toward him... (vidmahe kāmadevāya dhī).

Having consecrated [the deity] one hundred and eight times with the *manmatha-gāyatrī*: "O Great One, impel that desire within me," he should worship [the deity] with incense, lamps, food offerings (*naivedya*), and other services. Having offered a handful of flowers with the *hārda-mantra*, he should prostrate, saying: "Salutations to the one whose arrows are flowers, who brings joy to the world; salutations to Manmatha, the eye of the universe, beloved of Rati. You have been invoked, O Lord of Gods, O Ancient Supreme Person; I shall worship you this morning—be present, O Keśava! O You whose form rests upon the great serpent bed in the Ocean of Milk, I worship you this morning."

"Obeisance to the one who becomes present in the vicinity of the *damana* plant; I offer this auspicious *damana* to you in the morning, O Viṣṇu. In every way and at all times, obeisance to you; be pleased with me. Having thus petitioned the Lord of Gods and offered a handful of flowers again, one should place the worshipped *damana* upon the water-pot (*kumbha*). One should protect it on all sides with the *astra-mantra* and veil it with the *kavaca-mantra*. Alternatively, one should protect it with the *Vācaka-mantra* or the *Nṛhari-mantra*.

Then, having paid homage to the Brahmins and prostrated at the feet of the Guru, one should perform a vigil (*jāgaraṇa*) accompanied by the sounds of auspicious songs. Thus ends the section on the *damana*.

Having bowed to the Lord of Gods (Īśvara) at dawn, one should perform the ritual bath according to the prescribed rules. Having performed the daily worship separately, one should then perform the occasional (naimittika) rite. Accompanied by *damana* grass, *dūrvā* grass, sandalwood paste, and *akṣata* rice, one should offer it to the God of Gods amidst the resounding sounds of victory and auspicious hymns: "Oṃ! O God of gods, Lord of the universe, bestower of desired objects, O beloved of Kāmeśvarī, fulfill the desires residing in my heart. O God, accept this *damana* grass through your grace; complete this annual worship for the Blessed One. Indeed, this is the root mantra to be used in the offering of the *damana* plant, enclosed within the preceding and following mantras.

Having thus offered [the gifts] to the God, one should pray to the imperishable Viṣṇu with garlands of gems and coral, and with mandāra flowers and the like: "O Garuḍa-bannered Lord, this is the annual worship; as you always bear the forest-garland (vanamālā) upon your chest and the Kaustubha gem upon your heart, so too may you accept this Vāmana-thread garland (vāmanikī-mālā) in your heart. Whatever worship has been performed by me—whether knowingly or unknowingly—may all of that reach completion through your grace, O Lord of Ramā! Victory to you, O Lotus-eyed One! Salutations to you, O Creator of the Universe! Salutations to you, O Hṛṣīkeśa, O Primordial Great Being! [Whatever was done] deficient in mantra..."

"O Janārdana, whatever has been offered by me that was deficient in devotion or deficient in ritual, may all that become complete for me, O Lord. Having thus prayed to the Lord of Gods, one should prostrate on the ground like a staff. Then, one should worship the Guru with devotion using garments, gold, and other offerings; having performed the worship oneself, one should feed one's kinsmen and the Brahmins and cause them to complete the vow (pārayet). "This yields the merit born of an Aśvamedha sacrifice," so said the Blessed Śiva. Thus ends the ritual of offering the *damana* (the holy basil). If even a single *ghaṭikā* (24 minutes) of the twelfth lunar day (*dvādaśī*) is not available on the day intended for the completion of the vow (*pāraṇā*), then the thirteenth day (*trayodaśī*) should be taken for the offering of the sacred *damana*. If there is an obstacle to the offering of the *damana* during the month of Vaiśākha, it may be performed in the month of Caitra.

If the [observance] of Śrāvaṇa is not possible, it should be performed on the Vaiśākhī; thus ends the ritual for Caitra. On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, one should worship the Lord of the Universe situated in water with great joy until the eleventh day of the bright fortnight. And likewise in the Gāruḍa Purāṇa: "Those men who, having placed [the deity] in a vessel of water during the month known as Mādhava, worship Mādhava, they become deities upon the earth. O highly fortunate one, he who worships the Lord born from the Sālagrāma stone while situated in water—whether in a vessel of gold, silver, copper, or even clay—or an image, his merit is infinite."

Therefore, O highly fortunate one, one should worship Hari situated in the water while remaining bowed; it should be known that this rule regarding the duration of time for the warm water applies until the dissolution of all beings (*yāvad-ābhūta-saṃplavam*).

Having completed the daily worship with a vessel filled with scented water, and having passed the day by completing the worship of the Sun, one should lead the Lord to His own seat during the night. Having worshipped Him with the five services (*pañcopacāra*), one should sip the holy water (*tīrtha*) and dismiss Him. One should purify oneself, one's home, wife, and others with that holy water. On the twelfth lunar day (*dvādaśī*), however, at night, [one should worship] Him who lies in the water, situated within the water.

Thus ends the ritual for Vaiśākha and Jyeṣṭha. On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, the festival of the Lord’s sleep upon the Ocean of Milk (Kṣīrābdhi-śayana-utsava) should be performed; otherwise, according to the words of the Purāṇas, there will be drought. As stated in the *Bhaviṣya*: "When the Sun is in the sign of Gemini, one should put Madhusūdana to sleep; when He has entered the sign of Libra, one should again awaken the Lord. And in the *Garuḍa*: "If anyone does not put Hari to sleep while the Sun is in Gemini, then, through the collective action of the Vaiṣṇavas, a drought shall occur. Now, the procedure as declared in the *Bhaviṣya* regarding the festival of sleep is described: on the day of the breaking of the fast (pāraṇā), during the preceding night...

Sounding bells and other instruments, and having performed a grand and manifold worship of Viṣṇu, the Vaiṣṇavas should wear the *taptamudrā* (heated metal marks) according to the method taught by Śaunaka. All Vaiṣṇavas should do so in accordance with their respective traditions. In the Ṛgveda it is said: "The mortal does not eat that which is not his own body; those who carry the truth have attained it. Their purifier is spread out; the divine region is its seat; they have established it for us. Yājñavalkya said: "Therefore, for his own welfare, a man should worship Hari, the Lord of the gods, the one praised in the hymns (*mukhyaśloka*)."

"By means of fire they unite [the soul]"—thus says the Śatapatha Śruti. "O Viṣṇu, for the sake of crossing the ocean of births, the lords of men place upon their arms the well-heated discus and conch; indeed, O dear one, they apply the ancient marks and the heated weapons. "The wearing of the heated discus and other marks is for a Brāhmaṇa as obligatory as the Agnihotra sacrifice and the study of the Veda"—thus says the Padma Smṛti. The method of this practice, which has been briefly mentioned in the Śruti and Smṛti, is now set forth in detail as described by Śaunaka and others in the *Bahvṛca-pariśiṣṭas*.

Having worshipped the Blessed One with the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*), he should worship the discus and the conch with the two mantras beginning with *ṛkṣare paramenyoman* and *śanno mitraḥ śaṃ varuṇaḥ*. Then, with the two mantras beginning with *dvādaśāraṃ nahiṃ najjarāyāḥ* and *agnermarutve prathamasya pracetasaḥ*, he should place [the implements] into the fire. He should circumambulate the fire while reciting *vaiśvānarasya sumatau syāma*. Having offered sixteen oblations with the *Puruṣasūkta*, and having praised the Blessed One with the *Puruṣasūkta*, he should prostrate himself like a staff before it with the mantra *yo brahmāṇām*.

Then, taking up the Sudarśana [discus] with the mantra: "O Sudarśana, great flame, equal in radiance to ten million suns, O Viṣṇu, forever show the path to me who am blinded by ignorance," he performs the installation of the discus with: "Om, we meditate upon the great flame of Viṣṇu’s Sudarśana; may that Discus impel us. Then, taking up the Pañcajanya [conch] with the mantra: "O Pañcajanya, protect me—who am a sinner drowning in the terrible ocean of saṃsāra—from my own darkness and the accumulation of sins," he performs the installation of the conch with: "We know the Pañcajanya; we meditate upon Hayavāmana; may that Conch impel us."

The wise man who performs this "wearing of the conch" (*śaṅkhadhāna*)—being learned in the Veda (*śrotriya*), pure, and devoted to Brahman—is liberated from all sins and goes to the world of Viṣṇu. On the day of Śayanī (the day the Lord sleeps) and on the day of Bodhanī (the day He awakens), as well as at the Cakra-tīrtha, a man becomes purified by fire through the ritual procedure of the conch and discus (*śaṅkhacakra-vidhāna*). This is the rule for wearing the mudrās. Then, having performed the *nīrājana* (lustration) ceremony, the Lord Rāma, along with His Vaiṣṇava devotees, should be led to the water reservoir amidst the sounds of singing and musical instruments. Having offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), one should then cause the Lord to emerge from the water. Having performed the ritual placement of the feet (*aṅghri-nyāsa*) upon the bank and requested His blessing, one should place one's hand [upon Him] and seat Him.

Having washed his hands and feet and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should, while remaining covered, make the formal resolve (saṃkalpa). Then, having performed the ritual placement of mantras (nyāsa) upon the deity according to the *Svarṇadharma-anuvāka*, as well as the *Puruṣasūkta* and the *Uttara-nārāyaṇa*, and having bathed the Best of the Raghus with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), he should worship Him. Then, with the mantra "Atodeva," he should cause the Lord to sleep upon the excellent couch in the midst of Śvetadvīpa, amidst pure clusters of fruits and jewels, saying, "O God, sleep; salutations to You. Then, having performed a great worship with perfumes, garlands, incense, lamps, food, betel, and fragrant pastes, [he should proceed].

"O Lord of the World, when You sleep, this world sleeps; and when You awaken, it awakens. O Imperishable One, may You be gracious unto me. Having thus prayed, one should undertake these observances before Him: "O Lord of Śvetadvīpa, O Lord of Serpents, O Lord of Yogins, O Consort of Lakṣmī, grant me permission for the Cāturmāsya vow. Having obtained permission, like a woman whose husband is away with a conch in hand, [one should say]: "O Acyuta, from today until the conclusion of the Āghā festival, I shall perform this vow for the four months of the rainy season; grant me freedom from obstacles. Thus is the vow undertaken by me.

"O Lord of Ramā, by Your grace, may that which has been taken for the deity attain accomplishment without obstacle before You. O God, in this house of Yours, may there be success for the men who worship You without hindrance.

If death should befall these [deities], then let it be fulfilled through Your grace, O scion of Raghu. Having thus prayed to the deity, one should offer the *arghya* with a conch shell. In the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should avoid leafy vegetables;

likewise, in Bhādrapada, curd; in the month of Āśvayuja, milk; and in Kārttika, one should renounce meat. One should also avoid the powder of animal parts, leather, water-born [lotuses], *vīra*, *vīcapūraka*, and food that is not the remnant of a sacrifice offered to Viṣṇu.

One should avoid food offered [to others], burnt food, lentils (*masūra*), and black gram (*māṣa*)—these are the eight types of forbidden meat—as well as whatever fruits and roots are available in that region which are not palatable. According to the Smṛti: "During the four months of the rainy season, one should eat sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) and avoid cooked food; one should consume winter grains, rice boiled in milk, *mudga* beans, barley, sesame, peas, *kaṅgu*, *nīvāra*, *tūka*, *himalo-cikā*, *ṣaṣṭika* rice, *kāla-śāka*, radish, and *kemuketara*. One should not eat these while the Lord (the deity) is asleep. During these four months, one should subsist on sacrificial food and avoid hot water. Winter grains, rice boiled in milk, *mudga* beans, barley, sesame, peas, *kaṅgu*, *nīvāra*, *tūka*, *himalo-cikā*, *ṣaṣṭika* rice, *kāla-śāka*, radish, and *kemuketara* [are permitted]. All other [food] is prohibited.

The sages declare that the following are *haviṣya* foods—those not cooked in oil: white mustard, rock salt, asafoetida, cow’s curd and clarified butter, milk from which the cream has been removed, jackfruit, mango, *harītakī*, long pepper, cumin, citron, tamarind, plantain, *lavalī*, and *dhātrī* fruits, as well as jaggery and sugarcane products. Other such observances (*vrata*) are to be found in the Purāṇas.

Then, having praised the Protector of Creatures (Brahmā) and invoked auspiciousness for the king, they reached Śaṅkhatīrtha and gratified Hari with song, dance, and other offerings, and then honored the Vaiṣṇavas.

Having placed the Blessed Lord upon a palanquin amidst the sounds of singing and instrumental music, and having arrived at the temple, one should perform the great *nīrājana* ceremony for the Lord. Then, having dismissed the Vaiṣṇavas and seated the Deity comfortably, one should go to sleep. This is the festival of the Bed (*śayanotsava*) in the month of Āṣāḍha. Furthermore, the festival of the Sacred Thread (*pavitrāropaṇotsava*), which was described by Śaunaka and others as to be performed on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, must always be observed. Likewise, in the *Bahvṛca-pariśiṣṭa*: "He who performs the rite of the sacred thread according to the prescribed rule attains the merit of bathing in all holy waters and being initiated into all sacrifices; he also gains the favor of Hari. [End of verse fragment].

"One should not perform the *pavitraka* rite with thread seen by women; the Rākṣasas seize the fruit of his year-long worship and other merits," so it is said in the *Padma Purāṇa*. "One who does not observe the vow in the month of Kārttika, the swing-ride in Vaiśākha, the worship of the thread in Śrāvaṇa, and the offering of *damanaka* in Caitra, goes to hell. If there is an obstacle to the *pavitrāropaṇa* in Śrāvaṇa, Nārada says it must be performed until the full moon of Kārttika, even if Venus has set. Such is the necessity of the *pavitra* rite. Now, the origin of the *pavitra* is set forth from the *Prayogasāra*: "There was a king of the Nāgas named Kanīyas, whose name was Pavitra."

Having undertaken a vow of fasting, he performed Vedic penance for a hundred autumns, taking refuge in Maheśvara, the God of gods. By virtue of his propitiatory austerity, Śambhu—the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), the Remover of the Distress of those who bow to him, the Lord of Umā—manifested before him. Seeing that the God, together with the Lord of Serpents, was inclined toward him with favor, he requested this unsurpassed boon: "May I attain the status of being an ornament for [Śiva’s] neck. "So be it," replied the Destroyer of Tripura; and wearing it accordingly, he granted another boon to that pure one, the master of self-yoga: "Those who hold you in high regard, as you have been honored by me, shall perform your *japa*, fire-offerings (*homa*), and other rites."

"O you who possess the fruit of all [merits], this is my firm conviction: in this very month of Śrāvaṇa, or indeed under the asterism sacred to Viṣṇu (Śravaṇā), therefore let those who are devoted to daily and occasional rites worship you.

O sinless one, the Vaidikas perform the worship with a fire-oblation according to their capacity; likewise, the Tāntrikas, following your likeness and imitation, worship the deity by offering the *pavitra* while wearing the sacred thread (*nivīta*). Thus ends the origin of the *pavitra*. Now its performance is described according to the methods taught in various Āgamas: it should be made from threads of gold, silver, copper, linen, silk, lotus-fiber, or *kuśa* grass."

The sacred thread (*pavitra*) should be made from auspicious cotton spun by a Brāhmaṇa woman or a maiden, and not by those such as eunuchs. Having bathed, one should take a triple-stranded thread and, having tripled it again, purify it with the *Hṛdaya-mantra*.

Then, having washed it with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and the eight substances (*aṣṭau*), one should consecrate the sacred threads with conch-water using the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*), the *Gāyatrī*, and the mantra known as *Ārama*. They know the sequence of the five products of the cow to be milk, curd, clarified butter, feces, and urine. [The mantras for these are: "May you swell" (*āpyāyasva*) for milk; "O curd, you have come" (*dadhi krāvṇaḥ*) for curd; "You are splendor" (*tejo 'si*) for clarified butter; "You are semen" (*śukram asi*) for feces; and likewise, at the end of the *Gāyatrī*, the mantra "O Goddess, you whose door is fragrance" (*gaṃdhadvārām*) for urine. The *pavitra* should be fashioned.

The sequence for the *pañcagavya* is "trāḥ syuḥ," for the *pañcāmṛta* it is the *gāyatrī* verse beginning with "madhu vātā," and likewise for the purification of the thread (*sūtra-śuddhi*). Among these, the best purifier (*pavitra*) consists of three hundred and sixty threads;

the middling is recorded as having two hundred and seven; one should perform the lowest with one hundred and eighty. Alternatively, one may follow the sequence of nine threads, consisting of one hundred and eight, its half (fifty-four), or its half again (twenty-seven). The best of the three types extends from the knees to the thighs and up to the navel; one should fashion the *vanamālā* with one thousand and eight threads, or even by doubling the measure of the best purifier.

Beginning from the mirror up to the thread, the auspicious garlands fashioned thereon—hanging down as far as the feet—are proclaimed as the *vanamālā*. The *yajamāna-pavitra* (the purifier for the patron) should be made equal in length to the little finger;

the *adhivāsana-pavitra* (the purifier for the preliminary consecration) should be equal to the middle finger. One should fashion the auspicious *agni-pavitra* (the purifier for the fire) equal to the middle finger. One should prepare the common purifiers (*sādhāraṇa-pavitra*) with three threads. The best purifier should have one hundred knots, the middling fifty knots, and the lowest purifier should be beautiful with thirty-six knots. [Alternatively, it may be] thirty-six, twenty-four, or twelve [knots]. And with a single [thread]...

Some sages know [the knots] to be twenty-four or twelve years old; however, one should make the knot at the top of the thumb-joint. One should make the knots—well-rounded and very beautiful—half the size of that for the middle finger, and half the size of that for the little finger. In some cases, one should make nine knots of an odd number. By giving the thread to a person of the world (a non-initiate), there would be an inauspicious result for the maker; therefore, with supreme devotion, one should make the purifier beautiful, [anointing it] with saffron, yellow pigment, and camphor.

Then one should perform the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) over them with the mantra "Tad Viṣṇoḥ," or else the twelve-syllable mantra is traditionally prescribed as universal for all cases. In the best rite (*uttama*), the consecration should be performed three times; likewise in the middling (*madhyama*) it should be twice; and in the lowest (*kaniṣṭha*), it is traditionally prescribed as once. This concludes the characteristics of the *pavitra* (sacred grass rings). Then, having placed those *pavitra*s upon a beautiful bamboo mat and covering them with a clean cloth, one should set them down in front [of the deity]. One should fashion a bamboo rod measuring one *aratni* in length with thirty-six knots, and one should purify it with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) and with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).

Having placed that [garment] within the waistband, one should perform the mental bath (*mānasa-snāna*). Then, having provided protection on all sides, one should perform the fire-oblation (*agnihoma*). One should personally perform the great worship of the Blessed One and likewise carry out the great ablution (*mahā-snāna*) and the ritual services (*upacāra*). One should place before the Lord tooth-sticks, water, *kuśa* grass, clay, turmeric, costus (*kuṣṭha*), and yellow pigment (*gorocanā*). Likewise, one should place wooden sandals, leather shoes, an umbrella, a fly-whisk, and a fan. Furthermore, one should place grains such as rice and other cereals in front. Then, with prostrations like a staff and various hymns of praise...

One should properly ward off [the obstacles] with Vedic recitations (*japa*) and oblations (*homa*). "O Lord, that which was ordained by You for the sake of the knowledge of the ritual procedure—that I now perform as a purifying rite for these four deities.
May there be no obstacle here; O Lord of the Kurus, have compassion on me. O Viṣṇu, You are my supreme refuge in every way and at all times. O Lord of the World, I satisfy You through fasting.

May desire, anger, and the like not become slayers of the Veda for me. O Lord of Gods, from this day until the specific [concluding] day, protection must be provided by You for all of this; salutations to You. Thus...

Having informed the Lord of Devas and having prostrated at the feet of the Guru, Hari (the officiant) should perform the Pavitrāropaṇa rite together with the Vaiṣṇavas. Having filled an auspicious pitcher with holy water, he should place it in front of Viṣṇu upon a beautiful *sarvatobhadra* diagram, and there he should worship the threads (*sūtra*). With this mantra: "O Pavitra, come here from the world of Viṣṇu for the sake of purifying the year-long sacrifice; salutations to you," he should invoke the thread with the root mantra. The learned one should likewise meditate upon the triad of deities in the three [sections] beginning with the *uttama*, as well as the three qualities (*guṇas*), the three Vedas, and the triad of worlds.

Likewise, in the garland preceded by the forest of *prakṛti*, one should meditate upon the entire celestial realm (*dyuloka*) as the crown and the string adorned with its rays. *Oṃ! O you whose limbs are variegated with all ornaments, who are saluted by all deities, O Soul of the Universe, whose form is beauty—take refuge in this supreme string. Oṃ! O maker of all prosperity, Lord of Śrī, whose nature is identical to all knowledge, O support of all, whose form is the Earth, O creator of all, Prajāpati, O All-pervading Self, O Lord—in this thread, grant your presence; salutations to you. O you whose form blazes with all jewels, through the Brahma-light of the Cosmic Egg, [you are] the crest-jewel...*

Obeisance to the auspicious thread (*śrīsūtra*), which bestows all beauty upon the head and every limb, and which brings about the presence of all that is auspicious for this world. Having taken up the threads, beginning with the uppermost one, in sequence with the hand, one should consecrate them with these mantras and worship them with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*). Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Mahādeva are remembered as the deities of the three threads.

Oṃkāra, Āpa, Agni, Brahmā, Nāga, Śaśin, Sūrya, Śiva, and the Viśvedevas are the presiding deities (*adhidevatās*) of the nine threads. [The presiding deities of the rites are] Kriyā, Pauruṣī, Vīrā, Vijayā...

Having meditated upon and invoked Yeśā, Aparājitā, Manonmanī, Jayā, Bhadrā, Muktikā, and the deities of the *cit-granthi*, and having consecrated them with nectar (*amṛtīkṛtya*), one should worship the gods with perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), sprouts, incense, lamps, food offerings (*naivedya*), and betel leaves, as well as the sacred thread (*pavitra*). Then, the wise practitioner should tie upon the hand of the deity a sacred thread (*upavitraka*) made from *paṭṭa* cloth, which is auspicious in nature, beautiful, and pleasing to the eye. "Oṃ! To you who grant the full fruit of the vows performed throughout the year—for the sake of the offering of the sacred thread (*pavitrāropaṇa*)—I bow to this [thread] fashioned by Kandhara. Having held the sacred thread enclosed within the root mantra, he should then perform the lustration (*nīrājana*) for the deity.

Preceded by auspicious sounds, one should offer various kinds of food offerings (naivedya), betel leaf, and unguents. Then, one should worship the Lord with hymns such as "Victory! (Jitam). Next, one should invoke the Lord of Gods, the God of gods, with this mantra: "O Lord of Gods, O Ancient Puruṣottama, I have been invited; O Keśava, be present here. O You whose form rests upon the great serpent bed of the Milk Ocean, I shall worship you in the morning; be present before me. I offer this sacred thread (pavitraka) to you in the morning; in every way, [accept it] entirely."

"O Viṣṇu, obeisance to you; be gracious to me. Having thus prostrated like a staff upon the ground, he should again offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*). Then, having worshipped the threads and the water-pot (*kumbha*) situated before him, he should protect [the area] on all sides with the *astra-mantra* and veil it with the *kavaca-mantra*.

Alternatively, he should protect it with the *rakṣā-krama-mantra* or the mantra of Nṛhari. Having paid homage to the Brahmins and bowed at the feet of his guru, he should then perform a vigil (*ajāgaraṇa*) accompanied by the sounds of auspicious songs. Thus is declared the procedure for the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*); the rite has been told, O Nārada. This concludes the consecration of the sacred thread (*pavitrāvasana*). Then, having risen in the morning, he should meditate...

Having thus performed the daily worship as described, and likewise the offering of the sacred threads (*pavitra*), one should perform the lustration (*nīrājana*) with auspicious lamps preceded by the sound of auspicious instruments. Having praised the God worshipped by the gods with various hymns and bowed down to Him, one should then offer a thread to the God accompanied by auspicious sounds and the resonance of conchs, trumpets, and other instruments, together with sandalwood paste, flowers, and unbroken rice grains. *Oṃ Rāma, Rāma, salutations to You!

Accept this sacred thread for the sake of purification, which bestows the fruit of a year’s worship. Make this sacred thread [effective] today for whatever evil deed has been committed by me; O God, may I become pure.*

O Lord of the Gods, by His grace, this mantra—enclosed by the *mūla-mantra*—is indeed for the Pavitrāropaṇa rite. Then, one should offer water for the feet (*pādya*) and a livelihood (*vṛtti*) to the deities with their respective names. Thereafter, one should devotedly present the great preliminary food offering (*naivedya*). Then, one should perform the lustration (*nīrājana*) of the auspicious God, the beloved of Rāma. Having fanned Him with sacred chowries, one should then show Him a mirror. One should likewise offer various flowers and a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*). One should then pray to the Lord of the God of Gods with these mantras according to the prescribed rule: "With this [offering] consisting of garlands of gems and coral, and Mandāra flowers and the like, O Sāṃva..."

O Lord whose banner is Garuḍa, just as the *tsarī*, *pūjā*, *tāva*, *vāstu*, *vanamālā*, and the *kusumbha* flower are always held in Your heart, so too, O Lord, carry within Your heart these five-colored threads and this worship—whether performed knowingly or unknowingly by anyone.

May that worship of Yours be complete for me, even if it is marred by some obstacle or defect. O Janārdana, whatever has been worshipped by me lacking mantras, lacking ritual action, or lacking devotion, may that be made complete for me, O God. Thousands of offenses are committed by me day and night; considering me Your servant, forgive me, O Madhusūdana. [Salutations to] the one of fixed station.

On level ground, the wise man should bow with a mind full of devotion to Rāma, the Lord of the gods and the bestower of desired objects. Then, preceded by offerings of fragrance and other items, he should give the sacred thread (*pavitra*) to his preceptor.

He should then worship him with devotion using gold, garments, and ointments. He should likewise honor the Brāhmaṇas and Vaiṣṇavas with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and satisfy them with devotion through gifts of clothing, food, and gold coins. He should wear that arrangement of threads for a month, a fortnight, a day and night, or three nights, according to the requirements of place and time. Every day, after performing his bath and other duties, he should [wear] the threads.

One should cause [the deity] to be bathed with the water of the *arghya* offering and then re-enter the deity. Then, at the conclusion, having worshipped the deity specifically with flowers and sandalwood paste and having offered various kinds of food offerings (*naivedya*), one should then dismiss the sacred thread (*sūtra*) with the mantra: "O Pavitra, having duly completed this auspicious annual worship by me, you who possess purity, now go to the world of Viṣṇu, having been dismissed.

As long as the sacred threads remain upon the deity, one should remain composed, observing celibacy, eating sacrificial food (*haviṣya*), and devoted to the worship of the deity. One should perform the installation of the sacred thread (*pavitrāropaṇa*) at the proper time.

One should recite the mantra ten thousand times or perform a hymn of praise (*stotra*). Thus ends the *Pavitrāropaṇa* (the rite of offering the sacred thread), and thus ends the duty of the month of Śrāvaṇa. Now, on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, the *Karṇikotsava* (the festival of the ear-ornament) should be performed by Vaiṣṇavas along with the *Śayanī-utsava* (the festival of the Lord’s reclining), as stated in the *Bhavishyottara Purāṇa*: "When the month of Bhādrapada has arrived, on the eleventh day, the gift of a mat (*kaṭadāna*) to Viṣṇu shall take place; it destroys great sins. Having brought the Lord to the bedchamber according to the procedure for the *Śayanī-utsava*, one should perform the festival of the gift of the mat.

One should worship the God of gods, the Lord of the universe, who is accessible to yogis and free from all taint, with a resolve for the welfare of all. On this auspicious occasion of Bhādrapada, when [the month] has arrived, one should perform the gift of a mat (*kaṭadāna*). One should arrange a seat with many lotus centers on the right side. Then, having performed the great worship (*mahāpūjā*) as before, one should return to one's own home. Thus ends the festival of the gift of the mat. This concludes the religious duties of Bhādrapada. On the tenth day of the dark fortnight of Āśvina, the Vijaya festival must be observed by virtuous people everywhere who desire victory, while listening to the words of Hanumān.

The sons of Añjanā, filled with joy, informed him that the chariot had arrived. Having placed the Lord of Gods upon the chariot—adorned with all ornaments, holding a sword, bow, and arrows in his hands, the unborn and omnipresent one who had manifested by his own play to protect the world, accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa, Sugrīva, and others, along with elephants, horses, and foot-soldiers—he should lead him, attended by elephant-processions, toward the *śamī* tree. Forming the resolve, "I shall perform the worship of Viṣṇu at the *śamī*," he should worship Him. This is according to the *Viṣṇudharma*.

Having worshipped Śamī-yukta-sitārāma, who bestows fearlessness upon his devotees, for the sake of a journey free from obstacles along the aforementioned path, the man should thereafter worship the Śamī tree with these words: "O Śamī, you who pacify (śamayati) calamity, O Śamī, you who wear red garments, you who are the beloved speaker of Rāma, and you who are dear to the Earth, Arjuna, and Bāṇa—be the one who ensures my journey will proceed happily at the proper time and without hindrance, O you who are honored by the devotees of Śrī Rāma. Then, taking moist earth from the root of the Śamī tree along with unbroken grains (akṣata), he should sing:

Then, with the sounds of musical instruments, one should lead the Lord to the temple. Some should be bears there, and some should be monkeys; some should have red faces for the pleasure of the Lord of Kośala.

Having conquered the Rākṣasas and the Daityas, the enemies on the surface of the earth, and proclaiming "Rāma’s kingdom! Rāma’s kingdom! Rāma’s kingdom!", one should bring the Lord and establish him in health upon the divine throne. Then, having performed the *nīrājana* ceremony for the Lord of Gods, one should prostrate like a staff upon the ground. Afterwards, one should wear garments and other items that have been enjoyed [by the deity] together with one's kinsmen. Thus [says] Viṣṇu.

O best of the twice-born, having commenced the duties prescribed for the month of Āśvina from the eleventh day of the bright fortnight, one should perform the vigil (*jāgara*) and awaken the Lord according to the words of the Skanda Purāṇa: "He who performs the vigil before Dāmodara at the break of dawn in the month of Kārttika, O Govinda, shall obtain the fruit of a thousand cows. O Nārada, he who sings your praises facing the west during the final watch of the night dwells in Vaikuṇṭha together with his ancestors. That foolish man who does not perform the dawn-vigil in Kārttika goes to a terrible hell.

According to the injunctions of the *Padma Purāṇa*, one should perform the *nīrājana* rite and satisfy Hara with offerings according to the rules; likewise, having heard [the account] from the *Padma Purāṇa*, one should observe the vow for some time.

He who passes the month most dear to Dāmodara without bathing attains the womb of an animal, and so forth, as stated in the *Padma Purāṇa*. Then, in the bright fortnight of Kārttika, having performed the practice of heating the body (*taptāṅga-dhāraṇa*), one should place Mādhava upon the chariot according to the procedure prescribed for the *Śayanī* festival. With washed hands and feet, one should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) together with the Vaiṣṇavas on this day endowed with such qualities.

I shall perform the awakening of the Lord of Lakṣmī, or else one should recite the verses previously mentioned: "O God, who is praised by Brahmā, Indra, Rudra, Agni, Kubera, Sūrya, Soma, and others; awaken, O Lord, the abode of the universe, by the power of this mantra! O God, this Dvādaśī has been prepared for your awakening.

By you alone, who recline upon Śeṣa for the welfare of all the worlds, when the Lord of the Universe is asleep, this entire world remains asleep; when you have risen, everything moves. Arise, arise, O Mādhava! O Viṣṇu..."

With this [mantra], one should awaken the Lord from His bed of water: "Arise, arise, O Govinda, abandoning Your yogic sleep! Having awakened Him with this mantra amidst the sounds of bells and musical instruments, one should seat the Lord upon the bank and worship Him with great devotion. The Blessed One, whose compassion is like that of the moon, who has increased His lotus-eyes with a smile of love, having arisen for the sake of conquering the universe—may that Ancient Puruṣa, free from despondency, remove my inner fire of suffering. *Prājāpatya*, *Gāyatrī*, and *Vaiṣṇava* mantras grant all desires. [Page 66b] May the Lord, whose compassion is as vast as the moon, rise with a smile of love, expanding His lotus-eyes; may He, the Ancient Puruṣa, arise for the conquest of the universe and dispel my inner fire of distress.

Having offered three handfuls of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), one should recite the *Atharvaṇa* [mantras] with devotion. One should bathe Rāghava with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) while reciting the *Puruṣasūkta*, perform the *nīrājana* ceremony, and assign the mantras to the various parts. Then, one should gratify the Lord with garments, ornaments, sandalwood paste, garlands, incense, lamps, divine offerings, and betel leaves. Having performed this great worship (*mahāpūjā*) and taking water with unbroken grains of rice (*akṣata*), and having observed the vows month by month, one should offer them to Rāghava: "O Lord, may Rāghava be pleased with me for these various Cāturmāsya vows undertaken by me; may He be satisfied at the conclusion of this abundant observance. Thus, having completed the vows...

Having offered praise with the highest devotion through Vedic hymns, [the sage] praised the Lord of Ramā—who is known by the Vedas—as "Victory! Victory! and so forth. May the Wicked One (Khalu), who is the protector of the universe, be gracious; may all beings meditate upon auspiciousness with one another's minds; and may they attain the welfare of Adhokṣaja, offering spontaneous salutations. Having thus prayed for auspiciousness amidst the sounds of songs and musical instruments, and having performed worship, those who are freed from all sins go to the abode of Hari, which is filled with armies and mounts, and adorned with emeralds and tinkling bells.

May the victorious chariot of you who are worthy of worship by Brahmā and Śiva protect you—a chariot adorned with nets of jewels and pearls, with necklaces strung with unceasing gems, with golden jars possessing the luster of emeralds, with excellent banners, and with umbrellas that dispel the sins of the world. "Flee, flee, O enemies, O Rākṣasas, Diti-born ones, and Dānavas! For the protection of the worlds, the two lions among men have mounted the chariot! With these and other mantras spoken in the *Viṣṇudharma*, one should gratify [the deity] with reverence; then, filled with devotion, one should receive the grace-garland from Nṛhari. Victory to you, O Lord!

"O Mahādeva! O Jayarāma! O Lord of All! O Giver of Boons! O Protector of the Entire World! O Lord of the Universe! Victory to You, O Lord of Sītā! O God! Victory to You, O Destroyer of the Daityas! O God of Gods! O Support of All! Protect us who have come to You for refuge! With dances, musical instruments, and the sounds of ringing bells and cries of "Victory!", one should cause the chariot of Viṣṇu to be paraded all around the middle of the city.

First, the leaders of the Daityas, the gods, hosts of Siddhas, sages, Gandharvas, and humans should pull the chariot. As long as a man pulls even a single step of Kṛṣṇa’s chariot, [he attains great merit].

The Leader of Men (Narāyaṇa) makes those who go before, behind, or in front of His great chariot equal to those who perform hundreds of sacrifices. O Goddess born from my foot, those who beautify the chariot of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and cry out "Victory! attain eternal worlds. Madhusūdana, worshipped by men standing upon the chariot, grants them their desires and, at the end, the supreme goal. By seeing Govinda, Madhusūdana, seated in the chariot and swinging on the swing even once with devotion, men [attain liberation].

There is no rebirth for those who go to Janārdana by means of this chariot while it is wandering; even those Brahmins who know the Vedas should be known as the lowest of outcasts (śvapacas) if the Lord Śrī-Nṛkesarin, seated upon His chariot, passes by their house. They must perform worship, free from stinginess regarding wealth. O King, if He comes outside one's house due to negligence and is not honored, His ancestors remain turned away from him for a full year. Even women attain liberation if they are devoted to the chariot procession; through the waving of lights (nīrājana) and song, they are born within the divine circle.

"He who proclaims the greatness of the chariot festival (Rathotsava) in the Kali age, even if he be a dog, has given away the entire earth, including its mountains, forests, and regions"—according to this statement from the *Padma Purāṇa*, one should circumambulate the chariot, go home, perform the *nīrājana* ceremony for the Lord of Gods, and sleep while remembering Rāghava. Thus concludes the Great Festival of the Chariot. Regarding the *Traipura* festival on the full moon day: "Having seen [the deity], even a dog born of a low-caste woman becomes a Brahmin"—thus is the *Traipura* festival described in the *Skanda Purāṇa*. This concludes the duties of the month of Kārttika. In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, having observed a fast (*ekabhukta*), one should worship... [text ends]... Abhya.

Having worshipped Hari and fed the twice-born, one shall be liberated; thus says Kalipriya. He who passes the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, dear to Hari, by means of the *naktabrata* vow, goes to the eternal world of Viṣṇu; thus ends the duties for Mārgaśīrṣa in the Viṣṇudharma. Beginning from the bright eleventh day (*ekādaśī*) of Pauṣa, sleeping on the bare ground for the sake of pleasing Raghu, one should perform ablutions twice a day for the duration of a month. Abandoning enjoyments and with senses subdued, one should worship Rāma three times a day until the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, which bestows vast fruit. For a month...

Having performed the *Damanotsava* for twelve days, or even half of that, one should go to the abode of Hari and perform worship. Viṣṇu is to be worshipped with food offered to Him, as are other deities;

and that same offering should be given to the ancestors (*pitṛs*), for it is ordained to yield infinite merit. However, he who gives what remains from the ancestors' portion to the Supreme Soul (Viṣṇu), his ancestors become "seed-givers" (*retodās*) and partakers of suffering.

One should offer curd-rice accompanied by songs, instrumental music, and dances. Having worshipped Hari with devotion, one should then take [the remnants] by His grace. He who accepts the grace of Hari with devotion...

"He who eats, gives, and enjoys together with the Vaiṣṇavas attains the fruit of the vow. Thus ends the festival of curd-rice in the month of Māgha according to the Viṣṇudharma. On the full moon day of Phālguna (Tapasya), one should indeed perform the Holi festival; one should celebrate the Spring Festival for Him whose form is supreme bliss. When the clear morning has dawned at the rising of the sun on the first lunar day (pratipad), having performed the necessary duties and having satiated the ancestors and deities, one should worship the splendor of Holi for the pacification of all evils: "You have been worshipped by Indra and by Brahmā..."

And Śaṅkara said: "Therefore, O bestower of prosperity upon all beings, protect me from all dangers. At dawn, during the spring season, having worshipped the lover of Ramā (Kṛṣṇa) with sandalwood, flowers, and tender sprouts, and having offered the desired mango blossoms to the Lord amidst various songs, music, and dances for His pleasure—one should prepare a square courtyard in a clean and well-smeared house.

Having decorated it with auspicious colored powders and unbroken grains of rice, one should place a pedestal in its center, covered with a white cloth. In front of it, one should place a full water-pot adorned with fresh sprouts."

O Bhārata, while he is seated upon his throne, the consecration (abhiṣeka) should be performed with the chanting of the Veda, using *dūrvā* grass and mango sprouts. I shall describe the flower of the mango tree with its fresh spring shoots, which bestows happiness and increases longevity and health. Those people who, at the beginning of spring, drink mango flowers along with sandalwood paste, perform the worship of Kāma residing within the heart at the conclusion of the rite.

Thereafter, one whose soul is full of desire should give gifts according to one's capacity to the foremost of the twice-born, to the Sūtas, Māgadhas, and bards, saying, "May [Kāma] be pleased. Then, at the time of the meal, the sacred text was heard...

On the sixth day, one should first cause [the children] to eat food, and thereafter they may eat as they desire. At night, having seated the children upon white-clothed seats placed within a four-cornered enclosure, one should sprinkle them with water from a new jar mixed with mango sprouts.

O Pārtha, for him who performs the Phālguna festival in this manner as prescribed by the scriptures, all his heart's desires shall be fulfilled through my grace. When the winter season has passed and the springtime has arrived, on the morning of the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight, by eating mango blossoms together with sandalwood paste, a man, O Pārtha, will truly become happy for a hundred years.

Thus ends the description of the Spring Festival (Vasantotsava) as spoken by the Blessed Lord in the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*. This concludes the duties for the month of Phālguna. Now, regarding the duties during an intercalary month (*adhikamāsa*): remembering Hari, the husband of Sītā, one should give gold along with clarified butter and thirty-three cakes to a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*) who is learned in the Vedas and maintains a family. If this is not performed, the merit accumulated over twelve months quickly perishes. Thus ends the duties for the intercalary month in the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*. In all twelve months, during both fortnights, the festival of lightning (*vidyutsava*) should be observed, and on the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*), a vigil (*jāgara*) should be kept.

On the tenth day, having risen in the morning and performed the rites of friendliness (*maitrī*) and so forth, one should perform the worship of the deity and, with devotion, make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "O God of gods, Lord of the lords of gods, O Keśava, beginning from this tenth day, I shall observe your vow for three days; grant that it be free from obstacles. Having uttered this, one should offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) at the feet of Śrī Rāma. Having made the resolve with water from a conch shell, one should prostrate like a staff before the All-pervading Lord. This is the resolve for the tenth day. On the eleventh day, however, having cleansed the teeth with tooth-sticks (*parṇāya*), bathed, and performed the worship of the deity, one should perform the formal resolve for the vow. On the eleventh...

"Having remained without food on the eleventh day, I shall eat on the following day; O Acyuta, be my refuge, O Lotus-eyed One. Thus, according to the words of Devala, one should offer [the vow] with hands joined in a vessel.

Taking a Udumbara vessel filled with water and facing north, one should take the fast and then drink the water purified by mantras. This is the *saṃkalpa* for Ekādaśī. Having performed all necessary duties, one should offer the vow for Dvādaśī: "O Keśava, through this vow, be gracious to me who am blinded by the darkness of ignorance; O Lord, be well-disposed and grant me the vision of knowledge. This is the Dvādaśī [vow].

One should perform the vow for two or three days according to the manner described in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*. Because it is well-known, its performance has not been elaborated upon by us here. The primary Kṛṣṇajanmāṣṭamī and other rites are proclaimed in the scriptures; they should be understood from those specific Vaiṣṇava texts by Vaiṣṇava men. Due to their renown and for fear of excessive prolixity, they are not mentioned here. For one who summarizes what is already famous, there is an expansion of that which is famous. These rites beginning with Caitra have been stated by us for the satisfaction of the Lord, so that my mind, immersed in the bliss of Brahman, may become steady and fixed upon Your lotus feet.

O Lord of Janaki, let there be no distress for me from this; for this is not the moonlight of the moon, but rather the light revealed by Your grace. Since You have been pleased by my good deed, O Ramachandra, there is indeed none other than You. One should worship Rama with a steady mind, thinking "I am Rama," for whatever is undertaken by Rama is all for Rama, and he offers it back to Rama.

Who knows that this life is non-different from Rama? All this dissolves into Rama; therefore, cultivate equality with Rama. What is this wretchedness? It is merely the state of being the ten-necked one (Ravana).

O Maithili, this *Śrī Rāmārcanacandrikā*—which establishes the true gentleness of a yogi, the generosity of Vibhīṣaṇa, and manifold affection—is now determined by those such as yourself who rely upon the *Ārṣa-saṃhitā*. It is an elixir for the pacification of the forest-fire of worldly existence, proclaimed in five chapters (*paṭala*). May this *Śrī Rāmārcanacandrikā*, composed by the poet named Ānandavana for the pleasure of Hari, be [of benefit]. Thus ends the work of Ānandavana, disciple of the feet of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrī Mukundavana.
The fifth chapter of the *Śrīrāmārcanacandrikā* composed by [the author] is complete; and this *Rāmārcanacandrikā* is now finished. Saṃvat 1929.
